  * **On the Admin API**, `ProductVariant.soldLast30Days`, at all the shop's locations, and
    `daysOfStockLeft`: whole days what can be sold online lasts at that pace, none when out,
    null when nothing sold or its stock is not tracked. They read through the request's batch
    loader the low list uses, so a page of variants asks once; `read_inventory` as stock does.
  * **In the admin**, the product page says beside each variant "6 sold in 30 days · lasts
    about 20 days", and under a product sold as it is; a variant that sold none says nothing.
* **Consequences:**
  * A size that sells fast and one that does not are told apart where prices and stock are
    changed.
  * Not yet: the pace on the products list, sorting by it, or over other spans.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **The analytics' top products:** sales in money over a period, by product; not stock's
    pace by size, nor how long it lasts.

## ADR-371 · What was bought from each supplier: its purchase orders, what came of them and what it cost, and what is still to come, on the suppliers' list

* **Context:**
  * The suppliers' list (ADR-351) kept names, numbers and notes, and linked each supplier's
    purchase orders, but said nothing of how much the shop buys from it or still waits for,
    which is what is weighed before ordering again (INV-05).
* **Decision:**
  * **On the Admin API**, `supplier(id)`, and `Supplier.purchasing`: its purchase orders and
    how many are open, the units received on them and what they cost, the units open orders
    still await and what those cost, and when the latest was made. Worked out from the orders'
    lines when asked, a page of suppliers asking once; lines with no cost count in units and
    not in money; closed orders await nothing more.
  * **In the admin**, each supplier on the suppliers' list says "2 purchase orders · 17
    received for Rs 35,702.50 · 3 still to come, Rs 6,301.50 · last ordered" a day; in units
    alone where no cost was given, and nothing for a supplier never ordered from.
* **Consequences:**
  * Who the shop buys most from, and what it is owed in goods, is read where suppliers are kept.
  * Not yet: what was paid to a supplier, or how long its goods take to come.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A page of its own for each supplier:** the list already links its orders; a line on the
    list says the totals without another page to open.

## ADR-372 · How fast each product sells, on the products list: its variants' units sold in the last 30 days together, read through the same batch loader

* **Context:**
  * A product's page says how fast each of its sizes sells (ADR-370), but the products list,
    where staff look over the catalogue, said only what is in stock (CAT-04, INV-08).
* **Decision:**
  * **On the Admin API**, `Product.soldLast30Days`: its variants' units sold in the last 30
    days together, through the batch loader the variants use, so a page of 50 products asks
    the ledger once; `read_inventory` as stock does.
  * **In the admin**, each product on the list says "6 sold in 30 days" after its stock; a
    product that sold none says nothing more.
* **Consequences:**
  * Products that sell and those that sit are told apart on the list, out of stock or not.
  * Not yet: the list sorted by it. The catalog's search orders products by its own index and
    knows nothing of sales; a sort by them waits for a search that can join the two, or for the
    analytics' top products, which already rank what sells by money.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Sorting a page by sales in the admin:** it would sort only the 50 products on the page,
    not the shop's best sellers.

## ADR-373 · An order packed by scanning: each item read ticks off its line, one not in the order or one too many said at once, and the order packed once all of it is there

* **Context:**
  * A packer marked an order packed by eye. A wrong size or a missing piece was found by the
    customer, and in cash on delivery that is a refused parcel coming back at the shop's cost
    (APP-04, ORD-05).
* **Decision:**
  * **In the admin**, an order to pack offers "Pack by scanning" beside "Mark packed". Each
    barcode or SKU read, by a scanner at the keyboard, typed, or through the phone's camera, is
    found among the shop's variants as goods arriving are (ADR-363) and ticks off one of its
    line. An item the order has none of is said at once ("PC-10 is not in this order"), and so
    is one too many of a line already full. "Pack the order" is on only once every line is
    there, and packs it as "Mark packed" does.
  * **Nothing new in the core.** What is counted stays on the phone until the order is packed;
    the scan reads the variant's barcode or SKU as it is now, so an order line kept without one
    is found by its variant's.
* **Consequences:**
  * The wrong item is caught at the table rather than at the door. "Mark packed" stays for a
    shop without codes on its goods.
  * Not yet: the To pack list worked through order after order, or a record of who scanned.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Requiring a scan to pack:** shops whose goods carry no barcode or SKU could not pack at
    all.

## ADR-374 · The orders to pack scanned one after another: the To pack list opens the first to scan, and each packed brings up the next, until none is left

* **Context:**
  * An order is packed by scanning on its page (ADR-373), but a packer with forty orders went
    back to the list after each, found the next and opened its scanner again (APP-04, ORD-05).
* **Decision:**
  * **In the admin**, the To pack tab offers "Pack by scanning" to those who work orders,
    opening its first order with the scanner already open (`?scan=true` on the order's
    address).
  * Once an order is packed by scanning, its page offers "Scan the next to pack" with the next
    order's name: the first still to pack at the location the orders list shows, opened to scan
    in turn. With none left it says "Nothing more to pack" and links back to the list.
  * Nothing new in the core: the next is the orders list's own query, at its location.
* **Consequences:**
  * A packer works through the day's orders at one table, phone in hand, without the list in
    between.
  * Not yet: the packing slip printed as each is packed, or more than one packer kept from the
    same order.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Packing many orders in one screen:** a parcel is packed one at a time; one order on the
    screen is the one on the table.

## ADR-375 · What goes with a parcel, printed as it is packed by scanning: the packing slip or invoice offered once the order is packed, before the next

* **Context:**
  * Packing by scanning went from one order to the next (ADR-374), but the packing slip that
    goes in the parcel (ADR-028, ADR-331) was printed from the list, many at once,
    or from the order's page before packing; a packer working order by order had none to hand
    (ORD-06, APP-04).
* **Decision:**
  * **In the admin**, once an order is packed by scanning its page says "#1003 is packed." and
    offers "Print what goes with it": the order's print panel, packing slip or invoice, paper
    and language as last chosen, beside "Scan the next to pack". Printing is offered, not
    forced; nothing new in the core.
* **Consequences:**
  * The parcel leaves the table with its slip, and the packer goes on to the next.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Printing at once when packed:** a phone at the table often has no printer; the choice is
    the packer's.

## ADR-376 · How many orders each packer packed: the orders' own timelines, packing undone left out, for owners and managers and each packer their own

* **Context:**
  * Packing is the work of the shop's packers (APP-04), and orders are now packed one after
    another by scanning (ADR-373, ADR-374). Owners asked how many each packer packed today and
    this week, as the Confirmation Desk's agents are counted (COD-11, ADR-090, ADR-335).
  * Each order's timeline already says who marked it as packed and when, and who unpacked it.
* **Decision:**
  * **In the core**, `packers(from, before, first)` works it out when asked from the orders'
    timelines, as agents' performance does: for each member of staff or app, the orders they
    marked as packed in the period that nobody has unpacked since (packed still, or shipped),
    the units in them as their items stand, and the hours of the shop's day in which they
    packed any, with orders an hour. An order unpacked and packed again is the second packer's;
    packing undone counts for no one, though its hour still shows they were at it. Orders
    shipped without being marked as packed have no packer and are not counted. A partial index
    finds the packing entries by when (migration 0172). At most a year at a time.
  * **Who sees it:** owners and managers see every packer, and apps with `read_orders`; a packer
    sees their own count alone; other staff are refused.
  * **In the admin**, "Who packed what" on the To pack tab (for a packer, "What I packed") opens
    the count for today, the last 7 or the last 30 days in the shop's time zone: each packer by
    name, former staff and apps as the agents' page shows them, with orders packed, items and
    orders an hour, and the total for owners and managers.
* **Consequences:**
  * Owners see who packed what each day without a sheet of their own, and packers their own
    day's count, from what packing already records; nothing new is stored.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Counting every time an order was marked as packed:** a mistake undone would count, and an
    order packed twice would count twice.
  * **A counter kept as orders are packed:** a second record of what the timeline says, which
    unpacking would have to keep right.

## ADR-377 · A pickup's parcels checked off by scanning as its rider takes them: each by its label's tracking number, when and by whom kept, those still on the table listed

* **Context:**
  * A pickup asked of a courier (ADR-253, ADR-314) names the parcels the rider should take, but
    nothing said which the rider did take: a parcel left on the table, or taken without being on
    the sheet, was found only when the courier's tracking said so, days later (SHP-02, APP-04).
* **Decision:**
  * **In the core**, each of a pickup's parcels keeps when it was handed over and by whom
    (migration 0173). `courierPickupParcelHandOver(pickupId, trackingNumber)` checks off the
    pickup's parcel with that tracking number, spaces and case as a scanner or a thumb gives
    them; a parcel checked off already stays as it was and says so; a tracking number not among
    the pickup's parcels, and a pickup its courier has not taken, are refused with why. A
    pickup says how many of its parcels are handed over, and `parcels` lists them with when.
    Orders' work, as asking for the pickup is (`write_orders`).
  * **In the admin**, a pickup the courier took offers "Check off by scanning": the label read
    with the camera or its tracking number typed, each said as handed over with its order, or
    as checked off already, or not in the pickup; how many of how many are handed over, and the
    ones still to hand over, until all are. The pickup's row says how many are handed over.
* **Consequences:**
  * The packer knows before the rider leaves which parcels went, and which are still on the
    table, without reading the sheet line by line.
  * Nothing is told to the courier: its own scans say what it took, and a parcel the rider
    missed goes in the next pickup a day on, as before.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Unchecking a parcel:** a parcel is checked off only when its label is in hand; a mistake
    is rare and changes nothing the courier does. Left for when a shop asks.
  * **A courier without pickups through its API:** its load sheet is printed for the rider
    (ADR-150), with no pickup to check against; it waits for its own section.

## ADR-378 · Parcels handed to a courier's rider by hand: the parcels waiting recorded as a pickup the courier was not asked for, its load sheet printed and its parcels checked off

* **Context:**
  * Checking parcels off as the rider takes them (ADR-377) needed a pickup asked of the courier
    through its API (ADR-253). But PostEx's and Leopards' riders also come on their daily
    rounds without being asked for, and couriers to come, TCS and Trax among them, take no
    pickups through an API at all; the shop then printed the account's load sheet (ADR-150)
    with nothing to check it against (SHP-02, APP-04).
* **Decision:**
  * **In the core**, `courierPickupRecordByHand(input)` records the account's parcels waiting,
    the same a pickup would take, the longest waiting first and up to 200, as a pickup kept here
    alone: taken at once, by hand (migration 0174), the rider's name and code kept where given,
    the courier not asked. Its parcels then count as in a pickup, so none goes in another for a
    day, and are checked off as ADR-377 has it. Any courier account may record one; refused,
    saying why, when no account is connected or none of its parcels waits. The pickup event says
    whether it was by hand.
  * **In the admin**, "Hand parcels to a rider" beside asking for a pickup: the courier account,
    the rider's name and code if wanted, and "Hand over the parcels waiting", which opens their
    check-off at once. The pickup's row says "Handed to a rider by hand", with its load sheet to
    print.
* **Consequences:**
  * A rider who simply turns up is handled like one asked for: the sheet to sign, the parcels
    checked off, those left on the table in sight.
  * The courier learns of the hand-over from its rider's own scans, as before; nothing is sent to
    it.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Only for couriers without pickups through their API:** none of the couriers connected
    today is one, and their riders come unasked as often as asked.
  * **Checking off the account's load sheet without a pickup:** what the sheet listed would be
    lost once the parcels moved on; a pickup keeps it.

## ADR-379 · Parcels a rider took that the courier's tracking has not seen a day on: listed from the hand-overs against the parcels' status, with the rider and when

* **Context:**
  * Parcels are now checked off as the rider takes them (ADR-377, ADR-378), and the courier's
    tracking says of each parcel what the courier knows of it (ADR-149). A parcel the rider took
    but never scanned in, or lost on the way, stays "booked" in the courier's tracking; nothing
    put the two side by side, and the shop found out when the customer called (SHP-02, SHP-04).
* **Decision:**
  * **In the core**, `courierParcelsUnseen(first)` lists the parcels handed over at least 24
    hours ago, by the hand-over they were last in, that the courier's tracking still has as only
    booked: each with its booking, when it was handed over, the pickup, and that pickup's rider.
    The longest since handed over first. A parcel handed over again later counts from then. A
    partial index finds the bookings still waiting (migration 0175), which pickups' claim and
    load sheets read too.
  * **In the admin**, the Pickups tab opens with those parcels, when there are any: how many,
    and for each its order (linked), tracking number, courier, and when and to whom it was
    handed, with a word to ask the courier or the rider. In a pickup's check-off, a parcel not
    checked off that the courier's tracking already has says "The courier has it".
* **Consequences:**
  * A parcel gone missing between the shop and the courier shows a day after, with the rider
    who took it, instead of when the customer asks.
  * Nothing is sent to the courier; the shop asks it, as now.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Telling staff as it happens:** a day is how long couriers' first scans take at the
    slowest; a message before then would mostly be wrong. A message can follow once shops say
    the list is not enough.
  * **Checking the parcel off when the courier's tracking has it:** the check-off records what
    the shop saw leave; the courier's word is shown beside it, not written into it.

## ADR-380 · Parcels the courier has not seen on Home: their count among the next actions, a tap from the pickups that list them, for those who hand parcels over

* **Context:**
  * Parcels a rider took that the courier's tracking has not seen a day on (ADR-379) showed only
    on the Pickups tab, which staff open when a rider comes, not every day. Home is where they
    look first (ANL-01, ADR-121), as transfers to receive are (ADR-364).
* **Decision:**
  * **In the core**, Home's `parcelsUnseen` counts the same parcels `courierParcelsUnseen` lists,
    by the same rule, read with Home (`read_orders`).
  * **In the admin**, Home shows "N parcels handed over that the courier has not scanned in"
    below the next actions while there are any, for owners, managers and packers, who hand
    parcels over; a tap opens the Pickups tab, which lists them. Nothing while there are none,
    nor for other staff.
* **Consequences:**
  * A missing parcel is in front of the shop the morning after, without anyone opening the
    Pickups tab.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Among the next actions, with an amount:** the next actions are orders by stage, each with
    its money; a parcel unseen is a question for the courier, not a step in the order's way, and
    its cash is still the courier's to collect.

## ADR-381 · A parcel's hand-over on its order's page: when, to whom and whether by hand, and whether the courier's tracking has had it since, put together in the core

* **Context:**
  * A parcel's hand-over to its courier's rider (ADR-377, ADR-378), and whether the courier's
    tracking has had it since (ADR-379), showed only in the pickups. Staff answering a customer
    who asks where their order is open the order, not the pickups; the order's parcel showed its
    courier, tracking number and the courier's steps, but not that it had left the shop, when,
    or with whom.
  * The orders module keeps the parcel (a fulfillment); logistics keeps its booking and the
    pickups it went in. Neither reads the other's tables.
* **Decision:**
  * **In the core**, `Fulfillment.handOver` gives the parcel's last check-off in a pickup: when,
    the pickup, whether by hand, the rider's name and code where named, `seen` while the
    courier's tracking has had it as more than booked since, and `unseen` while it still has it
    as only booked a day on, by ADR-379's rule. Null for a parcel not booked through Hatti, or
    not checked off. It is resolved in the core, as an order's agreement is (ADR-057): logistics'
    `handOversOf` reads the hand-overs of a page's parcels at once through the request's loader,
    by their fulfillments, with an index on bookings' fulfillments (migration 0176) so that
    reading them never reads the shop's every booking. It is read with the order
    (`read_orders`).
  * **In the admin**, a parcel on the order's page says "Handed to Imran 6 hours ago", or
    "Handed over yesterday" where no rider was named, with "By hand, without asking the courier"
    where it was, and "The courier has it" once its tracking does. A day on without it, a warning
    says to ask the courier or the rider, with a tap to the pickups for owners, managers and
    packers, who hand parcels over; other staff see the warning alone. Nothing for a parcel never
    handed over.
* **Consequences:**
  * Staff answering a customer see on the order whether its parcel left the shop and whether the
    courier has it, without opening the pickups.
  * Only the last hand-over shows: a parcel handed over again, after a pickup it was missed in,
    shows that one.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **The hand-over as a step of the parcel's way:** its steps are what its courier and staff
    said of its delivery, kept as they were said (ADR-160); a hand-over checked off again, or
    unseen a day on, would need steps written and taken back.
  * **A field on the order:** a split order ships as parcels with bookings of their own; the
    hand-over belongs to each parcel.

## ADR-382 · Courier rules: an order booked without an account named goes with the first of the shop's rules its city and cash to collect match, else the default, and staff see which before they book

* **Context:**
  * Shops in Pakistan keep accounts with more than one courier: one that delivers well in
    Karachi, another for the rest of Sindh, a third trusted with dear parcels. Booking took the
    shop's default account unless staff chose one for the whole batch, so a packer booking a
    morning's orders either booked them all with one courier or picked the orders out by hand,
    batch by batch. Smart courier allocation is MVP work by rules (SHP-06), scored on couriers'
    records in V1.
* **Decision:**
  * **Rules, in the logistics module** (migration 0177, `logistics.courier_rules`): each names
    cities as Pakistan's list names them ("Pindi" is Rawalpindi, as delivery zones read cities,
    ADR-043), a range of the cash its courier is to collect (at least, and below, in minor
    units), or both, and the account that books what it matches. A shop keeps up to 50, in its
    order, replaced all at once by `courierRulesUpdate` (`write_settings`, as accounts are), read
    by `courierRules` (`read_orders`, as accounts are). A rule must name a live account of the
    shop's, and cities or cash; an account archived since leaves its rule passed over, and said
    so. A change records `courier_rules.updated`, on the activity log.
  * **Booking**: `ordersBook` without an account books each order with the account of the first
    rule its city and cash to collect match, else the shop's default; an account named books them
    all with it, as before. An order neither a rule nor a default is for is refused, with why,
    while the rest are booked. Without rules nothing changes.
  * **Seen before booking**: `courierAccountsFor` gives the account each of up to 250 orders
    would be booked with now, and the rule that chose it, by the same rule `ordersBook` follows.
  * **In the admin**, the Couriers settings page edits the rules: cities comma apart, the cash to
    collect at least and below, the account, each moved up or down or taken away, saved together,
    with what is wrong said by rule. The Shipping page's To book tab offers "By the shop's courier
    rules", chosen unless staff choose an account, and says under each order which courier it goes
    with.
* **Consequences:**
  * A morning's orders are booked at one tap, each with the courier the shop chose for its city
    and its cash, and staff see which before they tap.
  * Rules read the order as it is when booked: an order whose address changes after the preview
    is booked by its new city.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Rules by weight, product or the courier's record:** weight and products are SHP-07's rate
    cards; couriers' delivery and return rates by city (SHP-08, COD-12) are V1's scoring. Cities and
    cash are what shops choose couriers by today.
  * **The default account per city, kept on the account:** a rule for cash, or cities and cash
    together, would have no home; an ordered list says which wins where two match.

## ADR-383 · Couriers' rate cards: each parcel keeps what its account's card says it is likely to cost when the courier books it, and profit counts that until a statement says what it charged

* **Context:**
  * Profit (ANL-03, ADR-141) took off what couriers' statements charged for parcels
    ([ADR-088](#adr-088--a-parcel-keeps-what-couriers-statements-charged-for-it-which-cod-health-adds-up-for-those-that-came-back-a-statement-with-the-lines-of-one-imported-before-is-refused)),
    and statements come a week or two after the parcels. Until then every parcel cost nothing,
    so the last fortnight always looked more profitable than it was, and a shop deciding
    whether an ad paid or which courier to use read the wrong numbers. Couriers in Pakistan
    publish rate cards: a first half kilo and each half kilo after, within the city and to other
    cities, a share of the cash they collect, and a share again to bring a parcel back. SHP-07
    asks for rate cards and each order's shipping cost, for profit.
* **Decision:**
  * **A card per courier account, in the logistics module** (migration 0178,
    `logistics.rate_cards`): the city parcels go from, as Pakistan's list names it; the first half
    kilo and each half kilo after, within that city and to others, in minor units; the share of
    the cash collected and of the charge for a return, in hundredths of a percent, up to 20% and
    200%. Set whole by `courierRateCardSet`, taken away by `courierRateCardRemove`
    (`write_settings`, as accounts are), read by `courierRateCards` (`read_orders`); each change
    records `courier_rate_card.updated`, on the activity log.
  * **What a parcel is likely to cost** is worked out from the card as the courier books it,
    while its weight is known: out, by its half kilos (a part counting whole, one of no known
    weight counting one) within the card's city or beyond; the card's share of the cash to
    collect; and its share of out to bring it back. The worker keeps it on the booking, and the
    booking, as it is marked booked, carries it to the parcel through the orders module's
    `estimateParcelChargesIn`, as statements' charges reach parcels through its functions. A
    card changed later changes no parcel booked before.
  * **Profit counts it as the parcel stands** until a statement charges the parcel, and then the
    statement alone: out and the cash share while on its way or delivered, out and back once
    coming back, out once lost. The sales report's `shippingCosts` says so, and
    `shippingCostsEstimated` says how much of it is estimated. A parcel's
    `courierChargesEstimate` gives its own.
  * **Before booking**, `courierAccountsFor` gives, with each order's account, what its parcel is
    likely to cost with it if delivered.
  * **In the admin**, each courier account has a Rate card page under Couriers in settings; the
    Shipping page says "Goes with PostEx · about Rs 330" under each order the rules book; an
    order's parcel says what the courier charged, or until it says, "Likely courier charges:
    about Rs 337.48, by the rate card"; and analytics says under profit how much of couriers'
    charges in it is estimated.
* **Consequences:**
  * Profit for the last fortnight counts couriers' charges from the day parcels are booked, and
    the shop sees how much of it is estimate; statements replace the estimates as they come.
  * A card's mistakes show in profit until statements come; the card is the shop's own.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Couriers' own rate APIs:** PostEx and Leopards quote by API for some accounts only, and
    neither for returns; a card the shop keeps works for every courier, and for one Hatti does
    not book with, later.
  * **Weight slabs of the shop's own:** couriers price by the half kilo; a table of slabs is a
    next step if a courier's card needs it.
  * **Working the estimate out when the report is read:** the card may have changed since, and
    the parcel's weight is only known as it is booked.

## ADR-384 · Couriers' performance: how each courier's parcels shipped in a period went, everywhere and city by city, worked out from the parcels when asked

* **Context:**
  * A shop in Pakistan sends parcels with two or three couriers, and which one does best differs
    by city: one delivers in Karachi in two days and brings half of Quetta's back. COD health
    ([ADR-060](#adr-060--cod-health-follows-a-periods-cash-on-delivery-orders-worked-out-from-them-when-asked-its-rates-of-those-that-turned-out)) gives each courier's delivery and return rates, but not where, how long
    parcels took or what they cost. SHP-08 asks for delivery %, days to deliver and RTO % by
    city, so the shop can choose couriers by city, which courier rules (ADR-382) then do.
* **Decision:**
  * **`courierPerformance`** (`read_orders`, as COD health): for parcels shipped in a period of
    at most 366 days, each courier's parcels shipped, delivered, returned (refused or
    undeliverable, on their way back or back), lost and still on their way; delivered of those
    that arrived anywhere and returned of those delivered or returned; the average days from
    shipped to delivered, to a tenth; and charges, by statements else rate cards
    ([ADR-383](#adr-383--couriers-rate-cards-each-parcel-keeps-what-its-accounts-card-says-it-is-likely-to-cost-when-the-courier-books-it-and-profit-counts-that-until-a-statement-says-what-it-charged)), with what is estimated and each parcel's share. Beneath each, its busiest
    cities with the same figures, ten unless asked, fifty at most.
  * **Couriers go by the name parcels were shipped with**, however typed, as COD health's do,
    so parcels shipped by hand count with those booked; parcels with none named are "No courier
    named". Cities go by the order's shipping address, typed two ways counted once under the
    spelling most used.
  * **Worked out from the parcels when asked**, in one query grouping by courier and by courier
    and city, nothing stored: a shop's year of parcels is tens of thousands of rows.
  * **In the admin**, analytics has a Couriers section after cash on delivery, for the period the
    page shows: each courier's parcels, delivered %, came back % (in red from 30%, as COD
    health), days to deliver and cost per parcel; a courier opened shows its cities beneath it;
    and how much of the costs rate cards estimate.
* **Consequences:**
  * The shop sees which courier does best in each city, and writes courier rules from it.
  * Days to deliver count from when the parcel was made, as the courier booked it or staff
    shipped it by hand; a parcel the courier picks up days after booking counts those days.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **By courier account rather than name:** parcels shipped by hand have no account, and a
    shop's two accounts with one courier are one courier to the customer.
  * **ClickHouse's facts** (ADR-014): with V1's analytics; Postgres answers a shop's year well
    enough until then.
  * **Ranking couriers in each city for the shop:** the figures are few in most cities; the
    shop reads them and decides, until there are enough to choose by rule.

## ADR-385 · A courier rule may book with the cheapest of the shop's accounts by their rate cards, order by order, and is passed over where none has a card

* **Context:**
  * Courier rules ([ADR-382](#adr-382--courier-rules-an-order-booked-without-an-account-named-goes-with-the-first-of-the-shops-rules-its-city-and-cash-to-collect-match-else-the-default-and-staff-see-which-before-they-book)) send an order to one account by its city and cash; rate cards
    ([ADR-383](#adr-383--couriers-rate-cards-each-parcel-keeps-what-its-accounts-card-says-it-is-likely-to-cost-when-the-courier-books-it-and-profit-counts-that-until-a-statement-says-what-it-charged)) say what each account charges. A shop with two or three couriers finds one
    cheapest within its own city and another to the rest of the country, and the cheapest
    changes with the parcel's weight and the cash to collect. Writing a rule per city to follow
    that is work the cards already did. SHP-06 asks for the cheapest courier as a rule.
* **Decision:**
  * **A rule naming no account books with the cheapest** (migration 0179: `account_id` may be
    null): of the shop's live accounts with rate cards whose courier still books here, the one
    whose card prices the order's way out (by its city and weight) and the cash to collect the
    least; equal, the default account first, then the oldest. A return's charge is left out,
    since most parcels are delivered.
  * **Passed over without a card:** a rule for the cheapest matches as any rule does, by cities
    and cash; where no live account has a card it is passed over for the next rule, then the
    default account. The shop cannot save one until an account has a card.
  * **It may be for every order**, naming neither cities nor cash; a rule for one account still
    names one or the other, else it would stand in for the default account.
  * **Chosen as the order is booked and before**: `courierAccountsFor` gives the account the
    rule chose and what it is likely to cost, so the Shipping page says "Goes with Test courier ·
    about Rs 120" as it does for any rule. `CourierRule.accountId` and `CourierRuleInput.accountId`
    are null for the cheapest.
  * **In the admin**, a rule's "Book with" offers "The cheapest, by rate cards" after the
    accounts, saying what it does.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop with cards on its accounts needs one rule to send each order with the cheapest, and
    rules before it for the cities it wants a courier for whatever the price.
  * The cheapest by card is not the best: a courier that brings back half its parcels costs more
    than its card says. Couriers' performance by city (ADR-384) shows that; weighing it in is a
    next step.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A rule kind of its own (cheapest, fastest, best delivering):** one kind is all there is;
    a null account says it until a second comes.
  * **Counting what a return would cost, by each courier's return rate in the city:** the
    rates are few in most cities and move week to week; until they are steady, the card's price
    is what the shop can check.

## ADR-386 · Each morning the shop's alerts number hears how the day before went, from nine by its clock, once a day, and not of a day with nothing in it

* **Context:**
  * An owner in Pakistan runs the shop from a phone and reads WhatsApp first thing; opening the
    admin to see how yesterday went is a step most skip. ANL-07 asks for a daily summary on
    WhatsApp: yesterday's sales, deliveries, returns and the cash still owed. The shop already
    gives a number for Hatti's alerts ([ADR-157](#adr-157--the-shop-hears-on-whatsapp-when-a-variant-runs-low-on-stock-and-again-when-it-runs-out-at-the-number-it-gives-for-hattis-alerts-once-for-each-spell-of-low-stock-which-inventory-keeps-until-the-variant-is-stocked-above-the-threshold-again-the-worker-hears-each-levels-change-and-queues-the-alert-as-a-message-the-shops-credit-pays-for)), and the home already works out a day's figures
    ([ADR-121](#adr-121--the-home-says-how-the-shops-day-has-gone-from-midnight-in-its-time-zone-todays-sales-as-the-sales-report-works-them-out-and-the-parcels-delivered-and-turned-back-today-at-their-worth)).
* **Decision:**
  * **A message kind of its own, `daily_summary`**, Hatti's utility template
    `hatti_daily_summary` in English and Urdu: the day, its orders and their sales, parcels
    delivered and turned back, and the cash on delivery still to come. It goes to the shop's
    alerts number on WhatsApp, at the shop's cost as its alerts do, and the shop turns it off
    as it does any alert; on unless it does.
  * **Worked out as the home works out today**, for the day before by the shop's clock: the
    orders placed that day, cancelled ones aside, with the sales report's total sales, less what
    came back; parcels delivered and turned back that day at their worth; and the cash on
    delivery still to come as the home has it: on cash-on-delivery orders on their way, or
    delivered and not yet paid for. `yesterdayIn` in the orders module.
  * **A sweep of the worker**, every few minutes as the others: shops with an alerts number and
    the summary on are found with the system role, and each is told in its own transaction from
    nine in the morning by its clock, with the day in its message's key so it is told once a day.
    A day with no orders and no parcels delivered or turned back is not told: it would cost the
    shop for nothing.
  * **In the admin**, Messages in settings lists "Yesterday's summary" among what the shop
    hears, saying what it carries, to turn off.
* **Consequences:**
  * The owner hears each morning what the home would say of yesterday, without opening it.
  * A shop pays for one WhatsApp utility message on each day it had any orders or parcels.
  * A worker down all morning tells the shop late that day; down past midnight, that day's
    summary is not sent.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Off unless turned on:** few shops would find it; the alerts number is given on purpose,
    and the summary is turned off as easily as any alert.
  * **An hour of the shop's choosing:** nine suits most shops; a setting of its own can come
    when shops ask.
  * **To the owner's own number rather than the alerts number:** the alerts number is where the
    shop asked Hatti's word to go, and may be a manager's.

## ADR-387 · A courier rule may book with the best value: the account cheapest for each parcel delivered, weighing its rate card with how often its courier delivers to the order's city

* **Context:**
  * A rule for the cheapest account ([ADR-385](#adr-385--a-courier-rule-may-book-with-the-cheapest-of-the-shops-accounts-by-their-rate-cards-order-by-order-and-is-passed-over-where-none-has-a-card)) goes by the cards alone, and the cheapest courier
    to send with is often the one that brings the most back: a parcel refused costs its way out,
    its way back, and the sale. Couriers' performance ([ADR-384](#adr-384--couriers-performance-how-each-couriers-parcels-shipped-in-a-period-went-everywhere-and-city-by-city-worked-out-from-the-parcels-when-asked)) shows how often each courier
    delivers in each city; SHP-06 asks for allocation that weighs it.
* **Decision:**
  * **A rule naming no account picks one of two ways** (migration 0180, `pick`): the cheapest, as
    before and still the default, or the **best value**: the account whose card costs the least
    for each parcel delivered, its way out, the cash fee where delivered and the charge back
    where not, over how often its courier delivers: `(out + d × fee + (1 − d) × back) / d`.
  * **How often a courier delivers** comes from the shop's own parcels shipped in the last 90
    days, delivered of those delivered, returned or lost, under the name the courier ships them
    with: in the order's city once ten have arrived anywhere, else everywhere once ten have, else
    the shop's with every courier once ten have, else taken as always. `deliveryRatesIn` in the
    orders module gives them, grouped by courier and city, by courier, and the shop's whole, and
    is asked only where a rule picks the best value.
  * **A courier that never delivers is never picked** while another can be. Equal, the default
    account first, as for the cheapest.
  * **Through the API**, `CourierRule.pick` and `CourierRuleInput.pick` (`CHEAPEST`,
    `BEST_VALUE`); **in the admin**, a rule's "Book with" offers "The best value, by rate cards
    and deliveries", saying how it weighs them.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop sending most of its orders with one rule gets, city by city, the courier whose
    deliveries make it cheapest, and the choice follows the couriers as they do better or worse.
  * Two accounts with one courier share its record; a new courier with too few parcels is taken
    at the shop's rate until it has ten, so it is neither shunned nor favoured.
  * The sale lost when a parcel comes back is not counted; the courier's charges alone are.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Counting the margin lost on a return:** it differs by product and the rule does not know
    the order's margin when it is written; the charges are what the cards say.
  * **A delivery rate the shop sets per courier:** it would go stale; the shop's parcels already
    say it.
  * **Couriers' rates across shops:** a cross-shop record is the network data of V1 (06 §11),
    with its privacy questions; a shop's own parcels first.

## ADR-388 · A customer whose delivery failed is asked on WhatsApp whether to deliver it again or call them first, and the shop sees the parcels to rescue with each answer

* **Context:**
  * A parcel whose rider could not deliver it (not home, phone off, address not found) usually
    goes back to the shop after one or two more tries, both ways charged and the sale lost.
    Couriers' tracking tells Hatti of each try as a step, `attempted_delivery` ([ADR-160](#adr-160--each-parcels-way-is-kept-step-by-step-as-shopifys-fulfillmentevent-its-couriers-changes-recorded-once-from-the-workers-tracking-and-staffs-for-couriers-hatti-does-not-follow-the-orders-page-shows-them-the-latest-first-in-english-and-urdu-the-shipped-message-links-that-page-and-a-parcel-out-for-delivery-with-cash-to-collect-tells-its-customer-what-to-keep-ready)); the
    customer is often willing, and a word from them in time saves the parcel. COD-08 asks for a
    WhatsApp message to the shopper, and an instruction to the courier.
* **Decision:**
  * **Each failed try asks the customer** (`order_delivery_failed`, a kind the shop may turn off):
    the courier tried to deliver their order and could not; tell the shop whether to deliver it
    again or call them first. Two quick replies, `retry` and `call`, come back as the answers to
    confirmations do ([ADR-147](#adr-147--a-cash-on-delivery-order-waiting-for-its-customer-asks-them-on-whatsapp-to-confirm-it-with-confirm-cancel-and-change-address-buttons-and-its-link-their-answer-comes-through-the-webhook-as-an-event-and-the-worker-confirms-or-cancels-the-order-as-their-link-would)). Once per step, while the parcel is on its way; not for an erased
    customer's order, and never by email, as its answers come back on WhatsApp alone.
  * **The answer is kept on the parcel** (migration 0181, `rescue_answer` and
    `rescue_answered_at`, both or neither) and on the order's timeline as asked by the customer.
    It counts for the try it answers: a later try shows no answer until the customer gives one
    again. An answer once the parcel moved on, delivered or coming back, changes nothing.
  * **The shop sees the deliveries to rescue**: parcels on their way whose last step is a failed
    try, with the customer's name and city, how many tries, the courier's words for the last, and
    the answer, those answered first. `deliveriesToRescue` in the API (up to 100, with the whole
    count), a "Failed deliveries" tab among Returns in the admin, and a count on Home that leads
    there, for those who handle parcels coming back.
  * **Telling the courier stays the shop's** for now: the answer is for staff to pass on, by the
    courier's portal or call. Asking couriers through their APIs comes once one offers it.
* **Consequences:**
  * A failed delivery costs the shop one utility message, against a return's two charges.
  * The list follows couriers' tracking: a parcel out for delivery again leaves it, and comes
    back with its next failed try.
  * Couriers Hatti does not follow reach it only when staff record a failed try themselves.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A message with the order's page to choose a new time:** couriers in Pakistan take no
    appointments; two answers are what staff can act on.
  * **Answers changing the parcel's status:** the courier decides the next try; Hatti records
    what the customer asked, not what the courier will do.
  * **Asking only for cash-on-delivery orders:** a prepaid parcel refused is lost just the same.

## ADR-389 · A location lets customers pick orders up, with what to tell them; an order picked up waits ready for pickup once packed, its customer told where, is never booked with a courier, and completes when handed over at the counter

* **Context:**
  * Shops with a counter, a boutique or a warehouse in town, let nearby customers collect
    their orders: no courier's charge, no failed delivery, cash taken by hand. SHP-15 asks for
    store pickup with a message when the order is ready. Orders so far all went by courier or
    by hand to the customer's door, from the location they ship from ([ADR-355](#adr-355--an-order-ships-from-the-first-location-fulfilling-online-orders-that-has-all-of-it-the-primary-first-or-the-primary-and-from-another-chosen-on-its-page-until-it-is-packed-its-stock-committed-there-and-let-go-where-it-was-in-one-change)).
* **Decision:**
  * **A location offers pickup** when the shop lets it (migration 0182, `pickup_enabled` and
    up to 200 characters of `pickup_instructions`, such as the counter's hours), as Shopify's
    `locationLocalPickupEnable` and `locationLocalPickupDisable` do. Only an active location
    with its street address and city may, so customers can find it ([ADR-312](#adr-312--the-admin-lists-the-shops-locations-in-settings-those-out-of-use-too-and-adds-one-with-its-address-and-the-number-couriers-call-for-pickups-changes-it-and-whether-it-fulfils-online-orders-takes-it-out-of-use-and-puts-it-back-and-deletes-one-that-never-held-stock-the-primary-one-stays)); its address is
    not cleared while it does.
  * **An order is shipped or picked up** (`deliveryMethod`, `SHIPPING` by default). One
    picked up is collected at its location, which must offer pickup: the one named, or the
    only one that does. It has no delivery charge. It moves to another location only where
    pickup is offered, and merges only with another picked up.
  * **Packed, it waits at a stage of its own, `READY_FOR_PICKUP`**, in place of to book, on
    Home and in its own tab. The customer is told on WhatsApp, and by email when they gave one,
    that it is ready and where: the location's name, address and instructions
    (`order_ready_for_pickup`, which the shop may turn off); their order's page says so too.
  * **It is never booked or shipped**: a courier booking or a shipment by hand is refused with
    why. **"Picked up"** (`orderMarkPickedUp`) hands it over in one step: its stock leaves the
    location, a parcel with no courier is recorded as delivered, and what it still owed is
    taken at the counter, so the order completes. Returns, refunds and the timeline work as for
    any delivered parcel.
  * In the admin, a location's settings let customers pick up there; an order picked up says
    where, "Mark ready for pickup" packs it, and "Picked up" hands it over.
* **Consequences:**
  * Pickup orders come through the API for now; checkout and draft orders offering pickup come
    next, with the customer choosing where.
  * A parcel picked up has no courier and no tracking: no courier owes its cash, which is
    taken as it is handed over.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Pickup as a zero-charge delivery rate:** the order would still wait to be booked and
    could be given to a courier by mistake; a method of its own keeps couriers out.
  * **Cash at the counter recorded by hand:** handing over and taking the money happen
    together; one step keeps the order from completing unpaid.
  * **Pickup points apart from locations:** a shop's counter is where its stock is; a location
    keeps stock, address and orders in one place.

## ADR-390 · A draft order is shipped or picked up: one picked up names a location offering pickup, or the only one, has no delivery charge, and becomes an order picked up there; its link says the customer pays when they collect it

* **Context:**
  * Most orders a shop's staff take come from chats, as draft orders that the customer confirms
    through a link or staff place ([ADR-114](#adr-114--a-draft-its-customer-confirms-through-its-link-keeps-what-they-agreed-to-as-checkouts-orders-do-the-page-names-the-shops-policies-above-its-button-and-the-order-keeps-their-versions-and-where-it-was-confirmed-from)). Local pickup came to orders made through the API
    ([ADR-389](#adr-389--a-location-lets-customers-pick-orders-up-with-what-to-tell-them-an-order-picked-up-waits-ready-for-pickup-once-packed-its-customer-told-where-is-never-booked-with-a-courier-and-completes-when-handed-over-at-the-counter)), so a customer who said in the chat "I'll collect it" still had to be sent a
    courier's order, or one made by hand outside the admin.
* **Decision:**
  * **A draft is shipped or picked up** (migration 0183, `delivery_method` on drafts;
    `deliveryMethod` on `DraftOrderInput` and `DraftOrder`), as orders are. One picked up names
    a location offering pickup, or is collected at the only one that does; it has no delivery
    charge. Both are checked as the draft is saved, so staff learn then, not when placing it.
  * **Placing it, by staff or by the customer through its link,** makes an order picked up
    there, which goes on as any pickup order: ready for pickup once packed, the customer told
    where, and picked up at the counter.
  * **Its link** leaves out the delivery charge and says the customer pays when they collect
    it; it names them as the one collecting rather than an address to deliver to. An order's
    page picked up says the same.
  * **In the admin**, the draft form offers "Delivery" where a location offers pickup: delivered
    to the customer, or picked up at each such location, the delivery charge gone once picked
    up. The draft's page says where it is picked up and what is collected at the counter. An
    order picked up moves only to another location offering pickup.
* **Consequences:**
  * A draft picked up still keeps the customer's name, number and address, as a draft sent does:
    the number is how they are told it is ready.
  * Checkout offering pickup to shoppers comes next.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A zero delivery charge and a note:** the order would wait to be booked with a courier;
    the method of its own keeps couriers out, as for orders.
  * **Choosing the location only when placing:** a draft is agreed in the chat; where to collect
    is part of what the customer agreed to, so it is on the draft.

## ADR-391 · Checkout offers pickup at each location that lets customers pick up: chosen, the order has no delivery charge, the shopper's address is optional with the location's standing in, and the thank-you page says where to collect it

* **Context:**
  * Shops offer pickup at their counters ([ADR-389](#adr-389--a-location-lets-customers-pick-orders-up-with-what-to-tell-them-an-order-picked-up-waits-ready-for-pickup-once-packed-its-customer-told-where-is-never-booked-with-a-courier-and-completes-when-handed-over-at-the-counter)), but shoppers ordering on the storefront
    could only have their order delivered. Checkout is one page the core renders, working
    without JavaScript ([ADR-044](#adr-044--checkout-is-one-page-the-core-renders-and-storefronts-serve-on-the-shops-address-placing-a-cash-on-delivery-order-as-the-page-showed-it)), its totals worked out as it is posted.
* **Decision:**
  * **The page offers delivery or pickup** where any active location lets customers pick up
    and has its street and city: "Deliver to my address", or "Pick up from" each such location,
    its address and what the shop says of it, with no delivery charge. Delivered is the default;
    without such a location the page is as before.
  * **Picked up, the shopper's address is optional**: the location's street and city stand in
    for any they leave out, so the shop's rules by city (cash on delivery, advances) go by where
    they collect it. Their name and number are still asked, as the order is theirs and its
    ready message goes to the number.
  * **Placed, it is an order picked up there**, with no delivery charge, through the orders
    module's own placing, which checks the location again. A location that stopped offering
    pickup after the page showed it shows the page again.
  * **The thank-you page says where to collect it**, with what the shop says of collecting
    there, and that the customer is told on WhatsApp when it is ready; as it is seen again too.
* **Consequences:**
  * What the cart may hold is still what the locations fulfilling online orders have; an order
    picked up commits stock at its location as any order does.
  * The page's words for paying, such as an advance before the shop "sends your order", stay
    those of delivered orders for now.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A script switching the address away:** the page works without JavaScript; the address
    stays and is optional once picked up.
  * **Pickup as a delivery zone with no charge:** couriers would be booked for it; the
    location's own method keeps them out, as for orders and drafts.

## ADR-392 · An order may repeat another: placed for a customer with an open order not shipped yet, from the three days before, with an item in common, it names that order, and staff merge it in, cancel it as a repeat, or keep both

* **Context:**
  * Shoppers in Pakistan often place the same order twice: the page seemed stuck, they were
    not sure it went through, or they ordered again on WhatsApp after the storefront. Shops
    then pack and ship both, and the second comes back refused, with its return charges.
  * Merging an order into another of its customer's exists ([ADR-132](#adr-132--an-order-its-customer-placed-twice-is-merged-into-the-other-while-both-wait-to-be-packed-the-other-takes-its-items-and-discount-and-keeps-its-own-delivery-charge-as-one-parcel-the-order-merged-is-cancelled-as-merged-naming-it-and-counts-for-nothing-in-its-customers-history)), but staff have to notice
    the repeat first.
* **Decision:**
  * **An order is flagged as it is placed**, through every channel, when the same customer
    has an open order, not shipped yet, placed within the last three days (`REPEAT_DAYS`),
    with any variant in common. The most recent such order is named; the order keeps it
    (`repeat_of_id`).
  * **Its timeline says so**: "May repeat #1002, which the same number placed 20 minutes before
    with items in common and is not shipped yet: merge it in, cancel it as a repeat, or keep
    both".
  * **The API shows `Order.repeatOf`** while both are open and the earlier one is not shipped;
    once either ends, nothing is shown. Staff then:
    * merge it into the earlier order with `orderMerge`, as before;
    * cancel it as `DUPLICATE`, a new cancel reason; or
    * keep both with `orderRepeatKeep`, which clears the flag and says so on its timeline.
  * **The admin's order page shows a banner** linking the earlier order. Those who work orders
    get the three choices, with the merge offered only where merging is allowed (nothing paid).
    Merged, the earlier order's page opens. `DUPLICATE` is also among the cancel reasons staff
    pick from.
* **Consequences:**
  * The order is not held: a repeat is often a customer adding to what they wanted, so staff
    decide. Risk scoring already counts other recent orders from the number (COD-06).
  * The check is one indexed query per order with a known customer.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Refusing the second order at checkout:** a customer ordering twice on purpose would be
    turned away.
  * **Matching the whole basket:** a customer adding an item would not be caught; any item in
    common is enough for a hint staff can dismiss.

## ADR-393 · Abandoned checkouts: the number a shopper types is kept as they type it, the shop sees who left, and may remind them once on WhatsApp, after the delay it sets, with a link back to their items; an order the number places then recovers it

* **Context:**
  * Most shoppers who start a checkout leave without ordering. Shopify keeps their email and
    reminds them; in Pakistan the number is what shoppers give, and WhatsApp is where they
    answer. The checkout kept nothing the shopper typed until the order had it ([ADR-044](#adr-044--checkout-is-one-page-the-core-renders-and-storefronts-serve-on-the-shops-address-placing-a-cash-on-delivery-order-as-the-page-showed-it)).
  * Hatti's WhatsApp templates are shared by every shop, and a URL button can vary only the last
    part of its address ([ADR-147](#adr-147--a-cash-on-delivery-order-waiting-for-its-customer-asks-them-on-whatsapp-to-confirm-it-with-confirm-cancel-and-change-address-buttons-and-its-link-their-answer-comes-through-the-webhook-as-an-event-and-the-worker-confirms-or-cancels-the-order-as-their-link-would)).
* **Decision:**
  * **The checkout keeps the name and number** the shopper types, with the cart's items and
    their subtotal then: as the page is posted without placing the order, and as a small script
    on the page sends them once the number is whole, to `/checkouts/<secret>/contact` on the
    page's own site. The page's policy lets its scripts connect to that site alone
    (`connect-src 'self'`); the page works without the script, as with the pin's
    ([ADR-259](#adr-259--a-delivery-address-may-carry-a-pin-where-the-customers-phone-is-at-the-address-checkouts-and-customers-links-address-forms-add-it-by-the-pages-first-script-allowed-by-its-hash-it-is-kept-in-pakistan-and-near-the-city-typed-as-shopifys-latitude-and-longitude)). The storefront relays it to the core, from the shop's own pages only.
  * **The shop sees who left**: `abandonedCheckouts` lists them, the latest first, with the
    number masked for roles that see numbers masked; a checkout with a number is kept 30 days
    past its page's day.
  * **The shop may remind them once**, 30, 60, 180 or 600 minutes after they left
    (`checkoutRecoverySettingsUpdate`); never until it chooses. The worker's sweep queues one
    `checkout_reminder` message, which Meta counts as marketing, charged to the shop as its
    messages are, for shoppers who left within the last day and have ordered nothing since.
    Its button opens `/r/<secret>` on the core's address, which sends them on to their shop's
    storefront at a cart permalink of their items.
  * **An order recovers it**: one the same number places through checkout within 7 days, or by
    any way before the reminder is due, which then is not sent.
  * **Erasing a customer** takes what they typed from the checkouts they left; their file lists
    them.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shopper who types their number and leaves gets at most one message from the shop, and only
    where it chose to send them; the shop can't turn the kind off in its notifications, as
    checkout's setting is its switch.
  * The reminder's link names the items, not the discount code or the address typed: the cart
    permalink starts a new checkout.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A two-step checkout, the number first:** the page stays one form, as shoppers on slow
    phones finish it faster; the script keeps the number as it is typed.
  * **Keeping the checkout's own secret for the link:** only its SHA-256 is kept, so a reminder
    has a secret of its own.
  * **Reminding on by default:** each reminder costs the shop a marketing message, so it chooses.

## ADR-394 · The admin lists the checkouts shoppers left under Orders, for those who work orders and marketers, with a chat on WhatsApp for a whole number not yet ordered, and the reminder's delay is set with the checkout page's settings

* **Context:**
  * The core keeps the checkouts shoppers leave with their number and reminds them once if the
    shop chooses a delay ([ADR-393](#adr-393--abandoned-checkouts-the-number-a-shopper-types-is-kept-as-they-type-it-the-shop-sees-who-left-and-may-remind-them-once-on-whatsapp-after-the-delay-it-sets-with-a-link-back-to-their-items-an-order-the-number-places-then-recovers-it)); the admin showed neither.
* **Decision:**
  * **Orders links to "Abandoned checkouts"** for owners, managers, confirmation agents and
    marketers: the latest first, fifty a page, each with the name or "No name given", the
    number as the role sees it, the items and their subtotal, when they left, and whether they
    were reminded, not reminded, or ordered since, the order a link.
  * **A whole number not yet ordered offers "Message on WhatsApp"**, a `wa.me` link, so a
    shop that keeps reminders off can still write to them itself; a masked number offers none.
  * **The page says whether reminders are on** and after how long; owners and managers, who open
    Settings, get a link to change it.
  * **Settings → Checkout chooses the delay**, "Don't remind them" or one of the four, beside
    the page's other settings, and says each reminder is a marketing message charged as others.
  * **How customers are told** lists the reminder among the messages the shop can't turn off
    there, as checkout's setting is its switch.
* **Consequences:**
  * A packer or rider sees no abandoned checkouts; an agent sees them as they see numbers.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A tab of the orders list:** abandoned checkouts are not orders and have none of their
    actions, so they have a page of their own, linked from it.

## ADR-395 · A custom app is an access token the shop's owner or a manager makes, with a name and scopes none beyond their own role's, and a secret its webhooks will be signed with, kept sealed for the app alone; both are shown once and can be replaced, and removing the app revokes its token at once

* **Context:**
  * The Admin API has taken access tokens with scopes since its first slice, but only the seed
    made them. Shops here connect sheets, accounting and warehouse tools through developers they
    hire, as Shopify's custom apps let merchants do (DEV-04).
  * Webhooks (DEV-03) need a secret to sign with that the app's developer knows and Hatti can
    read: a token is kept only as its SHA-256.
* **Decision:**
  * **A custom app is an access token**, as `apps.access_tokens` already keeps them, with a name
    and its scopes; a new module, `@hatti/apps`, makes and lists them.
  * **Owners and managers alone make and change them** (`customAppCreate`, `customAppUpdate`),
    signed in as themselves: apps manage no apps, themselves included. The scopes given are ones
    the maker's own role has, each once, in the API's order. A shop keeps up to 20.
  * **The token and a webhook secret are shown once**, in the payload that makes them. The
    secret is sealed with the platform's SecretBox for that shop and app, as Meta's token is
    ([ADR-143](#adr-143--orders-placed-through-checkout-go-to-metas-conversions-api-from-the-worker-as-they-are-placed-confirmed-and-delivered-the-shop-choosing-which-is-purchase-each-moment-waits-in-postgres-until-meta-takes-it-or-its-seven-days-are-up)), and opened only for signing.
  * **Either can be replaced** (`customAppTokenRotate`, `customAppSecretRotate`): the old token
    stops working at once. **Removing** an app (`customAppDelete`) revokes its token.
  * Making, changing and replacing need the member to have proved who they are lately
    ([ADR-103](#adr-103--sensitive-actions-need-staff-to-have-proved-who-they-are-in-the-last-15-minutes-by-signing-in-or-confirming-with-the-strongest-factor-their-account-has-apps-are-not-asked)); removing does not, as it only takes access away.
  * Each change is an event on the activity log ([ADR-256](#adr-256--what-the-shops-staff-and-apps-change-goes-on-its-activity-log-each-event-a-request-of-the-admin-api-records-written-in-the-same-statement-as-the-outboxs-by-whom-and-to-what-never-what-it-recorded-in-a-table-of-its-own-kept-as-long-as-the-audit-log)) and in the audit log, with the
    token's and secret's last four characters, never either.
* **Consequences:**
  * A token made before apps had a secret is listed with none until one is made for it.
  * An app's scopes change from its next request; what it did before stays on the activity log
    by its token.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A table of apps apart from their tokens:** a custom app has one token, as Shopify's do;
    OAuth apps installed from a store, with tokens of their own per shop, come later.
  * **Showing the secret again on request:** Shopify does; once is enough here, as a new one can
    be made, and a leaked admin session reveals nothing.

## ADR-396 · Settings lists the shop's custom apps for owners and managers, each with what it may reach in words and the last characters of its token and secret; an app is made by choosing each resource's access, and its token and secret are shown once, to copy

* **Context:**
  * The core makes custom apps ([ADR-395](#adr-395--a-custom-app-is-an-access-token-the-shops-owner-or-a-manager-makes-with-a-name-and-scopes-none-beyond-their-own-roles-and-a-secret-its-webhooks-will-be-signed-with-kept-sealed-for-the-app-alone-both-are-shown-once-and-can-be-replaced-and-removing-the-app-revokes-its-token-at-once)); a shop's owner needs to make one for the developer
    connecting their sheet or accounting system, from their phone.
* **Decision:**
  * **Settings → Apps**, for owners and managers, lists the shop's apps: each with what it may
    reach in words ("Orders: Read and write"), or "Everything the API offers", when it was
    made, and the last four characters of its token and its signing secret, or that it has none
    yet.
  * **Making or changing an app chooses each resource's access**, "No access", "Read" or "Read
    and write", rather than the API's scopes by name; the core refuses any the member's role
    lacks.
  * **What is made is shown once**, with a button to copy each, until "I've copied it". A new
    token or secret is shown the same way. Removing asks once more, saying the token stops
    working at once.
  * Making, changing and replacing ask the member to confirm who they are when they have not
    lately.
* **Consequences:**
  * The activity log names apps' changes, a new token or secret among them.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A checkbox for each scope:** forty boxes on a phone, with read and write apart where
    write already reads.

## ADR-397 · A custom app subscribes to topics of the shop's events at https addresses; the worker makes one delivery an event and subscription for apps that may read what it names, posts it signed with the app's secret to a public address alone, and tries again with backoff for two days

* **Context:**
  * Apps the shop makes ([ADR-395](#adr-395--a-custom-app-is-an-access-token-the-shops-owner-or-a-manager-makes-with-a-name-and-scopes-none-beyond-their-own-roles-and-a-secret-its-webhooks-will-be-signed-with-kept-sealed-for-the-app-alone-both-are-shown-once-and-can-be-replaced-and-removing-the-app-revokes-its-token-at-once)) need to hear of orders, products, stock and customers as
    they change, rather than asking the API again and again (DEV-03; 08 §2).
  * The shop's events already go through the outbox to the worker, at least once each.
* **Decision:**
  * **Topics are Shopify's names**: `orders/create`, `orders/updated` (every change to an
    order), `orders/cancelled`, `orders/paid`, `fulfillments/create` and `/update`,
    `products/create`, `/update` and `/delete`, `inventory_levels/update`, `customers/create`
    and `/update`, and `app/uninstalled`. Each but the last needs the app to read what it names.
  * **An app subscribes itself** (`webhookSubscriptionCreate`, `Update`, `Delete`,
    `webhookSubscriptions`), or the owner or a manager subscribes it, naming the app; up to 50
    each, at https addresses on the public internet.
  * **The worker makes a delivery** for each subscription to a topic an event makes, once an
    event and subscription however often the event comes, for apps that may read it then. An
    app removed is told on `app/uninstalled`, and nothing else.
  * **The body names the resource by its ID**, with the topic, the event, when it happened and
    the shop, for the app to fetch through the API; headers say the topic, shop, event and
    delivery, and `X-Hatti-Hmac-Sha256` is the body's HMAC-SHA256 with the app's secret, in
    base64, as Shopify's is.
  * **A sweep posts what is due** every ten seconds, as images are fetched ([ADR-158](#adr-158--hatti-keeps-products-images-itself-the-worker-reads-each-from-the-shops-upload-or-fetches-it-from-its-url-never-reaching-a-private-network-checks-it-and-keeps-a-clean-copy-without-its-metadata-at-most-4096-pixels-a-side-the-api-serves-it-at-nine-widths-in-avif-webp-or-its-own-format-each-made-the-first-time-it-is-asked-for-and-kept-and-an-image-goes-from-storage-and-the-edge-with-its-media)): to
    addresses every one of whose IPs is public, connecting to those checked, following no
    redirect, five seconds to answer. Any 2xx is delivered; anything else is tried again after
    a minute, then twice as long each time up to six hours, until two days have passed.
    Outcomes are kept 30 days.
* **Consequences:**
  * An app gets an event at least once and may get them out of order; the event's ID tells a
    repeat.
  * A subscription failing for days is not turned off yet; the shop's admin will show it.
  * Development may post to plain http and private addresses with `WEBHOOK_PRIVATE_ADDRESSES`.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **The whole resource in the body, as Shopify sends:** it would need each module's shape in
    the worker and grows stale when deliveries are retried; the ID and the API's current answer
    cannot disagree.
  * **A queue per app:** the deliveries table is the queue, and the log the admin will show.

## ADR-398 · Each custom app on the shop's apps page shows its webhooks, the topic in words, where it goes and how its latest delivery went, with its last ten to open; one is added for a topic the app may hear, or removed

* **Context:**
  * Apps' webhooks are made and posted by the core ([ADR-397](#adr-397--a-custom-app-subscribes-to-topics-of-the-shops-events-at-https-addresses-the-worker-makes-one-delivery-an-event-and-subscription-for-apps-that-may-read-what-it-names-posts-it-signed-with-the-apps-secret-to-a-public-address-alone-and-tries-again-with-backoff-for-two-days)); a shop whose sheet stops
    filling needs to see whether Hatti sent, and what the app answered, without a developer.
* **Decision:**
  * **Under each app on Settings → Apps** ([ADR-396](#adr-396--settings-lists-the-shops-custom-apps-for-owners-and-managers-each-with-what-it-may-reach-in-words-and-the-last-characters-of-its-token-and-secret-an-app-is-made-by-choosing-each-resources-access-and-its-token-and-secret-are-shown-once-to-copy)), its webhooks: the topic in words ("An
    order is placed"), the address, and its latest delivery: delivered and when, trying again
    and when, with why it failed, given up, or nothing sent yet. "Recent deliveries" opens the
    last ten, each with its tries.
  * **The core gives each subscription its latest delivery** (`lastDelivery`) and a
    subscription's deliveries of the last 30 days (`webhookDeliveries`), to the app itself or
    the owner and managers.
  * **Adding one offers only the topics the app may hear**, from its scopes, at an https
    address; removing one is a tap.
* **Consequences:**
  * The activity log calls a subscription's changes a webhook's.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A page of its own for webhooks:** they are each app's, so they sit with the app.

## ADR-399 · Customers rate what their delivered order brought them on its own page, one to five stars a product with words if they like; each review waits for the shop, which publishes or hides it, unless its stars reach those the shop publishes by itself

* **Context:**
  * Shoppers in Pakistan buy from shops they don't know on the word of others who did, and a
    review from someone who never received the parcel is worth nothing: MKT-05 wants reviews
    from verified buyers, asked for on WhatsApp after delivery.
  * Customers have no accounts, but each order has its own page behind a link the shop already
    sends ([ADR-115](#adr-115--an-order-staff-or-an-app-placed-keeps-what-its-customer-agreed-to-in-confirming-it-through-its-link-the-page-names-the-shops-policies-and-the-order-keeps-their-versions-where-it-was-confirmed-from-and-when)), which knows the order, its items and that it was delivered.
* **Decision:**
  * **Written on the order's page once it is delivered:** each product it brought, once, with
    five stars to choose and a box for words, up to 2,000 characters. The page has no scripts,
    so the stars are radio buttons drawn as stars. What the customer said before is filled in,
    to change; one review an order and product, so a customer who bought a product twice
    reviews it twice.
  * **Kept by the catalog** (`catalog.product_reviews`), which the orders module already
    depends on: the product, the order, the customer, their name as "Ayesha K." from the
    order's address, the stars, the words, and pending, published or hidden.
  * **Waiting for the shop, unless** the shop chose to publish reviews of 3, 4 or 5 stars or
    more by themselves (`reviewSettingsUpdate(publishFrom)`); a changed review is judged again.
    The shop publishes or hides each through the Admin API (`productReviews`,
    `productReviewPublish`, `productReviewHide`), with `read_products` and `write_products`.
  * **Theirs, as their orders are:** a customer's reviews are in their own file ([ADR-102](#adr-102--a-customers-own-data-is-one-json-file-of-everything-the-shop-keeps-of-them-which-each-module-with-their-data-adds-to-the-blocklist-and-risk-scores-stay-out)),
    move with a merge, and go when they are erased.
* **Consequences:**
  * Products deleted since are not offered to rate; a deleted product takes its reviews with it.
  * The storefront does not show them yet, nor does WhatsApp ask for them: the next slices.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A review form on the storefront's product page:** anyone could write one; verified
    buyers would need accounts the shop's customers don't have.
  * **Publishing every review at once:** a shop's first one-star review from a rider's delay
    would sit on its product page before the shop saw it.

## ADR-400 · A shop may ask each delivered order's customer once on WhatsApp to rate what it brought, 1 to 14 days after its last parcel arrived, with the order's page; an order already rated is not asked about

* **Context:**
  * Customers rate what they bought on their delivered order's page ([ADR-399](#adr-399--customers-rate-what-their-delivered-order-brought-them-on-its-own-page-one-to-five-stars-a-product-with-words-if-they-like-each-review-waits-for-the-shop-which-publishes-or-hides-it-unless-its-stars-reach-those-the-shop-publishes-by-itself)), but few go back
    to it unasked; MKT-05 asks for reviews on WhatsApp after delivery.
* **Decision:**
  * **The shop says how many days after delivery**, 1 to 14, or never
    (`reviewSettingsUpdate(input: { requestAfterDays })`), the default. Fourteen at most, so
    the order's page, whose link lasts 30 days past the order's end, is still there to open.
  * **The worker asks once an order**, a `review_request` on WhatsApp with the customer's first
    name, the order and the shop, and a button to the order's page: the link its messages
    carried while it works ([ADR-160](#adr-160--each-parcels-way-is-kept-step-by-step-as-shopifys-fulfillmentevent-its-couriers-changes-recorded-once-from-the-workers-tracking-and-staffs-for-couriers-hatti-does-not-follow-the-orders-page-shows-them-the-latest-first-in-english-and-urdu-the-shipped-message-links-that-page-and-a-parcel-out-for-delivery-with-cash-to-collect-tells-its-customer-what-to-keep-ready)), a new one otherwise, now also for an order closed once
    delivered. Orders whose last parcel arrived up to three days past the day are still asked,
    so a sweep missed is made up; older ones are not.
  * **Not asked:** an order already rated on its page, its customer erased, or a shop that does
    not ask. Each order asked says so on its timeline.
  * **Utility, not marketing:** the message is about the order its customer received, as its
    delivery's news is; Meta prices it so unless it judges the template otherwise. Turned on and
    off by the reviews' setting, not the list of customers' messages, as the checkout reminder is
    ([ADR-393](#adr-393--abandoned-checkouts-the-number-a-shopper-types-is-kept-as-they-type-it-the-shop-sees-who-left-and-may-remind-them-once-on-whatsapp-after-the-delay-it-sets-with-a-link-back-to-their-items-an-order-the-number-places-then-recovers-it)).
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop that starts asking asks about orders delivered within its days and the three before,
    not its history.
  * The admin has no setting for it yet: the next slice.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Asking at delivery:** a customer who has not yet worn the suit has nothing to say of it.
  * **Asking again later:** one message is a request; two are a nag, and cost the shop twice.

## ADR-401 · A product's storefront page shows its published reviews, their average stars and the latest ten, through Shopify's review metafields and Hatti's product.reviews, and tells search engines as schema.org's AggregateRating

* **Context:**
  * Reviews written by buyers ([ADR-399](#adr-399--customers-rate-what-their-delivered-order-brought-them-on-its-own-page-one-to-five-stars-a-product-with-words-if-they-like-each-review-waits-for-the-shop-which-publishes-or-hides-it-unless-its-stars-reach-those-the-shop-publishes-by-itself)) are worth something only where shoppers decide: on
    the product's page, on its card in a collection, and in Google's results as stars.
  * Shopify themes read a product's stars from the standard `reviews.rating` and
    `reviews.rating_count` metafields, which review apps fill; the reviews themselves each app
    shows its own way.
* **Decision:**
  * **The product's storefront document carries them:** its published reviews' average, to one
    decimal place, how many, and the latest ten, each with its author as "Ayesha K.", its stars,
    its words escaped as articles' comments are ([ADR-220](#adr-220--articles-take-comments-as-their-blogs-shopify-comment-policy-says-posted-from-an-articles-page-through-the-storefront-held-for-the-shops-approval-where-the-blog-moderates-them-shown-escaped-as-text-in-the-articles-document-and-approved-marked-as-spam-or-deleted-through-the-admin-api)), and when it was published. A product
    with none carries nothing. The publisher rebuilds the product when one of its reviews is
    written, published or hidden.
  * **Themes read them as Shopify's:** `product.metafields.reviews.rating.value` (`rating`,
    `scale_min`, `scale_max`) and `product.metafields.reviews.rating_count.value`, and Hatti's
    own `product.reviews`, each with `author`, `rating`, `content` and `created_at`.
  * **Hatti Base shows them:** stars filled as far as the average under the title, leading to
    the reviews; the same on the product's cards; and the reviews below the product, each
    saying it was bought from the shop, in English and Urdu.
  * **`structured_data` tells search engines:** an AggregateRating, and the latest as Reviews,
    so Google may show the product's stars in its results.
* **Consequences:**
  * Only the latest ten show; a product with more shows its average of all of them.
  * Hidden reviews leave the page with the next build, and the edge forgets the page.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Fetching reviews as the page renders:** every product page would wait on the core; the
    document is already read for the page.
  * **Metafields alone:** a theme could show stars but no words.

## ADR-402 · Products' reviews have a page of their own in the admin, by status, waiting first, each published or hidden by those who change products; above them, for the owner and managers, from how many stars reviews publish by themselves and how many days after delivery customers are asked

* **Context:**
  * Reviews wait for the shop unless their stars reach those it publishes by itself
