## ADR-474 · Owners of a trademark or copyright complain of a store's listings from its rights page, naming them by their addresses and swearing to it; Hatti's people decide within 48 hours

* **Context:**
  * TNS-04 (V1) asks for notice and takedown of listings that infringe a trademark or copyright,
    or pass copies off as a brand's own: "replica" and "master copy" listings of well-known
    Pakistani labels are common (11 §6). Shoppers' reports (ADR-460) are about a store; a rights
    owner's complaint is about its listings, and must say whose right and swear to it.
  * Prohibited-items screening (ADR-473) catches the words a seller uses of a copy; it can't
    tell a brand's own goods from goods sold as that brand.
* **Decision:**
  * **Hatti's rights page on every store**, at `/report/rights` and `/ur/report/rights`, linked
    from its report page: the platform's markup in English and Urdu, as the report page is,
    answering while the shop is paused or behind its password. It asks what right (a trademark,
    a copyright, or fakes sold as the brand), whose, and its registration if any; who complains,
    whether as the owner or acting for them, an email and, if they say, a mobile; the listings,
    and how they infringe; and a good-faith statement sworn by ticking it and typing their name.
  * **Listings are named by their addresses**, whole or as paths, one on each line, up to 20.
    The storefront finds each among the store's own products and sends the core its ID, title
    and address as the store showed it; an address on another host, or of no product there, is
    refused on the form.
  * **The trust module keeps each complaint** (`trust.rights_complaints`), numbered `ipc_…`, due
    a decision within 48 hours, its complainant's address kept only as a hash with the shop's;
    five a day of one store from one address. No Admin API reads complaints.
  * **Hatti's people's queue** is the same command-line tool: `rights [--all]` lists each with
    its listings, the soonest due first and the overdue marked; `dismiss-rights` records why and
    names whom to write to.
* **Consequences:**
  * A brand finding copies of its goods on a Hatti store can tell Hatti, with what a decision
    needs, without an account.
  * Upholding a complaint, which takes its listings down and tells the store's owner with the
    complaint and a way to answer it, is TNS-04's next part.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **One page on Hatti's own site for every store:** the complainant would have to name the
    store and Hatti find it from any of its domains. On the store itself, the store is known
    and its products are at hand.
  * **Folding complaints into reports:** a report needs no statement, no owner and no listings,
    and a takedown of listings is not a takedown of the store.

## ADR-475 · A rights complaint upheld takes its listings off sale and holds them there, copies too, marked with its number; the store's owner is told who complained and how to reach them

* **Context:**
  * Rights owners complain of a store's listings, and Hatti's people decide within 48 hours
    (ADR-474). Notice and takedown (TNS-04) needs an upheld complaint to take the listings down,
    and keep them down: a seller who sets one on sale again, or copies it, undoes the decision.
  * The listings are the catalog's; the complaint is the trust module's. Neither reads the
    other's tables.
* **Decision:**
  * **The catalog holds products off sale** (`catalog.products.held_by`): its facade's
    `holdOffSale` makes each of the shop's products named a draft, its time to go on sale gone,
    marked with the complaint's number, `ipc_…`; `releaseHold` lets go every product so marked.
    Each goes through the catalog's own change, so its event takes it off the storefront as any
    change does.
  * **A held product doesn't go on sale:** putting it on sale by hand, many at once, from a file
    or at its time is refused with `HELD`, saying why and where to answer; other changes go
    through. A copy is held with it.
  * **`trust-reports uphold-rights`** holds the listings still the shop's, records the decision
    with what was done, and tells the store's owner at its alerts number and by email, at
    Hatti's cost: the listings, who complained (for whom, if an agent), the complaint's number,
    Hatti's words, and the complainant's email.
* **Consequences:**
  * An upheld complaint stops the listings selling within the minute, and they stay down.
  * The complainant's email goes to the seller, as the rights page says it may (ADR-474), so the
    two can settle it; Hatti's people let the listings go when they do.
  * The seller's own answer through Hatti, and letting go after it, are TNS-04's last part.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Archiving the listings:** an archived product goes back on sale with one change, and
    nothing says why it went.
  * **Deleting them:** the seller loses its work, and nothing is left to restore if the
    complaint was wrong.

## ADR-476 · The store's owner answers a rights complaint once, sworn, through a link in the notice; Hatti's people refuse the answer with why, or let the listings go

* **Context:**
  * An upheld rights complaint holds the store's listings off sale (ADR-475). Notice and
    takedown is fair only if the seller can answer: their own label, a licence, or a complaint
    about someone else's goods. Their admin works, but no Admin API reads complaints (ADR-460),
    and the answer belongs with the complaint.
* **Decision:**
  * **The notice carries a link**, `/rights/<secret>` on the core's public address: 24 random
    bytes, kept only as their SHA-256 digest on the complaint, found through a database function
    as appeals' links are (ADR-462). Only an upheld complaint has one.
  * **Its page**, in English and Urdu, never kept, indexed or framed, shows the complaint: the
    right, whose, the listings, the complainant's words and email, and Hatti's decision. It takes
    the owner's answer once, up to 2,000 characters, sworn in good faith by ticking a statement
    and typing their name, and shows Hatti's answer.
  * **Hatti's people** list the answers waiting, the oldest first, with `trust-reports
    counters`. `refuse-counter` answers one with why: the page shows it and the owner is told on
    WhatsApp; the listings stay held. `release-rights` lets the listings go, with why, once the
    complaint is withdrawn or settled or the answer holds: the catalog's hold is lifted from them
    and their copies, an answer waiting is upheld with the same words, and the owner is told to
    put them on sale again.
* **Consequences:**
  * TNS-04 is whole: a rights owner's sworn complaint, Hatti's decision within 48 hours, the
    listings held off sale, the seller's sworn answer, and the listings let go or kept down.
  * The complainant hears of the answer from Hatti's people, who have their email in the list.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Answering from the admin:** it would need an Admin API for complaints, which shows the
    shop more than its own answer needs.
  * **Letting the listings go on any answer, as the US DMCA's counter-notice does after ten
    days:** Pakistani law sets no such clock for platforms, and Hatti's people judge each.

## ADR-477 · A product says whether it comes stitched, its pieces, fabrics and season in Hatti's own words, in English and Urdu: kept by the catalog, set from its admin page, shown on its storefront page and given to themes

* **Context:**
  * Pakistani shoppers choose eastern wear by whether it comes stitched, in how many pieces,
    of what fabric and for which season before its size or colour (CAT-08, V1). Shops write it
    in titles and tags, each their own way: "3pc lawn", "Unstitched 3-Piece", "LAWN 25".
  * Filters across a store's collections (SRC-03) need the same words on every product, and
    Urdu pages need them in Urdu.
* **Decision:**
  * **Hatti's own words**, kept with the catalog: stitching (unstitched, semi-stitched,
    stitched), pieces (1 to 4), up to three fabrics of twenty (lawn, cambric, khaddar, karandi,
    chiffon, organza, jamawar and the rest Pakistani shops sell), and season (summer, winter,
    festive, all season), each with its English and Urdu words. A shop can't add its own; one
    left out is unsaid, and none said is none at all (`catalog.products.eastern_wear`).
  * **The Admin API** takes and gives them as `Product.easternWear`, with enums for each, on
    `productCreate` and `productUpdate` (null clears them); a copy keeps them. Search finds a
    product by their English words too.
  * **The admin's product page** has an Eastern wear card: three choices, the fabrics ticked,
    saved together.
  * **The storefront's document** carries each with its value and its words in both languages;
    Urdu pages show the Urdu. Themes read `product.eastern_wear` (each `value` and `label`, the
    fabrics a list, and a `summary` line) and `product.metafields.hatti.*`, as Shopify's themes
    read metafields. Hatti Base says the summary under the product's title.
* **Consequences:**
  * Every shop's lawn is the same lawn: filtering by them across a collection (SRC-03) is the
    next part.
  * Shops whose goods are not eastern wear see a card they can leave empty.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Free text, or tags:** what the shop already writes, which no filter can gather.
  * **Shopify's metafields, defined by each shop:** CAT-06's work, and each shop's definitions
    would differ again.

## ADR-478 · A collection's page filters its products by Shopify's filter parameters: availability, price, product type, brand, each option and the eastern-wear attributes, each value counted, as Shopify's collection.filters

* **Context:**
  * Shoppers narrow a collection by size, colour, fabric, price and what is in stock (SRC-03,
    V1). Shopify's themes do it with `collection.filters` and `filter.*` parameters, Dawn's
    facets among them; Hatti's themes should work the same.
  * The eastern-wear attributes (ADR-477) are Hatti's own words on every product, so a
    collection can be filtered by them across shops' different titles.
  * Storefront documents are in Valkey; there is no search index to count facets with.
* **Decision:**
  * **The storefront filters**, from the collection's product documents, fetched in one round
    trip where it has at most 1,000 products; a larger one is shown unfiltered, with no
    filters, as before.
  * **Shopify's parameters:** `filter.v.availability` (1 or 0), `filter.v.price.gte` and
    `.lte` in rupees, `filter.p.product_type`, `filter.p.vendor`, `filter.v.option.<name>`,
    and `filter.p.m.hatti.stitching`, `.pieces`, `.fabric` and `.season`. A filter's values
    are any of them, the filters all of them; a variant's filters (availability, price,
    options) hold of one variant together, so "L in stock" is an L that is. Parameters the
    page doesn't know are ignored.
  * **Shopify's `collection.filters`:** each filter's `label`, `param_name`, `type` (list or
    price_range), its `values` with `count`, `active`, `url_to_add` and `url_to_remove`,
    `active_values`, and for price `min_value`, `max_value` and `range_max` in paisa, as money
    prints them. A value counts the products the other filters leave. A filter whose products
    all have one value is left out, unless the shopper chose it. Labels are in the page's
    language; the eastern-wear values' too.
  * **The page:** `collection.products` and `products_count` are those the filters leave,
    `all_products_count` the collection's; its pages' links keep the filters, each as often as
    given, and its canonical address has none.
  * **Hatti Base** has a filter form that works without scripts: each filter's values ticked,
    the price from and to, the filters chosen as links that take each away, and one to clear
    them.
* **Consequences:**
  * A collection's page fetches all its products' documents, not a page of them: one round
    trip, kept for the page's own products, and the page is kept at the edge per address.
  * Option filters on Urdu pages go by the options' Urdu names where the shop gave them.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Counts from the core's search:** a round trip to Postgres for every collection page,
    where the documents are already at hand.
  * **Filters each shop chooses, as Shopify's Search & Discovery app:** a later part; the
    filters a collection's products have are shown meanwhile.

## ADR-479 · A collection's page is put in the order a shopper asks for, by Shopify's sort_by, and the search page's products are filtered and ordered as a collection's are

* **Context:**
  * Shoppers who filter a collection (ADR-478) also want it cheapest first or newest first, and
    Shopify's themes ask with `sort_by` and show `collection.sort_options`.
  * The search page lists what a search found; Shopify's themes filter and order it with
    `search.filters` and `search.sort_options` too.
* **Decision:**
  * **Orders, as Shopify names them:** a collection's own (`manual`, "Featured"), title A–Z
    and Z–A, price low to high and high to low by its cheapest variant, and date new to old
    and old to new, those without a date last. A search's: best first (`relevance`) and price
    either way. One not among a list's is its own order; ties keep it.
  * **Liquid:** `sort_by`, `default_sort_by` and `sort_options` (each `name`, in the page's
    language, and `value`) on `collection` and `search`; `search.filters` as a collection's.
    What the filters leave is put in order; pages' links keep the order and the filters.
  * **A filtered search** lists the products alone, as pages and articles have none of their
    filters; unfiltered, its pages and articles follow as before.
  * **Hatti Base:** one form for both, a snippet: the order to choose, the filters, the search's
    words kept, and the filters chosen as links that take each away.
  * Past 1,000 products, a list keeps its own order, as it does its filters.
* **Consequences:**
  * Best-selling, Shopify's other order, needs sales in the documents: not yet; asked for, a
    collection keeps its own order.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Ordering in the core:** each order a query, where the documents are already at hand.

## ADR-480 · Frequently bought together: the products a shop's customers bought in the same orders, recommended as complementary where the shop paired none with a product

* **Context:**
  * SRC-05 asks for recommendations: related products (ADR-434) and those frequently bought
    together. ADR-434 left the second for when shops had orders to learn from.
  * Complementary products are what the shop pairs with one (ADR-435): Hatti Base shows them
    on the product page and the cart offers them (ADR-437). Most shops pair none.
* **Decision:**
  * **The orders module works out what was bought together** (`boughtTogetherIn`): the other
    products in a product's 500 latest orders of the past year, not cancelled; a pair counts
    once two orders have both. Those in the most orders with it come first, then those bought
    with it latest; at most 10. Migration 0225 indexes order lines by product.
  * **The publisher** gives them as a product's complementary products where the shop paired
    none with it: the shop's own pairing always wins. They are as fresh as the product's
    document, which its stock's changes rebuild as it sells.
  * Shopify's complementary recommendations, Hatti Base's product page and the cart's
    cross-sells show them as they do the shop's pairings; products gone or sold out since are
    left out where they are shown.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop with no pairings gets cross-sells from its second repeated pair of orders on.
  * A product whose stock isn't counted is rebuilt only when it changes, so what was bought with
    it may lag.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Mixed into related products:** related ones are alike (the same collection, type or
    brand); bought together are what goes with it, which is what complementary means.
  * **A nightly job over every shop's orders:** documents already rebuild as products sell.

## ADR-481 · A commerce lexicon: a storefront's search finds what a word means in English, Roman Urdu or Urdu, "juta" the shop's shoes, after what holds the word as typed

* **Context:**
  * SRC-02 asks for search in Roman Urdu and Urdu with phonetic folding, script normalisation
    and a commerce lexicon. ADR-046 and ADR-240 fold Roman Urdu spellings and Urdu letters, so
    "qameez" finds "kameez". A shopper who types "juta" still finds nothing in a shop that
    wrote "shoes", nor one who types "لال" a "red" dupatta.
* **Decision:**
  * **`@hatti/pk` keeps a commerce lexicon:** groups of words that mean the same in English,
    Roman Urdu and Urdu script (clothes, shoes, jewellery and bags, fabrics, who and when it is
    for, colours), folded as searched words are. A kind of a thing is not the thing: khussas are
    shoes, but not every shopper asking for shoes wants them, so they are apart, as are kurtas
    and kurtis. Each word means one thing alone.
  * **A storefront's search** (the search page and predictive search) finds a product by each
    word as typed or by a word meaning the same, that one as a whole word: "lal" finds "red",
    but "red" in "embroidered" does not count. Every word must still be there. Products holding
    the first word as typed come first, then those holding only a word meaning the same, the
    newest first. Typos are forgiven as before where nothing matches.
* **Consequences:**
  * The lexicon is Hatti's, for every shop; a shop's own synonyms are a later part.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Translating the shopper's words with AI:** a call per search, and its answers vary.
  * **Synonyms in the search text kept with each product:** every product rewritten whenever the
    lexicon grows.

## ADR-482 · Products from a WooCommerce export: productsImport reads WooCommerce's product CSV, its variable products' variations the variants, as Shopify's file would make them

* **Context:**
  * ONB-06 asks for importers from WooCommerce, Daraz and spreadsheets. Many Pakistani shops
    moving to Hatti run WooCommerce. ADR-120 imports Shopify's product CSV; ADR-130 updates
    products from it.
  * WooCommerce's exporter (Products > Export) writes a row for each simple or variable product
    and a row for each variation, naming its product in Parent by ID or SKU. Variations carry
    their attributes' values, prices, SKUs and stock.
* **Decision:**
  * **The catalog reads WooCommerce's file into what Shopify's file would have made**
    (`readWooCommerceProducts`), so the import (ADR-120), its updates (ADR-130), images by
    address and stock go on as they do for Shopify's.
    * Simple products have one variant; variable products a variant for each variation, their
      options the attributes the variations name, at most three. A variation for any value of
      an attribute is left out, said by its row: Hatti's variants have values.
    * The price is the sale price, the regular price the price compared at; else the regular
      price. Weight in kg, g, lbs or oz becomes grams. Tax status none is untaxed.
    * The first category's last part is the product type; the others and the tags its tags.
      Published is on sale; drafts and private products are drafts. A handle is made from the
      name, `-2` and on where names repeat.
    * Stock is set where WooCommerce managed it; backorders allowed sells on at nothing.
    * Grouped and external products, and variations without their product, are said by row and
      left out.
  * **`productsImport` takes `format: WOOCOMMERCE`** (SHOPIFY by default); stock it sets says
    it came from WooCommerce's export in the stock history.
  * **The admin's import card** asks where the file is from.
* **Consequences:**
  * Daraz's seller exports, and the spreadsheet templates, are later parts of ONB-06.
  * WooCommerce's attributes that no variation varies by are left; they are not options.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **WooCommerce's REST API with the shop's keys:** a connection for a one-time move, and the
    file is what the shop already knows how to make.

## ADR-483 · Product taxonomy: a product's category in Google's product taxonomy and its condition, barcodes that are GTINs published as such, all three in the catalog feed

* **Context:**
  * CAT-18 asks for a standard product taxonomy, condition and GTINs, so Google Shopping and
    Meta's catalogs take a shop's products without each being fixed by hand.
  * The catalog feed (ADR-142) said every product was new and had no identifiers. Google
    rejects or limits products in categories that need them when neither a GTIN nor
    `identifier_exists` is given, and places products better when their category is said.
  * Shopify's product CSV carries `Product Category` (a path in Google's taxonomy) and
    `Google Shopping / Condition`.
* **Decision:**
  * **A product has a category and a condition** (migration 0226). The category is one of
    the paths of Google's product taxonomy Hatti offers (`PRODUCT_CATEGORIES`, those the
    shops it serves sell in: clothing and its traditional and ceremonial kinds, shoes,
    jewellery, bags, beauty, home and kitchen, electronics, toys, food and more), matched
    however it is spaced or cased; one Hatti doesn't offer is refused. Blank clears it.
    The condition is new, refurbished or used, new unless said. A duplicate keeps both.
  * **The Admin API** has `Product.category` and `condition`, both on `productCreate` and
    `productUpdate`, and `productCategories` lists the paths offered.
  * **Shopify's CSV** fills both from its columns; a category Hatti doesn't offer is left out
    and the product goes in.
  * **A barcode that is a GTIN** (8, 12, 13 or 14 digits whose check digit holds) is published
    in the storefront document as the variant's GTIN; other barcodes stay the shop's own.
  * **The catalog feed** says each product's condition, its `google_product_category`, its
    GTIN where it has one, and `identifier_exists no` where it hasn't.
  * **The admin's product page** has a card for the category and condition.
* **Consequences:**
  * The whole of Google's taxonomy (about 5,600 paths) is not offered: a shop picks from the
    few dozen its kind of shop needs, and the list grows as shops ask.
  * Meta's catalog reads the same feed, so it gets the same fields.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Google's numeric category IDs:** what Google prefers, but paths are what Shopify's CSV
    carries and what a merchant reads; Google takes either.
  * **A GTIN field of its own on variants:** barcodes already hold them, and a second field
    would be one more to fill in.

## ADR-484 · Pakistan's marketing calendar: the moments shoppers buy for, dated each year from Umm al-Qura a day later for the Islamic ones, each with a ready-made campaign

* **Context:**
  * MKT-16 asks for a Pakistani marketing calendar: Ramadan, Eid, 14 August, White Friday and
    the lawn seasons, with ready-made campaign kits.
  * Most of a Pakistani shop's year turns on these moments, and the Islamic ones move about
    eleven days earlier each year. Shops miss them by starting late: Eid's shopping starts in
    Ramadan's first weeks, and parcels take days.
  * Pakistan fixes Ramadan and the Eids by its own moon sighting (the Ruet-e-Hilal committee),
    usually a day after Saudi Arabia's Umm al-Qura calendar.
* **Decision:**
  * **The marketing module dates twelve moments for any year** (`marketingDatesOf`), with no
    table to keep up:
    * Ramadan, Eid ul Fitr (three days) and Eid ul Adha (three days) from the Umm al-Qura
      calendar, which ICU's data in Node has (`Intl`'s `islamic-umalqura`), a day later; said
      to be expected, since the sighting decides. Ramadan runs to the day before Eid, and can
      come twice in a Gregorian year.
    * Pakistan Day (23 March), Mother's Day (the second Sunday of May), Independence Day
      (14 August), 11.11, White Friday (the last Friday of November, to the Monday after) and
      12.12.
    * Seasons: lawn (15 February to April), winter collections (October and November) and
      weddings (November to the end of February).
  * **Each has a lead**, the days before it to start promoting: three weeks for Eid ul Fitr,
    two for most, one for the one-day sales.
  * **Each has a kit**: a discount code (EID26, AZADI26 and the like, the year's last two
    digits after a word), a percentage customers expect (14% for 14 August, 23% for
    23 March, 30% for White Friday), and a broadcast's words in English and Urdu naming both,
    short enough for one SMS campaign (ADR-458).
  * **`marketingCalendar(days)`** lists the moments to promote for from the shop's today, in
    its time zone, through `days` ahead (365 by default, at most 731): those not over whose
    promoting begins by then, soonest first. It needs `read_marketing_events`.
  * **The admin's Marketing calendar page** (linked from Marketing) shows each moment's dates,
    whether they are expected, what sells, and its kit; a tap makes its discount code, from
    its promoting's first day to its last day in the shop's time zone, through
    `discountCodeCreate`.
* **Consequences:**
  * A year when Pakistan's sighting matches Saudi Arabia's (Eid ul Fitr 2024) is a day off
    until the shop adjusts its code's dates; the page says the dates are expected.
  * Kits are suggestions: nothing is sent or made until the shop chooses. Broadcasts are
    written from the kit's words on the broadcasts page; WhatsApp needs an approved template.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A table of dates kept by hand:** right where the committee's announcements differ, but
    a chore each year that a missed update turns into a wrong date for every shop.
  * **The tabular Islamic calendar:** simpler, but further from the sighting than Umm al-Qura.

## ADR-485 · The store speed score: shoppers' own Core Web Vitals, counted by the storefront in histograms of 28 days, scored per device as Google judges them, with fixes

* **Context:**
  * OS-13 asks for a store speed score from real users' Core Web Vitals, with fixes a merchant
    can act on.
  * Lab scores (Lighthouse) measure one device on one network. Google ranks pages by what
    Chrome users actually saw over 28 days, at the 75th percentile, phones and computers
    apart. Most Pakistani shoppers are on mid-range Android phones and mobile networks.
  * Pages are cached at the edge and the same for every shopper (ADR-066), so measuring has to
    run in the shopper's browser. Sessions are already counted that way (ADR-180).
* **Decision:**
  * **Each shopper's page measures itself.** A small classic script in the page's head, beside
    the session's (not in staff previews), watches the browser's performance entries as
    Google's web-vitals library does: largest contentful paint until the shopper acts, layout
    shift as the worst window of shifts, interaction to next paint as the slowest tap, first
    contentful paint and time to first byte. It reports them once, with the page's kind (its
    theme's template), by `sendBeacon` to `/.hatti/vitals` when the page is hidden or left.
    Browsers without these entries report nothing.
  * **The storefront counts reports in histograms** (`StorefrontVitals`): a hash per shop per
    day in its time zone, a bucket count for each device (phone or computer, from the user
    agent), kind of page and metric, with Google's thresholds among the bucket edges, and page
    views. Kept 30 days in Valkey; nothing about a shopper is kept. Reports from robots, from
    browsers without a session cookie, from previews and over 1 KB are not counted, and an
    address may send as many reports as pages a minute.
  * **`storeSpeed`** (with `read_themes`) adds up the last 28 days to the shop's today. It
    gives, for each device, each metric's 75th percentile (a bucket's upper edge, "at most"),
    the share of good page views and Google's rating, for the whole store and each kind of
    page. The score is the share of good page views, averaged over the three Core Web Vitals,
    0 to 100, once a device has 20 page views.
  * **Fixes are drawn from what is slow** where 20 page views or more say so:
    * a main picture shown late on a kind of page (largest contentful paint);
    * pages that jump (layout shift);
    * slow taps (interaction to next paint);
    * a slow answer from the storefront, which is Hatti's to fix (time to first byte);
    * a blank page while it loads, once the answer is fast (first contentful paint).
    The poorest come first, then the most viewed.
  * **The admin's online store has a Speed tab**, for those who edit themes. It shows each
    device's score, measurements and ratings, and the fixes, each with what to do.
* **Consequences:**
  * Percentiles are as fine as the buckets: 2.5 s and 4 s are exact for largest contentful
    paint, and between them a 75th percentile reads "at most 3 s".
  * Interaction to next paint is the page's slowest interaction, not the 98th percentile
    Google takes on pages with very many. That is the same for nearly every shop page.
  * 28 days in Valkey is the whole history. A trend over months would need the worker to keep
    days in Postgres, as sessions are (ADR-180).
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Google's Chrome UX Report API:** only for origins with enough Chrome traffic, which most
    new shops lack, and not by page kind.
  * **Lighthouse runs from Hatti's servers:** a lab number, not what shoppers on Pakistani
    networks saw.

## ADR-486 · Vertical starter kits: what a kind of shop sells by, its smart collections, size charts and main menu links, set up in one go and safe to apply again

* **Context:**
  * ONB-13 asks for vertical starter kits: fashion (stitched and unstitched), jewellery, beauty,
    electronics, bakery and grocery.
  * A new shop opens empty (ADR-145). Its owner has to work out collections, a menu and size
    charts before adding products, and many stop there.
* **Decision:**
  * **Five kits, as data in the core** (`apps/core/src/api/starter-kits.ts`):
    * Fashion: Unstitched, Ready to wear, Lawn, Formal and Eid collection, with kameez and
      kurta size charts in inches.
    * Jewellery: Earrings, Necklaces, Bangles, Rings and Bridal sets.
    * Beauty: Skin care, Makeup, Hair care and Fragrance.
    * Electronics: Mobile accessories, Audio, Smart watches and Home appliances.
    * Grocery: Bakery, Mithai, Dry fruits, Spices and Deals.
    * Each also has New arrivals (everything priced, newest first) and a Sale of what is
      priced below its compare-at price.
  * **Collections are smart, filled by a tag** (`lawn`, `bridal`, `skin-care`), so a product
    is in its collection by being tagged, as Shopify shops do, and nothing has to be picked by
    hand.
  * **`starterKitApply(kit)`** (with `write_products` and `write_online_store_navigation`):
    * makes, through the catalog's and the online store's facades, the kit's collections the
      shop has no collection of that handle for, and the size charts it has none of that name
      for;
    * adds to the main menu a link to each of the kit's collections it does not link yet,
      after what is there;
    * says what it made and what it kept.
    So a kit can be applied again, or another after it: they share New arrivals and Sale.
    `starterKits` lists what each kit sets up.
  * **The admin's collections page offers a kit** while a shop has fewer than three
    collections. It shows what the chosen kit sets up, applies it in a tap, and says to tag
    products to fill the collections.
* **Consequences:**
  * Kits make no products, theme or policies. Policies have drafts of their own (ADR-056), and
    a theme preset per kind of shop is a later part of ONB-13.
  * The kits' names are English, as collections' titles are; shops put them in Urdu on the
    Urdu pages (ADR-238).
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Manual collections with sample products:** sample products have to be deleted, and
    manual collections filled by hand.
  * **Kits chosen when a shop opens:** opening stays one step (ADR-145). A kit is offered where
    its collections show.

## ADR-487 · Collaborators: staff invited for 1 to 90 days, whose access ends by itself

* **Context:**
  * ADM-07 asks for collaborator accounts: an agency running a shop's ads, or a freelancer
    shooting its products, given access that is time-boxed and ends without anyone
    remembering to take it back.
  * Staff join by invitation (ADR-101) and stay until removed. A role limits what they do
    (ADR-030), but nothing limits how long.
* **Decision:**
  * **An invitation may give access for 1 to 90 days** (`staffInvitationCreate(accessDays:)`).
    The days count from joining, not from the invitation, so a link opened on its seventh day
    still gives the days asked. The invitation's preview says them; sending it again keeps
    them.
  * **A membership keeps when it ends** (`identity.memberships.expires_at`, migration 0227),
    set when such an invitation is accepted. The owner's membership never ends (a check
    constraint), and a shop is not handed to a collaborator.
  * **Access ends at that moment, not at a sweep**:
    * `identity.resolve_staff_access` refuses a membership past its end, so every Admin API
      request after it answers `NO_SHOP_ACCESS`;
    * the staff list, the account's shops and the numbers and emails staff are told at leave
      it out.
  * **A worker sweep deletes ended memberships** every sweep interval, 200 at a time, through
    `identity.end_expired_memberships`, a function owned by identity's role. So the shop's
    staff count and room on its plan (ADR-154) come back.
  * **The admin's invitation form asks "Access for"**: for good, 7, 30 or 90 days. Staff
    show when a collaborator's access ends, and invitations their days.
* **Consequences:**
  * An agency asking for access itself, by the shop's handle, for the owner to approve, is the
    second part of ADM-07.
  * Extending a collaborator means inviting them again. The role can still be changed or the
    member removed sooner as for any staff.
  * A collaborator's actions are on the activity log under their own name, as any staff's.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A separate collaborator role:** what an agency may do is a role's question; how long is
    a separate one, so any role can be time-boxed.
  * **Days from the invitation:** the agency would lose days to a link opened late.
  * **Ending access only by the sweep:** access would last up to a sweep interval past its
    end.

## ADR-488 · Requests for access: an agency asks a shop by its address, its owner approves or declines

* **Context:**
  * ADM-07 asks for collaborator access that agencies request and owners approve, time-boxed.
    ADR-487 made the time box: invited staff whose access ends by itself.
  * An agency working for many shops would otherwise need each owner to find the invitation
    form, pick the role and send a link.
* **Decision:**
  * **An account asks a shop for access by its address** (`POST /auth/access-requests`, signed
    in): the shop's handle, a role other than the owner's, 1 to 90 days, and who they are and
    what for, in 300 characters. A link to the store is read as its handle in the admin.
    Requests are always collaborators': their access always ends.
  * **Kept by identity** (`identity.access_requests`, migration 0228). A request waits 7 days,
    then reads as expired.
  * **Limits:**
    * an account asks 10 a day, and one at a time of a shop (a unique index on those waiting);
    * a shop has 20 waiting at most;
    * no one asks a shop they work in.
  * **The owner is emailed** at the email their account proved, in their language, with a link
    to the staff page. The request stands if the email fails.
  * **The owner, or a manager for the roles below them, decides** in the Admin API:
    * `staffAccessRequests` lists those waiting;
    * `staffAccessRequestApprove(id, role, accessDays)` makes the membership, ending that many
      days from approval (ADR-487), within the plan's staff (ADR-154). The approver may give
      another role or fewer days. A member must have confirmed who they are recently;
    * `staffAccessRequestDecline(id)` declines it.
    Each goes on the audit log.
  * **The asker sees what became of their requests** (`GET /auth/access-requests`, the last 30
    days).
  * **An ended membership the sweep has not taken yet is cleared on joining again**, by request
    or by invitation, so a returning agency is not refused as one already working there.
  * **In the admin:**
    * the shops page links "Work for a shop? Ask it for access" to the form and to the asker's
      requests;
    * the staff page shows requests waiting, each approved or declined in a tap.
* **Consequences:**
  * Shop handles are public (each is the storefront's own address), so asking by one reveals
    nothing new. A request tells the owner only the asker's name and email.
  * An agency is not told by email when it is approved; it sees the shop on its next sign-in
    and on its requests.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Asking by the owner's email or phone:** this would reveal whose shop is whose, and the
    handle is what agencies already know.
  * **Approval with no time box:** an agency's access would last until someone took it back.
    Approved requests always end, as ADM-07 asks.

## ADR-489 · Metafields: custom data on products, variants and collections, as Shopify keeps it, typed by the shop's definitions and read by themes in Liquid

* **Context:**
  * CAT-06 asks for metafields: custom fields on what a shop sells, for care instructions, a
    lining, a fabric's weight, a collection's banner colour.
  * Themes and apps written for Shopify read them (`product.metafields.custom.care.value`,
    `metafieldsSet`). Hatti wrote only its own namespaces so far: reviews' stars (ADR-401) and
    eastern-wear attributes (ADR-477).
* **Decision:**
  * **Kept by the catalog** (`catalog.metafields`, migration 0229) on products, variants and
    collections. Each owner is a foreign key, so values go when their owner is deleted.
    * A value has a namespace, a key, a type and the value as Shopify keeps it: a string, JSON
      for the list and json types.
    * Types: single- and multi-line text, whole and decimal numbers, true or false, date, date
      and time, URL, colour, JSON, and a list of lines.
    * Each value is checked and kept in a standard form: numbers without leading zeros, dates
      in ISO 8601, JSON compact, colours in lower case.
  * **Definitions** (`catalog.metafield_definitions`) name a field of the shop's own for each
    kind of owner and fix its type. Values set after take the definition's type and refuse
    another. A definition is refused while values of the field have another type. Deleting a
    definition can delete its values with it.
  * **The Admin API, as Shopify's:**
    * `metafieldsSet` sets up to 25 at once, all or none; an owner keeps 100.
    * `metafieldsDelete` deletes by owner, namespace and key.
    * `metafields(namespace)` and `metafield(namespace, key)` on `Product`, `ProductVariant`
      and `Collection`, loaded for all owners at once.
    * `metafieldDefinitions`, and `metafieldDefinitionCreate`, `metafieldDefinitionUpdate` and
      `metafieldDefinitionDelete`.
    * Under `read_products` and `write_products`.
  * **Hatti's namespaces are its own:** `hatti` and `reviews` are refused, since the storefront
    writes them from what the shop keeps elsewhere.
  * **On the storefront:** `metafields.updated` names the products and collections whose pages
    change, a variant's by its product. Their documents carry their metafields, and Liquid reads
    them as Shopify's: `value` is of its type (a number, true or false, a list, an object for
    JSON), and `{ product.metafields.custom.care }` prints the value.
* **Consequences:**
  * Themes and apps written for Shopify's metafields work on Hatti's products, variants and
    collections.
  * `metafields` is a list, not Shopify's connection: an owner keeps 100, which one list holds.
  * Customers', orders' and the shop's metafields, metaobjects, and file and reference types
    come later. The admin's definitions and the fields on a product's page are the next part of
    CAT-06, and the metafield columns of Shopify's product CSV after that.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **One JSON column on each table:** no definition could fix a type, and a key could not be
    set or deleted on its own.
  * **Values parsed and kept by type in the database:** Shopify's API and its CSVs give strings,
    and Liquid parses them once on the page.

## ADR-490 · Custom data in the admin: the shop's fields defined in Settings, keyed from their names, and filled on a product's page by the kind of field their type takes

* **Context:** Metafields (ADR-489) were kept and read through the Admin API alone. Shop owners
  need to make their fields and fill them in without an app, as Shopify's admin lets them.
* **Decision:**
  * **Settings → Custom data** lists the shop's definitions by what they are for: products,
    variants and collections. Each shows its key, its type in words, and how many owners have a
    value. A definition is added there with a name, a type and an optional description:
    * its key is made from its name (`care_instructions`), in the `custom` namespace, and may
      be changed before it is added;
    * types are named in words ("Text, one line", "Yes or no", "List of lines").
    A definition is deleted with its values, after the owner confirms.
  * **A product's page has a "Custom fields" card**, with a field for each product definition
    of the kind its type takes:
    * a choice of yes, no or not said for true or false;
    * a box of many lines for long text and JSON, and for a list, one item to a line;
    * a date or web address field where the browser has one;
    * one line of text otherwise.
    Saving sets what was filled through `metafieldsSet` and deletes what was emptied through
    `metafieldsDelete`. A refusal names its field. Without definitions, the card links to
    Settings.
* **Consequences:**
  * Variants' and collections' values are set through the Admin API for now. Their pages'
    fields come later.
  * The admin checks no value itself: the core's checks (ADR-489) answer, in the field's words.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A free form of namespace, key and value on each product:** shop owners would have to keep
    keys and types consistent across products. Definitions keep them so.

## ADR-491 · Gateway settlements: the statements gateways send imported as they come, each line matched to a payment by the gateway's reference, and the fees and tax withheld kept beside it

* **Context:** Gateways pay a shop what its customers paid online days later. They pay less
  their fees and the income tax they withhold, with a statement of the payments it is for. The
  shop has to check that every payment was settled, and at what cost. Its accountant needs the
  tax withheld for the shop's return. Couriers' statements are reconciled already (ADR-066,
  ADR-269); gateways' were not.
* **Decision:**
  * **`paymentSettlementImport` takes a gateway account's statement as the CSV or Excel workbook
    the gateway sends.** Up to 20 title rows may come above its header. Its columns are found by
    the names gateways use:
    * the payment's reference ("Transaction ID", "Txn Ref", "Tracker");
    * what the customer paid ("Gross Amount", "Amount");
    * the fees ("MDR", "Commission") and the tax withheld ("WHT"), when it has them;
    * what was paid over ("Net Amount").
    Deductions count however signed, a refund's amount in brackets or below 0. A totals row is
    passed over. A row that cannot be read is reported with its column, and the rest import.
  * **Each line is matched to one of the account's paid payments by the gateway's reference or
    Hatti's, whatever their case:**
    * MATCHED when the line settled what was paid;
    * DIFFERS when it settled another amount;
    * UNMATCHED when no payment of the account has its reference;
    * REPEATED when its payment was settled before, or earlier in the same file;
    * REFUND when it takes money back.
    A payment is settled once: a unique index on its matched line says so.
  * **A dry run says what the import would do**: its counts, totals and the first 250 lines to
    look into. **An import keeps the settlement whole or not at all.** Its lines keep their fees
    and tax beside their payment, and its totals what the gateway paid over. A shop's imports run
    one at a time. A reference used before by the same account is refused.
  * `paymentSettlements` lists them, the newest first, and `paymentSettlement` reads one with its
    lines, which may be filtered by outcome. Owners, managers and accountants reconcile. Apps read
    with `read_orders` and import with `write_orders` too.
* **Consequences:**
  * The tax gateways withheld is kept per payment for the withholding report (TAX-03), with
    couriers' tax.
  * Payments never settled are not listed yet. The admin's page of settlements, and payouts
    across gateways and couriers, come next.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Gateways' settlement APIs:** few Pakistani gateways have one, and those that do differ.
    Every gateway sends a statement.
  * **Matching by amount and date:** two payments of one amount on a day are common. The
    gateway's reference is exact.

## ADR-492 · Gateway settlements in the admin: imported beside couriers' statements, checked before they are, and each opened on the lines to look into

* **Context:** Gateways' settlements were imported and read through the Admin API alone
  (ADR-491). The accountants who reconcile couriers' cash need to reconcile gateways' payouts
  the same way. Accountants cannot read the shop's gateway accounts, which are settings.
* **Decision:**
  * **The cash page links to "Gateways' settlements"**, a page for owners, managers and
    accountants:
    * the settlements imported, the newest first, each with what it paid over, its fees and tax,
      and its lines to look into in red;
    * an import of the statement for a gateway account chosen by name, a sandbox's said, checked
      first. The check counts its lines by outcome, says what was paid over after fees and tax,
      and lists rows it could not read. The import opens the settlement.
  * **A settlement's page** shows what customers paid, the fees, the tax withheld and what was
    paid over. Its lines open on those to look into when it has any. Each names its payment's
    order, or its row, and for another amount what the payment was.
  * **The core gives what the page needs:**
    * `paymentSettlementAccounts`, the live accounts by name and sandbox alone, for those who
      reconcile;
    * a settlement's `issueCount`, counted from its lines;
    * its `gatewayName`.
* **Consequences:**
  * Payouts across gateways and couriers on one page, and the tax withheld by both for the
    shop's return (TAX-03), come next.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Giving accountants `read_settings`:** they would see every setting, not only which
    accounts exist.
  * **A settlements tab on the cash page:** the cash page is about couriers' cash on delivery.
    A page of its own keeps both short.

## ADR-493 · Payouts and tax withheld: gateways' and couriers' statements over a period, by who paid and by month, and each that withheld tax for the shop's tax credit

* **Context:** Gateways (ADR-491) and couriers (ADR-067) pay the shop less their fees and the
  income tax they withhold. The tax is the shop's credit against its own income tax, claimed in
  its return with the certificates the payers give. The shop needs what it was paid in a period,
  what that cost, and the tax withheld from it, with each statement to show for it.
* **Decision:**
  * **`payoutsReport(from, before)`** in the core adds up the statements imported in a period of
    at most 400 days. It reads them through each module's facade:
    * the payments module's settlements;
    * the logistics module's remittances, a courier's collected, charges and paid counted as
      gross, fees and net.
  * It reports:
    * the totals: statements, gross, fees, tax withheld and net;
    * each source, a gateway by its name or a courier as staff named it in any case, the most
      paid over first;
    * each month in the shop's time zone;
    * each statement that withheld tax, with its reference, in the order imported.
  * It reads 2,000 statements of each kind at most and says when a period has more. Owners,
    managers and accountants see it; apps need `read_orders`.
* **Consequences:**
  * Statements are dated by when they were imported, not by the payout's own date, which
    statements write in many ways. Imported promptly, they fall in the right month.
  * Sales tax withheld (TAX-03's second half) is not kept apart from income tax: no statement
    seen so far writes it apart.
  * The admin's page for the report comes next.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A table of payouts kept as statements are imported:** a second copy to keep in step. Both
    modules' statements are few, so adding them up when asked is cheap.

## ADR-494 · Payouts and tax withheld in the admin: a month or Pakistan's tax year, who paid, and the statements that withheld tax to download for the shop's return

* **Context:** The payouts report (ADR-493) was read through the Admin API alone. The shop's
  accountant reads it by the month, and by the tax year when the return is due. Pakistan's tax
  year runs from 1 July to 30 June.
* **Decision:**
  * **The cash page links to "Payouts and tax withheld"**, for owners, managers and
    accountants. The page reads the report for this month, last month, this tax year or last tax
    year, each from midnight on the first in the shop's time zone. It shows:
    * what was paid over, the tax withheld, the fees, and what customers paid;
    * each gateway or courier, with its statements, fees and tax;
    * each month, when the period has more than one;
    * each statement that withheld tax, with its reference and date.
  * **The statements that withheld tax download as a CSV file**, made in the browser: date in
    the shop's time zone, who paid, gateway or courier, reference, and the four amounts. Headings
    are in the admin's language.
  * A period with more statements than the report counts says so, and to choose a shorter one.
* **Consequences:**
  * The certificates gateways and couriers issue for the tax are not kept with the statements.
    The page reminds the shop to keep them.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Rolling periods, as analytics has:** tax is reckoned by month and by tax year, so rolling
    periods would not match the return.
  * **A CSV made by the core:** the page has every line already. Making it in the browser saves
    a round trip and an endpoint.

## ADR-495 · Invoice series: an order's invoice numbered in the shop's own series when first printed, counted afresh each tax year from 1 July, with no number skipped or given twice

* **Context:** Invoices went by their order's number (ADR-190). Order numbers are not an invoice
  series: drafts and cancelled orders take them too, and they never start again. FBR asks a
  registered seller's tax invoices to be numbered serially, and accountants expect a series a
  year with no gaps (TAX-05). Pakistan's tax year runs from 1 July to 30 June.
* **Decision:**
  * **An order's invoice takes the next number in the shop's series the first time it is
    printed,** written `INV/2026-27/00001`, and keeps it however often it is printed again.
    Printing an invoice is issuing it, through the same `orderDocument` query. A packing slip
    issues nothing.
  * **The series starts again at 1 each tax year,** the year of the day the invoice is issued in
    the shop's time zone.
  * **No number is skipped or given twice:**
    * a shop's invoices are issued one transaction at a time, under a lock of the shop's own;
    * the counter is taken in the same transaction as the invoice, so a print that fails gives
      its number back;
    * an order printed in two places at once is numbered once.
  * **A cancelled order without an invoice gets none.** One issued before it was cancelled keeps
    its number, and prints marked cancelled. Nothing prints, and nothing is issued, while an
    order of the batch is past the plan's limit.
  * The invoice prints its number and the day it was issued under the order's number and date,
    in English and Urdu. `Order.invoice` gives the number and when it was issued.
* **Consequences:**
  * A refund on an invoiced order should be a credit note in a series of its own. The counters
    are kept by kind for that, and credit notes come next.
  * Debit notes, for an invoiced order whose total rises, come later.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Issuing an invoice when the order is confirmed or shipped:** most cash-on-delivery orders
    are never invoiced, and confirmed orders are often cancelled. Numbering on print keeps the
    series to the invoices the shop actually gives.
  * **A Postgres sequence:** sequences skip numbers when a transaction rolls back.

## ADR-496 · Credit notes: money refunded on an order whose invoice was issued goes on a credit note numbered in a series of its own, printed against the invoice it corrects

* **Context:** Once an invoice is issued (ADR-495), it can't be changed. Money given back later
  has to go on a credit note: numbered in a series, naming the invoice it corrects, with the
  sales tax it takes back. Section 39 of the Sales Tax Act asks registered sellers for just
  this (TAX-05).
* **Decision:**
  * **A refund recorded on an order whose invoice was issued takes the next credit note number,**
    `CN/2026-27/00001`. It is numbered in the same transaction as the refund, by hand or through
    a gateway, under the shop's series lock. The series counts afresh each tax year, as
    invoices do.
  * **A refund before the invoice is printed gets no credit note:** the invoice, once printed,
    says what was refunded.
  * **Lock order:** the refund asks whether the order has an invoice before taking the series
    lock. A print holding that lock never waits on an order that already has its invoice, so a
    refund holding its order's row and a print never wait on each other.
  * `Refund.creditNote` gives the number and when it was issued.
  * **The CREDIT_NOTE document prints a page for each credit note of the orders asked for**, under
    the shop, the order and the invoice it corrects:
    * what was refunded;
    * the sales tax of it;
    * its value without the tax, for a shop with an STRN;
    * the refund's note.
    Orders without credit notes are refused.
* **Consequences:**
  * Debit notes, for invoiced orders whose totals rise in an edit, come later.
  * The admin's order page doesn't show the numbers, or print credit notes, yet.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A credit note for every refund:** a refund before any invoice corrects nothing that was
    issued.
  * **A credit note made when printed, as invoices are:** a refund on an invoiced order always
    needs one, and numbering it with the refund keeps the series in the order money went back.

## ADR-497 · Invoices and credit notes in the admin: an order's invoice number and its refunds' credit notes on its page, and credit notes printed beside slips and invoices

* **Context:** Invoices (ADR-495) and credit notes (ADR-496) were numbered and printed through
  the Admin API alone. Staff answering a customer, or the shop's accountant, need the numbers
  where the order is.
* **Decision:**
  * **An order's page says when its invoice was issued, and its number,** under when the order
    was placed. Each refund in "Payments and refunds" names its credit note when it has one.
  * **The print panel offers credit notes beside packing slips and invoices,** a page for each,
    on the paper and in the language chosen. The invoice's hint says the first print issues it.
    Once an invoice is printed, the order is read again so its number shows.
* **Consequences:**
  * Orders' lists don't show invoice numbers yet, and orders can't be searched by them.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A tab of invoices and credit notes on the order:** a line under the order's date and one on
    each refund say all there is, without another place to look.

## ADR-498 · Hatti's status page: Hatti's people post incidents and maintenance with a command, and the core serves them at /status, as JSON and to every shop's admin

* **Context:** When checkout, a courier or WhatsApp breaks, shops need to know it's Hatti's
  problem, that Hatti knows, and when it will be fixed. Otherwise every shop rings support at
  once. Planned downtime needs to be announced ahead. The launch checklist calls for a public
  status page (BIL-06).
* **Decision:**
  * **Incidents are kept by the trust module, which already holds what Hatti's people decide**
    (ADR-460). An incident belongs to no shop, so the application login only reads it, and only
    the system login, through Hatti's people's command, writes it.
  * **An incident says which of Hatti's parts it touches and how badly.** The parts are:
    storefronts, checkout, admin, online payments, couriers, WhatsApp, SMS and email. The
    impact is degraded or outage.
  * **Updates follow it until it ends.**
    * An incident goes investigating, identified, monitoring, resolved.
    * Maintenance goes scheduled, in progress, completed. Maintenance begun early begins then.
    * The last status ends it, and an ended incident takes no more updates.
    * An update may change the impact or the parts.
    * Titles and updates may come in Urdu too.
  * **The command is `pnpm --filter @hatti/core status-incidents`,** with `list`, `open` and
    `update`. Incidents begin as they are posted. Maintenance may be posted up to 60 days
    ahead.
  * **The core serves the page at `/status`, in English and Urdu, in Pakistan's time.** It shows:
    * the worst state overall;
    * each part's state, the worst of what goes on and touches it;
    * what goes on now, with every update, the latest first;
    * maintenance to come;
    * what ended in the last 14 days.
    Who posted an update isn't shown.
  * **`/status.json` has the same,** open to any origin, for monitors.
  * **Both stay up when the core is down.** The edge may keep them for 30 seconds, and serve them
    for a day after the core stops answering.
  * **`platformStatus` gives every member of a shop's staff, whatever their role:**
    * incidents going on;
    * maintenance going on or beginning within a day;
    * the status page's address.
    It is for the admin's banner.
* **Consequences:**
  * No probe posts or changes an incident yet. The page says only what Hatti's people post.
  * Shops aren't told on WhatsApp or by email. Telling every shop at once would cost more
    than a banner they see as they work.
  * There's no subscribing to updates, and no uptime history yet.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A hosted status service:** another vendor and login, and its page wouldn't be in Urdu
    or in Pakistan's time.
  * **A static page written to storage on each change:** it would stay up without the edge,
    but it would need writes to the bucket from the command, and the admin would still need
    the API.

## ADR-499 · The admin's banner: what goes on at Hatti above every page of a shop's admin, asked every minute, in the staff's language where Hatti wrote it in Urdu

* **Context:** Staff working in the admin are the first to notice when bookings fail or
  messages lag. A banner where they work tells them Hatti knows, before they ring support
  (ADR-498, BIL-06).
* **Decision:**
  * **Every page of a shop's admin asks `platformStatus` when it opens, and every minute after,**
    as often as the edge keeps the status page. The admin shows a banner under the header while
    anything goes on, or maintenance begins within a day. Nothing shows while all is well, or
    while Hatti can't be asked.
  * **Each incident's line gives:**
    * its title;
    * its status, how badly, and the parts it touches;
    * maintenance's times, in the shop's time zone;
    * what Hatti said last;
    * a link to the status page.
    In Urdu the admin shows Hatti's Urdu title and words where Hatti gave them, else its
    English.
  * **An outage has a red edge, and anything else an amber one.** Maintenance not yet begun is
    amber even when it will take things down.
  * The test core answers `PlatformStatus` with all well unless a test answers it, and leaves it
    out of what was sent. Pages' tests stay as they were.
* **Consequences:**
  * A staff member can't dismiss the banner. It goes when the incident ends.
  * Nothing else of the admin changes while Hatti is down: its pages fail as they would.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Asking only when the admin opens:** staff keep it open all day.
  * **Pushing incidents to open admins:** the admin has no channel from the core for them yet,
    and a minute is soon enough for news a person posts.

## ADR-500 · The shop's tax profile: its province, filer status and Tier-1 kept with its tax settings, and the admin guiding it through what an online seller must register

* **Context:** Since the Finance Act 2025, every online seller must register for sales tax.
  Couriers and gateways may refuse to serve one that hasn't. From 1 July 2026, the income tax
  they withhold from a seller not on FBR's Active Taxpayers List doubles: 2% online and 4% on
  cash on delivery, instead of 1% and 2%. Most small shops don't know where they stand (ONB-12,
  TAX-02).
* **Decision:**
  * **The tax module keeps three more things beside the NTN and STRN (ADR-190).** The shop says
    each one itself:
    * the province its business is registered in;
    * whether it is on the Active Taxpayers List: active, inactive or unknown, unknown taken as
      not on it;
    * whether it is a Tier-1 retailer.
    `taxSettingsUpdate` changes them with `write_settings`, recorded in the event and the audit
    log as before.
  * **`TaxSettings.withholding`** gives the percentages its filer status means couriers and
    gateways withhold.
  * **`TaxSettings.guidance`** gives the steps of registering, each DONE or TO_DO, in order:
    * an NTN;
    * sales tax registration;
    * the Active Taxpayers List;
    * the province.
    Notes follow for a shop like this one:
    * FBR's digital invoicing, for one with an STRN;
    * monthly returns, for a Tier-1 retailer, for whom the 2% collected is an advance.
  * **The admin's sales tax page shows the steps above its form, with what the shop is
    withheld,** and takes the profile in its registration section. Each step says how to do it:
    * IRIS for an NTN and returns;
    * an SMS of ATL and the CNIC to 9966 to check the list.
    It links to IRIS and says rules change each budget.
* **Consequences:**
  * Hatti doesn't check the filer status with FBR. It is what the shop says.
  * There are no referrals to tax advisers yet.
  * The rates are Hatti's constants, to change with each budget.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Asking FBR for the filer status:** FBR has no public API for the list, only its SMS
    service and pages.
  * **Guidance as a page of its own:** the steps belong beside the numbers they are about.

## ADR-501 · Products from a shop's Instagram posts: productsImport reads its posts as Instagram gives them, each a draft product made of what its caption says

* **Context:** Most Pakistani shops sell on Instagram before they have a store. Their
  catalogue is their posts: a photo, then a caption with the name, the price, the sizes or
  colours, and hashtags. Typing it all again is what keeps them from opening a store (ONB-04).
* **Decision:**
  * **`productsImport` takes format INSTAGRAM, read as JSON.** It accepts Instagram's API media
    list, with or without `data`, or `posts_1.json` from Instagram's own download of a shop's
    information. The posts go through the same import as Shopify's and WooCommerce's files
    (ADR-120, ADR-482). The admin's import page offers it, with a hint on what it reads, and
    takes `.json`.
  * **Each post with a caption becomes a draft product,** never on sale until staff check it.
    It is read from the caption:
    * **Title:** the caption's first line that says something, without emoji or hashtags.
    * **Description:** the rest of the caption.
    * **Price:** the amount after "Rs" or "PKR", before "/-", or after "Price". Where a caption
      names two and says sale, now or was, the lower is the price and the higher is compared at.
      Amounts under Rs 50, such as "3 piece", aren't taken. A caption without a price is priced
      at Rs 0 and said so.
    * **Sizes and colours:** from lines saying "Sizes:" or "Colours:". They become options with
      a variant for each combination.
    * **Tags:** its hashtags, up to 10.
    * **Eastern wear (CAT-08):** stitched or not, its pieces, its fabrics and its season.
  * **Photos come by address,** as the API gives them. A carousel's photos are taken, and its
    videos are not. Instagram's download keeps its photos inside its ZIP, so those posts are
    said to need their photos added by hand.
  * Instagram's download writes text as UTF-8 read as Latin-1, and it is mended.
  * The same title twice keeps a handle of its own.
* **Consequences:**
  * Hatti doesn't connect to a shop's Instagram account yet. The shop gives the file.
  * Captions written otherwise, or in Urdu script, give only their title and hashtags.
  * Reading them with the AI gateway comes later.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Instagram's API through Meta's login:** it needs Meta's app review for each permission,
    and the import should not wait on it.
  * **Asking the AI gateway for every caption:** it costs a call for each post, and gives
    different answers for the same caption. The rules give the same draft each time, and
    staff check it either way.

## ADR-502 · The store builder: a shop set up from a few lines saying what it sells, its kit, theme colour, About us page and home page SEO, leaving what it set

* **Context:** A new owner faces an empty store: collections, colours, pages and SEO, each
  behind its own screen. Most can say in two lines what they sell. That should be enough to
  start (ONB-03).
* **Decision:**
  * **`storeBuildPlan(description)` says what the lines would make of the shop, changing
    nothing.** `storeBuild` does it:
    * **Kit:** the starter kit (ADR-486) whose words the lines name most, such as lawn, kurtas,
      jhumkas, serum, chargers or achar; or the kit given. No kit when they name none.
    * **Colour:** the kit's accent, one buttons read well on, or the colour given. It is set in
      the main theme's `config/settings_data.json`, keeping its other settings, where the shop
      has a main theme.
    * **About us:** a page at `about-us` of the lines, a paragraph each, escaped.
    * **Home page SEO:** the shop's name as the title, and as the description the first sentence
      of 50 characters or more, else the lines, at most 160 characters.
  * **What the shop set already stays.** A page at `about-us` and home page SEO it set are left
    as they are. The kit, applied again, makes nothing twice. The payload says what was made and
    what was left.
  * `storeBuild` needs the scopes of everything it changes: products, navigation, pages, themes
    and settings. The admin's online store has a "Build from a description" tab for owners and
    managers. It previews the kind of shop, the colour, what search engines see and the page's
    paragraphs, then builds in a tap.
* **Consequences:**
  * The lines are read by their words, not by the AI gateway. A description in Urdu script names
    no kit, and the About page is still made of it.
  * There's no reading of an Instagram handle's bio yet. Products come by the Instagram import
    (ADR-501).
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A model writing the page and choosing the kit:** a call per shop for what its words
    already say, and a page in words the owner didn't write.
  * **Overwriting what the shop set:** a store built from two lines must not undo the work of a
    shop that has more than two lines' worth.

## ADR-503 · Auto-crop: a product's photos cropped to the product against a plain backdrop, in the shape asked, through the crops a shop makes, leaving busy photos

* **Context:** Most of a small shop's photos show a product on a sheet or a wall. They are taken
  from too far, off centre, in whatever shape the phone made. A grid of them looks untidy beside
  a brand's. Cropping each by hand (ADR-257) takes a minute a photo (CAT-21).
* **Decision:**
  * **`productAutoCropMedia(productId, aspectRatio, mediaIds)`** crops the product's photos to
    the product in each. It takes the photos given, or all its ready images, in one of four
    shapes: square (the default), 4:5, 3:4 or 4:3.
  * **The product is found on a copy at most 256 pixels a side.**
    * The backdrop is the colour of most of the photo's border: each channel's median, which a
      corner's shadow doesn't move.
    * If less than 85% of the border is within 40 of that colour, the photo is not on a plain
      backdrop. It is left as it is, as `BUSY_BACKGROUND`.
    * The product is the bounds of the rows and columns at least 1% of which differ from the
      backdrop, so dust is not the product. A photo with none is `NO_SUBJECT`.
  * **The frame:**
    * The product plus a margin of 8% of its longer side, widened or heightened to the shape and
      centred on the product.
    * Where that is larger than the photo, the frame is as large as the photo allows. It is
      moved to stay within the photo.
    * A frame that is the whole photo leaves it whole.
  * **The crops go through `productUpdateMedia`'s path:** checked, their clean copy made and
    kept beside the whole image's, the product's version bumped. The whole photo is kept, to be
    cropped again, by hand or in another shape. A crop the shop made is replaced.
  * The admin's product photos card has a shape and "Crop to the product". It then says how many
    photos were cropped and how many were left, and why.
* **Consequences:**
  * Background removal and lifestyle backgrounds wait for an image model behind the AI gateway.
    The other half of CAT-21's V1 is not done.
  * A product the colour of its backdrop, white kurta on a white sheet, is found in part or not
    at all. The shop crops that one by hand.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **libvips's own trim:** it takes the top-left pixel as the backdrop. A shadow there trims
    nothing, and a busy photo is trimmed to nonsense rather than refused.
  * **A model finding the product:** a call per photo for what a plain backdrop already tells.
  * **Padding photos to the shape:** that needs a new image made, with a colour that matches. A
    crop keeps the photo the shop took.

## ADR-504 · Partners: agencies open development stores, closed to shoppers until handed to their clients as any shop is handed over, and see every store they built, brought or work in

* **Context:** In Pakistan, agencies and freelancers set up many stores for others. They need to
  build a store before its owner has an account or has paid, and hand it over when it is ready.
  They need to see the stores they work for in one place. Collaborator access (ADR-487, ADR-488)
  lets them into a client's store, but not build one for a client to receive (PRT-01).
* **Decision:**
  * **Joining:** an account joins Hatti's partner programme from `/auth/partner` with a business
    name and, optionally, an https website. It is given a referral code of eight letters and
    digits that read apart, for the stores it brings (PRT-02). Changing its details keeps the code.
  * **Development stores:**
    * A partner opens one from `/auth/partner/stores`, as an owner opens a shop (ADR-145), and owns
      it while building it. The shop is marked `development` in the shop directory.
    * It counts against none of the five shops an account may own. A partner builds at most 20 at
      once.
    * Its storefront answers every page with Hatti's "This store opens soon" page, in English and
      Urdu: 503, never kept, not indexed. Scripts get the same in a line. Its staff's previews show
      the store as it is.
  * **Handing it over is the handover every shop has (ADR-104).**
    * The partner invites the client as a manager, the client adds a second factor, and the
      partner hands the shop to them.
    * The first handover of a development store opens it, in the same transaction. The shop is no
      longer `development`, the store is kept as transferred to the client, and an event republishes
      the shop's document.
    * The partner stays on as a manager, as a previous owner does, for the client to keep or remove.
  * **The dashboard** (`GET /auth/partner`) lists the partner's stores, newest first:
    * development stores, still being built or handed over;
    * stores referred by the partner;
    * clients' stores where the partner works through staff or collaborator access, though not as
      owner.
    Each store has its handle, the partner's role there and, for a collaborator, when their access
    ends. A shop the partner owns as a merchant is left out.
  * In the database, the identity login may only update a shop's `development` flag, and only from
    true to false. It may record in the outbox only the event saying a store was handed over.
  * The admin has a page for partners, linked from the shop choice. It has a join form, a form to
    open a development store, and the list of stores with their kind and role. A store's name opens
    it.
* **Consequences:**
  * A development store's checkout is not closed. Shoppers can't reach it with the storefront
    closed. Its staff may place test orders, and those count against the free plan's month as any
    shop's do.
  * Referred stores and revenue share come with PRT-02. The referral code is given now, so links
    made with it last.
  * Store transfer to someone with no account yet waits for them to sign up and accept the
    invitation. The handover itself is unchanged.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A separate transfer flow by email:** it would duplicate the handover's checks (a manager, a
    second factor, one owner throughout) for no gain.
  * **The storefront password for development stores:** a shop's password is its own to set and
    share, while a development store must stay closed until handed over, whatever its builder sets.
  * **A plan of its own for development stores:** billing stays as it is until shops are billed
    differently by kind.

## ADR-505 · Partners' revenue share: 20% of each plan invoice a store they brought pays, recorded as it is paid, owed until Hatti's people pay it into their bank account

* **Context:** Agencies and freelancers bring Hatti most of the stores it doesn't find itself.
  They will send merchants Hatti's way, and keep them there, if they earn from it while the
  store pays. Pakistan's partners are paid in rupees by bank transfer, not by card or PayPal
  (PRT-02).
* **Decision:**
  * **What a partner earns:** 20% of each plan invoice paid by a store they brought, for as long
    as it pays. A store they brought is one whose owner opened it through the partner's link, or
    a development store they handed to its client (ADR-504).
    * Message credit earns nothing.
    * A development store the partner still builds earns nothing: its plan is the partner's own
      to pay.
  * **The referral link** is `/sign-up?ref=<code>`. The admin keeps the code in the browser from
    the page the link opens until a shop is opened. That carries it across signing up and an
    email's link. Opening the shop sends the code, and `/auth/shops` records the store as the
    partner's, as referred.
    * A code that is no partner's is ignored. So is the opener's own code. Neither stops the shop
      opening.
    * A store has one partner at most, for good.
  * **Recording the share:**
    * As billing says an invoice is paid, the worker records the share through
      `identity.record_partner_earning`, in the shop's own transaction.
    * The function is SECURITY DEFINER and works only for the shop of the transaction asking, so
      the worker reads none of identity's tables (as with ADR-193).
    * The 20% is fixed in the function, so no caller can pass another. Each invoice earns once,
      so a re-delivered event changes nothing. The share is rounded down to the paisa.
  * **The partner's view:**
    * The dashboard (`GET /auth/partner`) adds their earnings: earned, paid out and still owed,
      and the latest 50 shares, each with its store, invoice and whether it has been paid.
    * The partner gives an account title and a Pakistani IBAN (PK, two digits, four letters, 16
      digits) to be paid into. The two are given together or not at all.
  * **Paying out:** Hatti's people run `partner-payouts list` to see who is owed what and into
    which account. Once the transfer is made, `partner-payouts pay <partner> <reference>` marks
    everything that partner was owed as paid, with the transfer's reference.
  * The admin's partner page shows the referral link, the earnings and their shares, and the
    payout account form.
* **Consequences:**
  * Shares are not taken back when Hatti refunds an invoice. Plan invoices are not refunded today
    (ADR-154), and when they are, the refund will need a clawback line.
  * Withholding tax on commissions paid to partners isn't deducted yet. Hatti's accountants deduct
    it when they pay, and record only the net.
  * Payouts are by hand, once a month, until there are enough partners for a bank's bulk
    transfer file.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Billing recording the share itself:** billing would have to read which partner brought a
    shop, and that is identity's.
  * **A share for a fixed term, such as 24 months:** a share for as long as the store pays keeps
    partners looking after their stores.
  * **Paying into a wallet to spend on Hatti:** partners run businesses, and they need rupees in
    the bank.

## ADR-506 · Push notifications for staff: Web Push to the browsers each member turns on, for the news their role does, encrypted and signed with node's crypto, once each

* **Context:** Shops run from their owners' and agents' phones. A COD order that waits an hour to
  be confirmed is more likely to be refused at the door, and a WhatsApp alert costs the shop
  credit and lands among its customers' chats. The admin is already installed on phones as a PWA
  (ADR-295), so the browser's own push service can reach it for free, with the admin closed
  (APP-03).
* **Decision:**
  * **What is pushed, and to whom:**
    * A new order, to owners, managers and confirmation agents.
    * An order held for review for its risk (at stage needs_review), to the same roles, in place
      of the new-order push.
    * A courier's statement of cash remitted, to owners, managers and accountants.
    * A variant fallen to the shop's low-stock threshold, and again when it runs out, to owners
      and managers. It goes with the WhatsApp alert's spell (ADR-157): the low-stock handler
      pushes it, since a spell is found once.
    * A part split from an order is nothing new, and isn't pushed.
  * **Subscribing:**
    * Each member of staff turns notifications on in each browser, from Your account, for the
