      kinds their role does. The admin asks the browser's permission, subscribes it with Hatti's
      VAPID public key, and sends the subscription (endpoint, P-256 key, auth secret) through
      `pushSubscribe`.
    * A subscription is kept by shop and endpoint in `messaging.push_subscriptions`, under the
      shop's row-level security. A browser another member signed in on before is theirs now.
    * Apps are refused. No scope is asked: a subscription is the member's own, and pushes go by
      role.
  * **Sending:**
    * The worker hears the events and pushes in each member's own language (English or Urdu),
      with a link into the admin to the order, the courier's statement or the product.
    * Recipients come from identity's `staff_phones` function, for the shop of the transaction
      alone (ADR-193).
    * Each push is recorded by its key in `messaging.push_deliveries`, so an event heard twice
      pushes once.
    * Orders' pushes are urgent; low stock's are normal.
  * **The protocol without a library:** messages are encrypted for each browser by RFC 8291
    (aes128gcm: ECDH on P-256, HKDF, AES-128-GCM), and requests are signed by RFC 8292 (an ES256
    JWT for the push service's origin, good for 12 hours). node's crypto has every part. The
    tests decrypt a message as a browser would and verify the signature.
  * **Forgetting subscriptions:** a subscription its push service answers 404 or 410 for is
    deleted. So is one that has failed 20 times in a row; one push that goes resets the count.
  * **Turning it on:** `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`, `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` and `VAPID_SUBJECT`, all three or
    none, for the API and the worker alike, made once by `pnpm --filter @hatti/core vapid-keys`.
    Without them nothing is pushed, and the admin says so.
  * **The admin's service worker** shows the push (title, body, the shop's icon, a tag so that a
    newer one replaces it) and opens the admin's own page when it is tapped. It focuses an open
    admin rather than opening another. A link that would leave the admin's origin opens the home
    instead.
* **Consequences:**
  * iPhones get pushes only once the admin is added to the home screen (iOS 16.4 and later). The
    card says so there instead of offering a button.
  * Changing the VAPID keys orphans every subscription: browsers subscribed with the old key.
    Each member turns notifications on again.
  * A push is sent once and not tried again, as the alerts are. One lost to a push service's
    outage is lost. The order is still on the home and the desk.
  * Pushes carry the shop's name, the order's number and amount, and a product's name, through
    Google's, Mozilla's and Apple's push services. The content is encrypted end to end, but each
    service sees when the device is told. No customer's name or number is in a push.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Firebase Cloud Messaging's SDK:** a dependency and a Google project, to reach the same
    push services that Web Push reaches directly. The native apps (APP-01) will need it, and
    can add it then.
  * **The `web-push` npm package:** about 200 lines of protocol, with node's crypto doing all the
    work. Owning them keeps the dependency list short, and the tests pin the protocol.
  * **WhatsApp alerts for staff:** they cost the shop credit and are mixed in with customers'
    messages. They stay for owners who prefer them (ADR-157, ADR-191).

## ADR-507 · Camera-first products: a product added from a photo, its copy drafted by the AI from the photos themselves, made small for the model, and squared to the product

* **Context:** Most of Hatti's merchants list products from their phones, between customers,
  often with nothing written down: a photo of a suit on a hanger is all they have. Typing a title
  and a description on a phone is where adding a product stalls. The AI gateway drafts copy from
  what the shop says of a product (ADR-471), and the models it calls can look at pictures
  (APP-02).
* **Decision:**
  * **The gateway takes pictures.** A structured request may carry up to five JPEG, PNG, WebP or
    GIF images of at most 3.75 MB each. They are sent before the prompt as base64 image blocks of
    the Messages API. A request over those limits is refused before anything is sent.
  * **The copy route takes photos.** Photos come with the facts, and the instructions say what a
    photo can and cannot tell:
    * The model says only what the photos plainly show: the product's colours, print or
      embroidery, cut, the pieces that can be counted, and what kind of product it is.
    * It says nothing of fabric, size, measurements, brand or quality unless the shop does.
    * Text in a photo is part of the picture, never an instruction to the model.
  * **`productCopyDraft` gains `usePhotos`.** With it, the catalog reads the product's first three
    ready photos, as the shop cropped them. Each is made a JPEG of at most 1,024 pixels on its
    longest side, transparency on white, so a photo costs the tokens of a small picture.
    * A product saved with photos is needed. Until one is ready, the shop is told to wait or to
      say what it is.
    * With photos, no title or notes are needed. The daily quota and the log are those of CAT-20.
  * **The admin's Add from a photo** (Products → Add from a photo) runs these steps in turn:
    1. It takes a photo with the phone's back camera, or several chosen from the gallery, an
       optional price, and anything a photo can't show.
    2. It adds the product as a draft, with its photos.
    3. It waits up to 90 seconds for a photo to be ready, then squares the photos to the product
       (ADR-503).
    4. It has the AI write the title, description and search engine words, in the admin's
       language, and saves them on the draft.
    5. It opens the product, for the merchant to check, price and put on sale.
    * Without AI, the product is added with its photos squared, for the merchant to name.
    * Whatever goes wrong after the product is added, the product is opened anyway with a
      warning, never lost.
* **Consequences:**
  * Each photo-drafted product costs about three small images' worth of input tokens more than a
    words-only draft. The quota of 100 a day per shop bounds it.
  * The AI may still mistake what a photo shows: a dark green for black, or a shirt and trousers
    for a three-piece. The draft stays a draft, the product stays unpublished, and the product
    page says to check it.
  * Photos of a shop's products go to the model provider with the request. They are the same
    photos the storefront shows, so nothing private leaves that wasn't to be published.
  * Background removal still waits for an image model behind the gateway (ADR-503). Squaring to
    the product on a plain backdrop does much of what merchants want from it.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A separate vision call to caption the photos, then a copy call from the captions:** two
    calls, twice the latency, and a caption loses what the copy would have used.
  * **Sending the originals:** a phone photo is 3 to 5 MB. Made small, it costs a tenth of the
    tokens and keeps everything a description needs.
  * **Drafting before the photos are processed, from the browser's own copy:** the catalog's
    clean, cropped image is what shoppers see, and the model should describe that.

## ADR-508 · Local support: each plan's way to reach Hatti's people, requests from the admin kept for them and answered with a command, and a help centre in English and Urdu

* **Context:** Pakistan's merchants expect to reach a person, on WhatsApp or by phone, in Urdu or
  English. The pricing (docs/product/03) promises each plan a way: Free the help centre, Starter
  WhatsApp, Growth priority WhatsApp, Pro priority WhatsApp and a call. Until now the admin said
  nothing about how to reach Hatti, and nothing kept what a shop asked (BIL-05).
* **Decision:**
  * **Each plan's tier is the billing module's constant.**

    | Plan | Way | Priority | Answered within |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | Free | Help centre and requests | 3 | 48 working hours |
    | Starter | WhatsApp | 2 | 24 working hours |
    | Growth | Priority WhatsApp | 1 | 8 working hours |
    | Pro | Priority WhatsApp and calls | 1 | 4 working hours |

  * **Hatti's own lines come from the host's configuration:** `SUPPORT_WHATSAPP` (a Pakistani
    mobile), `SUPPORT_PHONE`, `SUPPORT_EMAIL`, and `SUPPORT_HOURS` with `SUPPORT_HOURS_UR`, both or
    neither. `hattiSupport` gives any member of a shop's staff the shop's plan and tier and the
    lines its plan allows: the WhatsApp number from Starter, the phone line on Pro alone, the
    email and hours to all. No scope is asked: help is for everyone at the shop.
  * **A request from the admin is kept** in `billing.support_requests`, under the shop's tenant
    isolation:
    * Who asks is the signed-in member of staff, never an app. They give a topic, 10 to 2,000
      characters in their words, the language for the answer, and an optional Pakistani mobile to
      call back on.
    * The shop's plan when it asked sets the request's priority.
    * A shop has at most five requests open, so a stuck shop is answered rather than flooding the
      queue.
    * The shop closes a request when it is answered enough or no longer needed.
  * **Hatti's people answer with a command,** `pnpm --filter @hatti/core support-requests`, as
    for transfers (ADR-254):
    * `list` shows the requests waiting across shops, the most urgent then the oldest first, with
      the system login.
    * `answer sreq_… --by --text` answers one, in the shop's tenant. A request is answered once.
    * The answer, and who gave it, shows on the shop's Help page.
  * **The admin's Help page** (Help, for every role) has three parts:
    * A help centre of short articles in English and Urdu, searched in either language, kept with
      the admin so it works offline and on Free.
    * How to reach Hatti, as the plan allows: a wa.me link, a phone link, an email link, and the
      hours in the admin's language.
    * The request form, and the shop's last 20 requests with their answers.
* **Consequences:**
  * WhatsApp and calls happen outside Hatti: a conversation on Hatti's support number is not
    kept with the shop's requests. Requests are the record Hatti keeps.
  * Working hours are promised, not measured: nothing yet alerts Hatti's people to a request past
    its time. The priority-then-age order is what keeps the promise.
  * Without the support lines configured, shops see requests alone, which is honest for a host
    without a support team.
  * The help centre's articles ship with the admin: changing one is a release. Video tutorials
    (BIL-05) wait for a place to host them.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A support desk product (Zendesk, Freshdesk):** another account for each merchant, priced
    per agent in dollars, and English first. The requests table and the command do what Hatti's
    few people need now, and a desk can read the table later.
  * **Requests by WhatsApp alone:** Free has no WhatsApp, and a request typed in the admin
    carries the shop and its plan without asking.
  * **Answering from an internal web tool:** Hatti's people answer transfers and reports with
    commands already, and a web tool for Hatti's own people is its own project.

## ADR-509 · TCS, the third courier: bookings, tracking, cancellations and cities through its COD API, with the shop's own account and the city it ships from

* **Context:** TCS is Pakistan's largest courier by network, and many shops already hold an
  account with it. SHP-01 names PostEx, Leopards, TCS and Trax for the MVP. PostEx (ADR-149) and
  Leopards (ADR-162) were behind the courier adapter interface, and TCS was not.
* **Decision:**
  * **`TcsCourier` implements the adapter interface** against TCS's COD API
    (`api.tcscourier.com/production/v1/cod`, `TCS_URL` to point elsewhere):
    * Shops connect their own account with five credentials: the API client ID, user name,
      password, cost centre code and the city they ship from.
    * The client ID goes in the `X-IBM-Client-Id` header. The user name and password go in each
      request's body, never in an address.
    * A booking sends the parcel from the account's city to the city as TCS's list names it,
      overnight. It carries the weight in kilograms (half a kilo where none is known), the cash
      to collect in whole rupees with paisa rounded up, the order's name as the reference, and
      what is in the parcel.
    * A pickup code, where the shop gives one, is another cost centre of the same account.
    * TCS's consignment number, which it reports only in a sentence ("Your generated CN is:
      …"), is read from the end of that sentence. A booking without one is refused rather than
      kept without a tracking number.
    * Tracking asks about each parcel in turn and takes its delivery status, else the latest of
      its checkpoints. A parcel TCS does not know is left out. TCS refusing the account, or not
      answering, stops the round.
    * Cancelling uses `cancel-order`. The cities TCS delivers to are listed once a day for
      matching parcels' cities (ADR-233), and the last list is kept while TCS cannot give one.
  * **TCS's statuses map to Hatti's** through `logistics.courier_statuses` (migration 0239), as
    for the other couriers. A status no row names waits as one on its way.
  * **No pickups or load sheets through the API:** TCS takes them through its own portal and
    riders. `pickups` is null, so the admin offers none for TCS.
* **Consequences:**
  * Shops with a TCS account book, track and cancel from Hatti as with PostEx and Leopards.
    Courier rules (ADR-382) and rate cards (ADR-383) take TCS accounts like any other.
  * The adapter follows TCS's published API documentation and is tested against a stand-in.
    It must be tried against TCS's sandbox with a real account before shops rely on it, and
    statuses TCS says that no row maps need rows added as they are seen.
  * The city a shop ships from is a credential, typed by staff. A city TCS does not know refuses
    the booking with TCS's own message.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **TCS's newer token API:** it needs an OAuth client registered per merchant and is not yet
    offered to most accounts. The COD API is what TCS gives merchants today, and the adapter can
    change behind the same interface.
  * **Trax in the same change:** Trax's API is a different shape, and one courier per change
    keeps each reviewable. Trax follows.

## ADR-510 · Trax, the fourth courier: bookings by Trax's city IDs from the shop's pickup address, tracking, cancellations and cities through its merchant API

* **Context:** Trax is the last of the four couriers SHP-01 names for the MVP. PostEx
  (ADR-149), Leopards (ADR-162) and TCS (ADR-509) were already behind the courier adapter
  interface.
* **Decision:**
  * **`TraxCourier` implements the adapter interface** against Trax's merchant API
    (`sonic.pk/api`, `TRAX_URL` to point elsewhere):
    * Shops connect their own account with its API key and the ID of the pickup address they
      registered with Trax. The key goes in the Authorization header, never in an address.
    * A booking names the parcel's city by Trax's ID for it, from Trax's list of cities, kept a
      day; a city Trax does not list is refused before anything is booked.
    * The parcel is picked up from the account's pickup address, or another given as the pickup
      code, on the day it is booked in Pakistan.
    * It is booked by Trax's regular service in its Rush mode, with the weight in kilograms
      (half a kilo where none is known). Cash on delivery is in whole rupees, paisa rounded up,
      and an order paid ahead is booked as one with nothing to collect.
    * Trax answers `status` 0 for done. Its field errors are said as its own words.
    * Tracking asks about each parcel in turn and takes the latest status of its history, by its
      time. A parcel Trax does not know is left out, and Trax refusing the account stops the
      round. Cancelling uses `shipment/cancel`.
  * **Trax's statuses map to Hatti's** through `logistics.courier_statuses` (migration 0240).
    The parcel history helper reads Trax's and TCS's timestamps alike.
  * **No pickups or load sheets through the API:** `pickups` is null, as for TCS.
* **Consequences:**
  * The four couriers of SHP-01's MVP are bookable from Hatti with the shop's own accounts.
    Courier rules (ADR-382) and rate cards (ADR-383) take Trax accounts like any other.
  * As with TCS, the adapter follows Trax's published documentation against a stand-in. It
    must be tried on a real account before shops rely on it. Trax's service and mode IDs are
    fixed to its regular next-day service for now.
  * Couriers' own airway bills are still not fetched: Hatti prints its own labels (ADR-150).
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Choosing Trax's service and mode per booking:** no other adapter offers a choice yet, and
    the booking flow has nowhere to ask. A shop wanting another mode books it in Trax's portal.
  * **Naming the city by text, as PostEx takes it:** Trax books by its own city IDs. Its list,
    kept a day, is also what ADR-233 matches parcels' cities against.

## ADR-511 · Humane dunning: an overdue period's owner reminded the day it ends, with three days left and with one, each once, and the admin saying by when, the store open throughout

* **Context:** A paid plan whose period ends unpaid stays a week, then the shop is on Free
  (ADR-154), and its owner hears once the plan has ended (ADR-169). BIL-04 asks for a grace period
  in which the storefront never goes dark abruptly. The week of grace existed, and Free keeps the
  store open. But nothing told the owner during that week: the first word after the renewal's
  invoice was that the plan had gone.
* **Decision:**
  * **Three reminders while a period is overdue:** the billing sweep reminds the owner on the day
    the period ends, on the fourth day after (three days left) and on the sixth (one day left).
    The days are `BILLING_LIMITS.overdueReminderDays`.
    * Each is sent once. `billing.subscriptions.overdue_reminders` (migration 0241) counts those
      the period has had. A paid invoice's new period, or Free, sets it back to none.
    * A sweep that comes late, after a worker was down, sends one reminder for the days it
      missed, never a burst.
    * A reminder needs the renewal's open invoice. Free chosen for the period's end is no
      overdue period and is not reminded.
  * **`billing_invoice.overdue`** carries the invoice's name, the plan, the amount, the whole days
    left before Free and when that is. The worker tells the owner on WhatsApp at the shop's
    alerts number and by email, in their languages, at Hatti's cost, as for the other bills
    (ADR-169, ADR-195). The new `payment_overdue` message says the days left and that the store
    stays open either way. Its dedupe key is the invoice and the days left.
  * **The admin's billing page says by when:** `BillingSubscription.freeAt` is the period's end
    and the week of grace. The overdue banner reads "Pay its invoice by {date} to keep your plan;
    after that your shop is on Free, and its store stays open either way."
* **Consequences:**
  * An owner who missed the renewal's invoice hears up to four times before the plan goes: the
    invoice, then three reminders. The plan's end is never a surprise.
  * The storefront stays open through it all. Lapsing to Free locks only what Free does not
    include (ADR-263, ADR-264), as before.
  * The WhatsApp template `hatti_payment_overdue` must be approved by Meta like the other bill
    templates. Until then the email carries the reminder.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A reminder every day of the week:** too many for an owner who means to pay on payday. Three
    spaced ones say the same with less noise.
  * **Retrying a card on file:** Hatti keeps no cards. Auto-debit by wallets (BIL-01's remainder)
    would make reminders rarer, not unnecessary.
  * **A longer grace:** a week matches how Pakistani merchants are paid and pay. The reminders
    make the week enough, and paying after Free still brings the plan back (ADR-154).

## ADR-512 · Sales tax on Hatti's invoices: provincial sales tax on services at Hatti's registration, kept on each invoice with its authority, rate and number, and paid on top of the price

* **Context:** Hatti's plans and message credit are priced exclusive of provincial sales tax on
  services (docs/product/03). Its invoices must carry the tax and Hatti's registration numbers
  (BIL-02). The rate depends on the revenue authority: PRA 16%, SRB, KPRA, BRA and ICT 15% as
  standard (docs/research/03 §6.7). Until now Hatti's invoices carried none.
* **Decision:**
  * **Hatti's registration comes from the host's configuration:** `BILLING_TAX_AUTHORITY` and
    `BILLING_TAX_REGISTRATION`, both or neither, with `BILLING_TAX_RATE` where the rate is not the
    authority's standard one (a reduced rate for IT services, say), and `BILLING_NTN`. Without
    them, invoices carry no tax, as before.
  * **Each invoice keeps its tax** (migration 0242): the tax on the price less any credit, at the
    rate in basis points, halves of a paisa rounded up. It also keeps the authority and Hatti's
    number as they were when the invoice was made, so a later change of registration never
    rewrites an issued invoice. `amount`, what the shop pays and every payment is checked
    against, is now the price less the credit plus the tax.
  * **Origin-based:** the tax follows Hatti's registration, not the shop's province. Hatti
    registers where it is based, as the research advises, and charges that authority's rate on
    every invoice.
  * **What is not Hatti's revenue stays apart from it:**
    * Credit bought adds the credit alone to the wallet, never its tax.
    * A partner's share (ADR-505) is of the invoice less its tax. `billing_invoice.paid` carries
      the tax for it.
  * **Shown where the shop sees its bills:**
    * The invoice's page lists the price, any unused period credited, the sales tax with its
      authority and rate, the total, and Hatti's registration and NTN.
    * The admin says how much of an open invoice is tax.
    * `BillingInvoice` gains `tax`, `taxRate`, `taxAuthority` and `taxRegistration`.
* **Consequences:**
  * Turning the registration on raises what shops pay by the rate, as the pricing always said it
    would. Invoices already issued keep their amounts.
  * Destination-based tax, charging each shop its province's rate, needs Hatti registered in
    every province and the shop's province from its tax profile. The invoice already stores the
    authority per invoice, so that change is in how the authority is chosen, not in the data.
  * Hatti files and pays the tax with its authority outside Hatti's own systems. Monthly totals
    by authority can be read from the invoices.
  * Get an adviser's sign-off before turning it on, as the research notes cross-province
    disputes.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Prices inclusive of tax:** the pricing page promises prices exclusive of it. Inclusive
    prices would cut Hatti's revenue by the rate wherever it registers.
  * **A tax line on the payment rather than the invoice:** the invoice is the tax document. Its
    tax, authority and number must not change once issued.

## ADR-513 · The merchant admin's edge headers: a content security policy that runs only the admin's own scripts and Google's and Facebook's sign-in, written to `_headers` by each build with HSTS, framing refused and the camera alone allowed

* **Context:**
  * The admin keeps its session's tokens in the browser's storage, where any script on its
    origin could read them. ADR-265 left the admin's origin a strict content security policy
    "with the infrastructure".
  * ADR-164 added Google's sign-in script, and ADR-419 added Facebook's SDK for Embedded Signup.
    Neither was allowed for anywhere, and no header was sent at all: Vite served the admin in
    development alone.
  * The edge is Cloudflare (docs/architecture/10). Its static hosting reads headers from a
    `_headers` file beside the files it serves.
* **Decision:**
  * **One module says the headers:** `apps/admin-web/src/edge/headers.ts`. Each build writes them
    to `dist/_headers`, and `vite preview` sends them, so the built admin is tried under the same
    policy. `vite dev` sends none, because React's refresh runs inline there.
  * **Scripts:**
    * Allowed: the admin's own origin, `https://accounts.google.com/gsi/client` and
      `https://connect.facebook.net`.
    * Nothing inline and nothing evaluated: no `'unsafe-inline'` and no `'unsafe-eval'`. The
      built page loads one module script by its address, and the bundle uses neither `eval` nor
      `new Function`.
    * A test finds every `script.src` the admin's source sets and checks the policy allows each
      one, so a new third-party script fails the build's tests until the policy names it.
  * **The rest of the policy:**
    * Styles may be inline, because React's style props and Google's button set them. The tab a
      document is printed in is the admin's own, and inherits the policy, so styles and fonts
      from Google Fonts are allowed for the documents' fonts.
    * Images, media and connections may go to any `https:` address. Photos and files go
      straight to storage by presigned addresses wherever storage is, and come back from the
      image route.
    * Frames may show any `https:` page: the theme editor frames the shop's storefront at its own
      domain (ADR-325), and Google and Facebook frame their sign-in.
    * `object-src` and `base-uri` are `'none'`. Forms post only to the admin's origin.
    * No one may frame the admin (`frame-ancestors 'none'`, and `X-Frame-Options: DENY` for older
      browsers). Insecure requests are upgraded.
  * **Other headers on every path:**
    * HSTS for two years, with subdomains, ready for the preload list.
    * `nosniff`.
    * `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, so the shop's addresses inside the admin never leave as
      referrers.
    * `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups`, because Google's and Facebook's
      sign-in answer from pop-ups the admin opens.
    * A permissions policy that allows the camera (barcodes and photos) on the admin's origin and
      nothing else: microphone, location, payment and USB are refused.
  * **Caching:**
    * The page and `sw.js` are asked for again every time, so a new build reaches staff at once.
    * `/assets/*`, named by content, is kept for a year and marked immutable.
    * The service worker never precaches `_headers`, because ADR-295's rules keep only the
      admin's own files.
* **Consequences:**
  * Script injected into the admin is refused. Checked in Chromium against `vite preview`: the
    sign-in page renders with no violation, and an inline script added to the page does not run.
  * A third-party script the admin starts loading needs its address in the policy and in this
    ADR's test.
  * `connect-src https:` would let script already running send data anywhere. The policy's
    guard is that no foreign script runs, not where data goes. Narrowing connections to
    storage's own origin waits for that origin to be known when the admin is built.
  * Responses from `/auth` and the Admin API are the core's, and are not documents. The edge's
    worker that routes them to the core passes them through without these headers.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Nonces on a server-rendered page:** the admin is a static page that the edge and the
    service worker serve from cache, so there is nothing to put a fresh nonce in. With no inline
    script, nonces protect nothing more.
  * **The refresh token in an HTTP-only cookie:** this is ADR-265's other answer. It needs
    `/auth` to share a site with the admin and CSRF defences on every refresh. The policy keeps
    foreign script out first. Moving the refresh token into a cookie can still come later.
  * **A `<meta>` policy in index.html:** a meta tag cannot carry `frame-ancestors`, cannot report
    violations, and would not cover the service worker's script.

## ADR-514 · The admin keeps the shop's last data for use offline: Home, the orders and customers lists' first pages, the orders and customers opened and the account, in the browser's storage for the session that read them, shown offline with how old they are and forgotten on signing out

* **Context:**
  * ADR-295 made the admin open offline, but showed none of the shop's data there. Keeping
    orders and customers in the browser's storage was left for later: shops share phones, and
    the session's own keeping of data had to be thought through first.
  * Staff lose their connection in markets, warehouses and on the road. A packer who opens the
    admin there finds a page saying only that they are offline.
* **Decision:**
  * **What is kept** (`src/offline/kept-data.ts`):
    * Home's counts and stock.
    * The first page of the orders and customers lists, as last searched.
    * The orders and customers opened.
    * The account and its shops (`/auth/me`), without which no shop opens.
    * At most 40 queries and about 1.5 MB, the newest first. Nothing else the admin reads is
      kept: settings, reports and other pages are left out.
  * **Kept for the session that read it:**
    * Saved in the browser's storage under the session's id, a second after the last query that
      succeeded.
    * Put back into the query cache when the admin opens, only for that same session. Each query
      is restored as old as its data.
    * A different session on the same phone, or none, finds nothing, and what was kept is
      forgotten at once.
    * Signing out forgets it, here or in another tab.
    * Data older than three days is not shown.
  * **Offline:**
    * The admin tells its queries at once that the browser is offline. They wait for a
      connection instead of failing over the data they show.
    * Home, the lists and the order and customer pages show what was kept, with "As Hatti last
      saw it, 2 hours ago." The notice above every page says Hatti shows what it last saw.
  * **Online:** each kept query is stale, so its page fetches it again as it opens. Nothing old
    is shown once a connection is back.
  * Saving changes offline stays as ADR-295 left it: the work waits for a connection.
* **Consequences:**
  * Staff can read the orders they were working on, and Home's counts, with no connection.
  * The data is what the API gave that member. A confirmation agent's kept customers have their
    numbers masked as the API masks them (ADR-027). It sits in the phone's browser storage, where
    anyone with the unlocked phone could read it. The limits, the three days and signing out keep
    that small. Staff who share a phone should sign out when they hand it on.
  * Only what staff opened is kept. An order never opened online cannot be read offline.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **TanStack Query's persister packages:** they keep the whole cache unless told otherwise, and
    know nothing of sessions. The few dozen lines here keep what is chosen, for one session.
  * **IndexedDB:** it holds more, but the kept data is small, and synchronous storage lets the
    cache be filled before the first render, with no flash of a loading page.
  * **The service worker caching the API's answers:** the Admin API is GraphQL over POST, which
    the Cache API does not keep. The worker would also have to know which session a response
    belongs to. ADR-295 keeps the worker out of the shop's data.

## ADR-515 · Automatic discounts: a percentage or an amount off the items, or free delivery, given without a code to every cart and checkout that qualifies; the one taking most off the items applies with free delivery beside it, and with a code only where each combines with codes, else whichever takes more

* **Context:**
  * Codes (ADR-062) need the shopper to know and type one. A shop running an Eid sale wants it
    taken at the cart by everyone, as Shopify's automatic discounts are.
  * The feature catalog plans automatic discounts, buy X get Y, tiers and combinations for V1
    (CHK-06).
  * Until now a cart and a checkout held one code at most, and nothing else took anything off.
* **Decision:**
  * **What they are** (`pricing.automatic_discounts`, migration 0243):
    * A title shoppers see ("Eid sale").
    * What it gives: a percentage or an amount off the order's items, or free delivery, checked
      as codes' offers are.
    * An optional minimum for the items, and the dates it runs between.
    * Whether a code may be used with it.
    * A shop keeps 25 at most, running, scheduled or ended.
    * The Admin API makes, lists, changes and deletes them under the discount scopes.
  * **Which apply** (`chooseDiscounts`, a pure function in pricing). Of those that run and whose
    minimum the items reach:
    * The one taking most off the items applies, the oldest of equals.
    * The oldest that gives free delivery applies beside it.
  * **With a code:**
    * The code is checked as before.
    * It applies beside the automatic discounts where every one applied combines with codes.
    * Where one doesn't, the code applies alone, unless the automatic discounts take more off
      the items. On a tie the code wins, because the shopper chose it.
    * A code set aside stays in the cart. Shopify's cart marks it as not applicable. The checkout
      says it can't be used with the automatic discount, which takes more off.
    * Each takes its share of the items as they come before any discount. Together they take no
      more than the items.
  * **Cart and checkout:**
    * The cart's JSON gains `automaticDiscounts`, each with its title, kind, value and amount.
      `totalDiscount` counts the code and the automatic discounts together. The storefront gives
      them to Liquid as Shopify's `discount_application`s of type `automatic`.
    * Hatti Base lists them with what they take off. Free delivery by an automatic discount reads
      "delivered free", not "with the code".
    * The checkout page shows the automatic discount's row beside the code's. Its digest changes
      when an automatic discount applied changes, so a page shown before is shown again.
  * **Orders:**
    * Placing an order recomputes the discounts in its own transaction.
    * The order keeps the titles of the automatic discounts it was placed with
      (`orders.automatic_discounts`) beside its codes.
    * Only a code applied has its use counted. Automatic discounts have no limit on uses.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop runs a sale without handing out codes. Shoppers see it in the cart, on the checkout
    page and on the order's page.
  * Every cart read asks for the shop's running automatic discounts: one indexed query on a
    small table.
  * Discounts still apply to the whole order. Products or collections, buy X get Y and tiers need
    each line's share kept, and come next with their own ADR. The admin's screen for automatic
    discounts is the next slice.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Codes marked automatic in `pricing.discount_codes`:** an automatic discount has no code, no
    limit on uses and no once a customer. A table of its own keeps both kinds' rules plain.
  * **Shopify's combination classes (order, product and shipping discounts, each choosing what
    it combines with):** product discounts don't exist yet. One flag, "combines with codes",
    covers what shops can make today, and the classes can grow from it.
  * **Every running automatic discount applying at once:** two sales the shop forgot to end would
    stack. The best one applying is what shoppers expect.

## ADR-516 · The admin's automatic discounts, on the discounts page below the codes: each with what it gives in a line and whether it runs; started with a title shoppers see, what it gives, a minimum, dates and whether codes go with it; ended at once or deleted

* **Context:** ADR-515 gave shops automatic discounts through the Admin API. Merchants run their
  shops from the admin, whose discounts page held codes alone (ADR-276).
* **Decision:**
  * **Where:** below the codes on the same page, under "Automatic discounts". A line says that
    every order that qualifies gets them in the cart without a code, and that the one taking most
    off applies with free delivery beside it.
  * **Each discount:**
    * Its title as shoppers see it, its summary from the API ("10% off orders of Rs 3,000 or
      more; with codes"), and whether it runs, starts later or has ended.
    * When it starts or ends, in the shop's time zone.
  * **Starting one:**
    * A title, required.
    * What it gives: a percentage off, an amount off or free delivery.
    * A minimum, whether codes can be used with it, and the days it starts and ends, read as the
      shop's days as codes' are.
    * The API's problems are shown under the form by field.
  * **Ending and deleting:** "End it now" sets its end to now. Delete asks first, saying orders
    placed with it keep its title.
  * **Who:** owners, managers and marketers, as for codes (`write_discounts`). The page is not in
    the other roles' sections.
  * In English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop starts an Eid sale from a phone without making a code. The cart, checkout and order
    say it by its title.
  * Changing an automatic discount's value or minimum in place is through the API only for now.
    Ending one and starting another does the same from the admin.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A page of its own:** shops think of codes and sales together, and the rule between them
    (ADR-515) reads best side by side.
  * **Editing in place:** a discount that runs while its value changes would give carts opened
    a minute apart different totals. Ending one and starting the next keeps each order's discount
    plain, as Shopify suggests for running sales.

## ADR-517 · Discounts for some products or collections: a code or an automatic discount names up to 100 of each, and takes a percentage or an amount off only their items, its minimum being what they come to; free delivery stays for the whole order

* **Context:**
  * Codes (ADR-062) and automatic discounts (ADR-515) took something off a whole order's items.
  * Shops in Pakistan run sales on part of what they sell: 20% off the lawn collection, Rs 500
    off khussas, a code for one new product. Shopify's basic discounts are "for specific products
    or collections" as often as for the whole order.
* **Decision:**
  * **What it names:** `productIds` and `collectionIds` on both, in the pricing module's tables,
    up to 100 of each, as the catalog's IDs. Naming neither is for the whole order, as before.
    The Admin API takes and gives them as public IDs on `DiscountCode`, `AutomaticDiscount` and
    their inputs.
  * **Checked:**
    * Each must be one of the shop's own, asked through the catalog's facade
      (`productsAndCollectionsIn`), never its tables.
    * An ID that is not found, or is no product's or collection's, is a `NOT_FOUND` error at its
      place in the list.
    * A product or collection deleted later stays on the list and matches nothing.
  * **Which items:** a line is the discount's when its product is named or is in a named
    collection, smart collections included. Checkout asks the catalog which of the named
    collections the cart's products are in (`collectionsOfProductsIn`), one query, and only when a
    discount names a collection.
  * **What it takes:**
    * A percentage of those items.
    * An amount off once an order, no more than those items come to.
    * Its minimum is what those items come to, as Shopify's is.
    * Automatic discounts still compete by what each takes off (ADR-515), now each on its own
      items. Together they take no more than the order's items.
  * **Free delivery:** stays for the whole order. Naming items for it is refused, and making a
    discount free delivery forgets what it named.
  * **A code for none of the cart:** refused with "isn't for the items in your cart", in English
    and Urdu, and counted as a try (ADR-063). A cart says it does not apply.
  * **Orders:** keep the discount as one amount, as before. Returns and tax share it over the lines
    by their totals (ADR-096), not by which lines it was for.
  * **The abandoned-checkout offer** (ADR-426): it knows only what the items came to, so a code
    for some items is not offered.
* **Consequences:**
  * "20% off the Eid collection" and "Rs 500 off this product" work in the cart, at checkout and
    on the order, beside codes and other automatic discounts by the rules of ADR-515.
  * A cart's discounts need one more query when a discount names collections.
  * The admin's discounts page does not yet choose products and collections; ADR-518 will.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Discounts kept on each line:** the order would know which line had what off, as Shopify's
    allocations do. That changes how orders, refunds, invoices and returns read their money.
    One amount an order is what they all read today, and a later ADR can split it.
  * **An amount off each item:** Shopify offers it, but shops here think of "Rs 500 off" as off
    the order. Once an order keeps the sum plain at checkout.
  * **Collections copied onto the discount as product lists:** that is wrong as soon as a smart
    collection's products change. Asking at checkout follows the collection as it is.

## ADR-518 · The admin's discounts for some products or collections: a new code or automatic discount applies to the whole order or to products found by name and collections chosen from the shop's, shown as chips taken off with a tap; free delivery has no such choice

* **Context:** ADR-517 let codes and automatic discounts be for some products or collections
  through the Admin API. The admin's discounts page made them for whole orders only (ADR-276,
  ADR-516).
* **Decision:**
  * **Where:** in both forms, under what the discount gives, an "Applies to" choice: the whole
    order, or some products or collections.
  * **Choosing:**
    * Products are found by name, as menus find them (ADR-291), and added with a tap; one
      already chosen is not offered again.
    * Collections are chosen from the shop's own, asked for only once "some" is chosen.
    * What is chosen shows as chips, collections marked so, each taken off with its button.
    * A line says the discount takes off only these items, its minimum is theirs, and free
      delivery is always for the whole order.
  * **Checked:**
    * "Some" with nothing chosen is stopped before it is sent, saying to choose one or make it
      for the whole order.
    * The API's errors on the lists are named "Applies to".
  * **Free delivery:** the choice is hidden while the discount gives free delivery, and nothing of
    it is sent.
  * **The list:** each discount's line from the API says what it is for ("Rs 500 off 2 products
    and 1 collection").
  * In English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop makes "20% off the Eid edit" or "Rs 500 off khussas" from a phone.
  * Which products and collections an existing discount is for is not listed by name, nor
    changed in place. A shop ends one and starts another, as for its value (ADR-516).
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A picker showing the whole catalog:** shops with thousands of products scroll forever on a
    phone. Finding by name is what the drafts and menus already do.
  * **Choosing variants:** Shopify allows it, but shops here run sales on products and
    collections. Variants would add a step for little gain.

## ADR-519 · Buy X get Y: a code or an automatic discount gives, in each full group of X + Y of its items, the Y cheapest at a percentage off, free unless it says less; spending tiers are automatic discounts with rising minimums

* **Context:**
  * "Buy 2 get 1 free" and "buy one, get the second half off" are how Pakistan's fashion and
    beauty shops run their biggest sales. Shopify calls these "Buy X get Y".
  * Codes and automatic discounts (ADR-062, ADR-515) took a share or an amount off items, now for
    some products or collections (ADR-517), or gave free delivery.
* **Decision:**
  * **A fourth kind:** `buy_x_get_y`, for codes and automatic discounts alike. It has:
    * `buyQuantity` and `getQuantity`, 1 to 100 each;
    * `percentage`, how much off the items given: 100, free, unless it says less.
  * **Which items:** those it is for, its products and collections or any (ADR-517), count and
    are given alike.
  * **What it gives:**
    * Every full group of X + Y of its items gives Y.
    * The cheapest items are given, each at its own price, rounded half up, as Shopify gives the
      lowest-priced items.
    * Six items for buy 2 get 1 make two groups, so two items are free.
  * **With others:**
    * Among automatic discounts it competes by what it takes off now, as any does (ADR-515).
    * One that gives nothing yet, too few of its items, is not applied.
    * As a code, too few of its items is refused: "needs 3 of its items in your cart", in English
      and Urdu.
    * A minimum, if it has one, is what its items come to.
  * **Changing one:** a percentage alone changes how much the given items take off and keeps it
    buy X get Y. Giving another kind makes it that kind and forgets its quantities.
  * **The cart's JSON:** says the kind, and the amount it takes off now as its value. Themes
    showing a discount's value read it as an amount off.
  * **Orders:** keep the discount as one amount, as before (ADR-517).
  * **The abandoned-checkout offer** (ADR-426) does not offer a buy X get Y code: its message
    names a percentage or an amount.
  * **Tiers** ("5% off Rs 3,000, 10% off Rs 5,000") need no kind of their own. The shop makes
    one automatic discount for each step, each with its minimum, and the one taking most off the
    order applies (ADR-515).
* **Consequences:**
  * "Buy 2 get 1 free on lawn" works in the cart, at checkout and on the order, and through the
    Admin API.
  * The admin's forms don't yet make buy X get Y; ADR-520 will.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Different items bought and given** ("buy a kurta, get a dupatta free"): Shopify allows it,
    but sharing one set keeps the groups plain and covers the sales shops run here. A later ADR
    can add a second set.
  * **Giving the dearest items:** that is kinder to shoppers but costs the shop more than it
    meant. The cheapest is what Shopify and the shops' own posters mean.
  * **A cap on uses an order:** every full group gives, as shops expect from "buy 2 get 1". A cap
    can come later if shops ask.

## ADR-520 · The admin's buy X get Y: both discount forms offer items for others bought, with items bought and given, two for one unless changed, and how much off those given, free unless changed; for the whole order or some products and collections

* **Context:** ADR-519 added buy X get Y to codes and automatic discounts through the Admin API.
  The admin's forms offered a percentage, an amount or free delivery (ADR-276, ADR-516).
* **Decision:**
  * **What it gives:** both forms offer a fourth choice, "Items for others bought".
  * **Its fields:**
    * Items bought and items given, side by side, 2 and 1 unless changed.
    * How much off the items given, 100% unless changed.
    * A line says the cheapest items of each group are given, and 100% off makes them free.
  * **Which items:** the "Applies to" choice (ADR-518) says which items count and are given: the
    whole order's, or some products and collections.
  * **Checked:** the API's errors on the quantities are named "Items bought" and "Items given".
  * **The list:** each discount's line from the API says what it gives ("Buy 2, get 1 free of 1
    collection").
  * In English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** a shop starts "Buy 2 get 1 free on lawn" from a phone, as an automatic
  discount or as a code.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A separate form for buy X get Y:** it shares the title, dates, minimum, items and, for a
    code, its limits with the others. One form with one more choice keeps them together.
  * **Presets ("Buy 1 get 1", "Buy 2 get 1"):** two plain fields cover every case and read just
    as clearly.

## ADR-521 · A draft order takes one of the shop's discount codes: checked against its items as checkout checks a cart's, setting what comes off or making delivery free, followed as the items change, and counted as a use when the draft becomes an order, in the same transaction

* **Context:**
  * Staff take orders in WhatsApp and Instagram chats as drafts (ADR-031). A draft took an
    amount off typed by hand.
  * Shops advertise codes in those same chats: "use EID10". The staff member then had to work
    out 10% of the items, and the code's limits never knew.
* **Decision:**
  * **On the draft:** `discountCode` on its input and on `DraftOrder`, one code at a time, as the
    shop wrote it. It replaces an amount off typed by hand, and giving both is refused.
  * **Checked:**
    * Against the draft's items, through the pricing module's facade, as checkout checks a cart
      (ADR-063, ADR-517, ADR-519): its dates, minimum, uses, items and groups.
    * Its collections are asked of the catalog's facade.
    * A code that takes nothing is refused with why, on the input's `discountCode`.
  * **What it sets:** the draft's discount, or its delivery charge to nothing for a free-delivery
    code. When the items change, the discount follows them. Removing the code takes the discount
    off.
  * **Placed:**
    * When the draft becomes an order, whether staff complete it or the customer confirms it
      through its link (ADR-114), the code is checked again. Its dates or uses may have changed.
    * The order is placed with the code, and the code's use is counted in the same transaction,
      inside a savepoint.
    * Its uses may have run out meanwhile, or the customer, known now by their number, may have
      used a code that is once a customer already. Then the order is undone, the draft stays
      open, and staff are told why.
  * **Orders placed by staff without a draft** keep their amount off, as before. A draft is how
    staff take an order with a code.
* **Consequences:**
  * "EID10" works in a chat as on the storefront, and counts against the same limits.
  * The orders module now depends on the pricing module's facade, as checkout does.
  * The admin's draft page doesn't yet take a code; ADR-522 will.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Counting the use when the code is typed on the draft:** a draft that is never placed would
    use the code up. Counting with the order is what checkout does.
  * **Codes on orderCreate as well:** staff placing an order directly agree its price there and
    then. A draft is where a chat's code belongs, and it is one step away.

## ADR-522 · The admin's draft page takes a discount code beside the amount off: while a code is given the amount is the code's to set and is not asked, the draft shows its discount by the code, and emptying the code takes it off

* **Context:** ADR-521 let a draft take one of the shop's discount codes through the Admin API.
  The admin's draft form asked for an amount off alone (ADR-277, ADR-334).
* **Decision:**
  * **On the form:** for a new draft and an open one, a "Discount code" field under the delivery
    charge and the amount off. Codes are typed in capitals. A line says the code works out what
    comes off and counts as used when the order is placed.
  * **With a code:** the amount off is not asked, since the code sets it. Saving sends the code
    alone.
  * **Taken off:** emptying the code brings back the amount, empty, and saving sends the amount
    typed and takes the code off.
  * **On the draft:** its discount reads "Discount (EID10)" when a code set it.
  * **Refused:** the API's refusals are shown under the form, named "Discount code", with why:
    the code has ended, isn't for these items, and so on.
  * In English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** a staff member types the code the customer sent in the chat, and the draft
  works out the rest.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Choosing from the shop's codes:** a shop may have thousands of codes, and the customer
    names theirs. Typing it is quicker and what checkout asks of shoppers.

## ADR-523 · Plans gate more of what the pricing leaves out: custom apps, automations and the abandoned checkout reminder from Starter, cashback and Meta's conversions API from Growth; refused when made, connected or turned on, those already are kept

* **Context:**
  * The pricing (docs/product/03-pricing-and-business-model.md) gives each plan more than room
    for staff, locations and orders. Free leaves out custom apps, automations, abandoned checkout
    recovery and conversion APIs. Starter leaves out loyalty and the conversions API.
  * Until now, plans gated only a domain of the shop's own and payment gateways (ADR-264). A shop
    on Free could use everything else that Starter and Growth are priced for.
* **Decision:**
  * **Four more features of a plan**, kept beside its limits in the billing module:
    * `customApps`: making custom apps (ADR-395). Starter and above.
    * `automations`: turning a recipe on (ADR-425), and the abandoned checkout reminder (ADR-393),
      with the offer that follows it (ADR-426). Starter and above.
    * `loyalty`: turning cashback on (ADR-453). Growth and above.
    * `conversionsApi`: connecting Meta's dataset (ADR-143). Growth and above.
  * **Asked as ADR-264 asks:** each module asks `PlanAllowance.excludes` before it makes, connects
    or turns one on. A plan that leaves the feature out is refused with its name, such as "The
    Free plan doesn't include automations: choose a bigger plan to turn it on".
  * **What is already on is kept.**
    * An app made, a recipe or reminder on, or a dataset connected on a bigger plan goes on
      working after a move to a smaller one.
    * It can still be changed or turned off. Once off, it is turned on again only on a plan that
      includes it.
  * **`BillingPlan`** says which of the four each plan includes, for the admin's plan cards.
  * **Back in stock and COD to prepaid** are automations, and are gated with them. Hatti sends
    them from its own number, but they are recipes the pricing counts as automations.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop sees in its plan what the pricing promises, and upgrading is how it gets more.
  * Nothing stops working for a shop that moves down. A shop can't turn a feature off and on to
    get it back on a plan that leaves it out.
  * Free and Starter can't connect Meta's pixel, which shares the dataset's connection with the
    conversions API. The pricing gives Starter the pixel alone; it waits until the pixel can be
    connected on its own.
  * The admin's plan cards don't yet list the four; ADR-524 will.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Turning features off when a shop moves to a smaller plan:**
    * Automations would stop sending mid-campaign, and apps an integrator relies on would break.
    * Domains and gateways already stay connected on a move down (ADR-264). Features keep the
      same rule.
  * **Gating in the GraphQL resolvers:** the modules' services are what the worker and other
    callers use. The check belongs where the feature is turned on, as ADR-264 put it.

## ADR-524 · The admin's plan cards say which of the features a plan gates each includes: automations and abandoned checkout reminders, cashback, Meta's conversions API and custom apps, beside its limits, domain and payments

* **Context:**
  * Plans now gate custom apps, automations, cashback and Meta's conversions API (ADR-523).
  * The admin's plan cards listed only a plan's orders, staff, locations, payments and domain. An
    owner choosing a plan couldn't see what the rest came with.
* **Decision:**
  * Each card lists the four, after the domain line, as the payments and domain lines do: what the
    plan includes ("Cashback"), or what it leaves out ("No cashback").
  * They are listed in the order an owner looks for them: automations and abandoned checkout
    reminders first, then cashback, Meta's conversions API, and custom apps.
  * In English and Urdu, from the plans the API gives (`BillingPlan`), never written into the
    admin.
* **Consequences:**
  * An owner sees what moving up gets them before choosing.
  * A feature a plan refuses says which plan the shop is on, and the cards say which plans include
    it.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Listing only what each plan includes:** Free's card would be shorter, but cards would be
    harder to compare line by line. The existing lines say "No" too.
  * **Disabling the switches on the automations, apps and Meta pages for a plan without them:**
    the API's refusal already says why and which plan the shop is on, and what was on before stays
    usable. The switches can follow once they read the plan.

## ADR-525 · A shop's support request still open past its plan's time is flagged to Hatti's people once: the worker's sweep marks it, logs it and emails Hatti's support address the list, and the command says when each request is due

* **Context:**
  * Each plan promises an answer within its hours (ADR-508): 48 on Free, 24 on Starter, 8 on
    Growth and 4 on Pro.
  * Hatti's people list what waits with a command. Nothing told them when a promise was about to
    be broken, or had been.
* **Decision:**
  * **Due:** a request is due its plan's hours after it was asked, counted on the clock. The plan
    is the one the shop was on when it asked.
  * **Flagged once:**
    * The support module's `overdue` marks each request still open past its time, in the same
      statement that finds it (migration 0247), with the system role.
    * The next sweep finds only those late since. An answered or closed request is never flagged.
  * **Told:**
    * The worker sweeps as its other sweeps do. Each request flagged is logged as a warning, with
      its public ID, shop, plan and when it was due.
    * One email per sweep goes to Hatti's support address (`SUPPORT_EMAIL`) through SES. It lists
      the late requests, the most urgent first. Each item gives the shop, plan, priority, topic,
      hours late and the shop's words, with the command that answers it.
    * Without the address or SES, the log alone says so. An email SES refuses is logged.
  * **The command's list** shows when each request is due, or LATE once it is past.
* **Consequences:**
  * A broken promise reaches Hatti's people's inbox within one sweep, at most ten minutes by
    default, and the log feeds whatever alerting watches it.
  * A request is flagged once. Only the email tells of it, and the list's LATE marks it after.
  * Hours on the clock are stricter than working hours. A Friday-evening request on Pro is late
    by Saturday morning. Hatti's hours are words shown to shops, not a schedule the core keeps.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A message to Hatti's people on WhatsApp:** it needs a template Meta approves and a number
    for Hatti's people. Email reaches the inbox support already works from.
  * **Flagging after the email went:** a sweep that failed between the two would flag twice or
    not at all. Marking in the statement that finds a request keeps two workers from both
    telling of it; the warning in the log is there however the email went.
  * **Working hours:** they need Hatti's own calendar of hours and holidays, which the core
    doesn't keep.

## ADR-526 · Every storefront says it is "Powered by Hatti", as Shopify's powered_by_link does; a shop on Starter or above may hide it, and one hidden before stays hidden on a smaller plan

* **Context:**
  * The pricing shows "Powered by Hatti" on Free and lets paying plans remove it. It's how
    shoppers who like a store find Hatti, and part of what Free pays for.
  * Storefronts said nothing of Hatti, and themes ported from Shopify that print
    `powered_by_link` printed nothing.
* **Decision:**
  * **`powered_by_link`** is a global on every storefront page, as on Shopify: a link to Hatti's
    site, `rel="nofollow"`, opening a new tab, with campaign parameters saying it came from a
    storefront.
    * It reads "Powered by Hatti", and "ہٹی کے ذریعے" on Urdu pages.
    * It's blank while the shop hides it.
  * **Hatti Base** prints it at the foot of its footer, under the link to report the store.
  * **Hiding it:**
    * Hiding it is a preference of the online store, `hidePoweredBy`, kept with the shop's
      preferences (migration 0248) and published in the shop's document.
    * The plan gates it, as ADR-523 gates the rest: `removeBranding`, Starter and above. Free is
      refused with the plan's name.
    * One hidden before stays hidden after a move to Free. Showing it again is always allowed;
      hiding it again needs a plan with it.
* **Consequences:**
  * Free stores carry Hatti's name to their shoppers, linked so Hatti can count what it brings.
  * A theme that leaves `powered_by_link` out shows nothing. Hatti doesn't put the link into
    themes that don't ask for it, as Shopify doesn't.
  * The admin doesn't yet have the switch; ADR-527 will.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Showing it again when a shop moves down to Free:** it would change a shop's storefront by
    itself when its plan changes. Keeping what was set matches ADR-523 and ADR-264.
  * **Translated words from the theme's own locale files:** every theme would need the same
    words. The storefront gives them, as Shopify does.

## ADR-527 · The admin's storefront settings show or hide "Powered by Hatti" with a switch, saying the core's refusal on a plan without it, and the plan cards say which plans hide it

* **Context:** Storefronts say "Powered by Hatti", which shops on Starter and above may hide
  (ADR-526). Owners need a place to hide it, and to see which plans let them.
* **Decision:**
  * **Online store → Storefront** has a "Powered by Hatti" section after the return window, for
    owners and managers as the rest of the tab is.
    * A switch shows it, with what shoppers see either way, and Save sends the change alone.
    * On a plan without it, the core's refusal is shown in its words, which name the plan.
  * **The plan cards** add a line: "Hide "Powered by Hatti"", or ""Powered by Hatti" on your
    storefront" for Free (ADR-524).
  * English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:**
  * An owner hides it where the storefront's other settings are, and learns from the refusal and
    the cards which plan to choose.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Hiding the switch on Free:** the owner wouldn't know it can be hidden at all. Showing it,
    with the core's refusal naming the plan, says what to do.

## ADR-528 · The status page shows each part's last 90 days: a bar a day by the worst it was, and its uptime, counting incidents that took it down and not maintenance posted ahead

* **Context:** The status page says how each of Hatti's parts works now and lists the last 14
  days' incidents (ADR-498). A shop choosing Hatti, or a monitor, asks how it has worked over
  months, and the page couldn't say.
* **Decision:**
  * **The snapshot carries each part's history**, worked out from the incidents when the page is
    asked for; nothing new is kept.
    * Its days are Pakistan's, the last 90 with today the last, each with the worst the part was
      that day and how many minutes it was down, rounded up.
    * Its uptime is the share of the time since the first day's midnight it wasn't down, in
      percent, rounded down to two places, so a minute down never shows as 100%.
  * **Down is an incident's time down.** Incidents that took a part down count from when they
    began until they ended, or until now; overlapping ones count each minute once.
    * Maintenance posted ahead shows on its days and is not counted against uptime, as status
      pages usually do. Slowness shows and isn't counted either.
    * An incident counts by the impact it came to have, from its start: incidents keep no
      history of their impact.
  * **The page** shows under each part a row of bars, coloured by the day's worst, saying the
    day and what happened when pointed at, then its uptime, in English and Urdu. The page's
    shared styles gain the bars, light and dark.
  * **`/status.json`** gains `history`: each part's uptime and days.
* **Consequences:**
  * Anyone sees how reliable each part has been, from what Hatti's people posted, cached at the
    edge with the rest of the page.
  * It's as true as the incidents posted. Probes that post incidents themselves remain to come.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Keeping a row a day per part:** a second record of what the incidents already say, to keep
    in step with them when one is corrected. 90 days of incidents are few to read.
  * **Counting maintenance against uptime:** stricter, but unlike other status pages, and it
    would punish telling shops ahead.

## ADR-529 · The sales report's true profit lines are on Growth and bigger plans: smaller plans get them null, with the report saying so, and gross profit stays on every plan

* **Context:** The pricing gives true profit analytics, profit after couriers' charges,
  write-offs and claims (ANL-03, ADR-141), to Growth and bigger plans. The sales report gave it
  to every shop.
* **Decision:**
  * **Plans say whether they include it.** `trueProfit` is on Growth and Pro, as `BillingPlan`
    says, and `PlanAllowance` answers it as it does other features.
  * **The report asks each time it is read.** On a plan without it, every `Sales`'
    `shippingCosts`, `shippingCostsEstimated`, `writeOffs`, `claimsRecovered` and `profit` are
    null, now nullable, and `SalesReport.trueProfit` says false.
    * Gross profit and margin, from the cost of goods as Shopify's reports give them, stay on
      every plan.
    * Unlike features turned on, nothing is kept after a downgrade: it is only shown, and shows
      again when the shop's plan includes it.
* **Consequences:**
  * The plan's promise holds in the API as in the admin. Apps reading `profit` must allow null.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Refusing the whole report on smaller plans:** sales over time are on every plan.
  * **Computing the lines and hiding them in the admin:** the API would still give them.

## ADR-530 · The admin's analytics show gross profit where the plan leaves true profit out, saying which plans give it, and the plan cards say which plans do

* **Context:** The sales report gives profit null on plans without true profit (ADR-529). The
  analytics page's profit figure read it as always there.
* **Decision:**
  * **Analytics** shows, where profit is null, a gross profit figure against the period before,
    saying under it that profit after couriers and returns is on Growth and bigger plans.
  * **The plan cards** add a line: "True profit, after couriers and returns", or "Gross profit
    alone" (ADR-524).
  * English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:**
  * An owner on a smaller plan still sees what the orders made before couriers and returns, and
    learns which plan gives the rest.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Hiding the figure:** the owner wouldn't know true profit exists.

## ADR-531 · A shop on Starter connects its Meta pixel alone, without the conversions API's token, and its storefront loads it while orders go to no conversions API; Free connects neither

* **Context:** The pricing gives the Meta pixel to Starter and the conversions API to Growth and
  bigger plans. Connecting Meta needed a token for the conversions API (ADR-143), and Starter
  could connect no token (ADR-523), so Starter had no pixel at all; Free could connect one.
* **Decision:**
  * **A dataset may have no token.** Migration 0249 makes the token and its hint nullable,
    together or neither. Connecting needs the pixel's ID; the token is for the conversions API.
  * **Plans say whether they include the pixel.** `pixels` is on Starter and bigger, as
    `BillingPlan` says. A plan without it connects nothing; one connected before stays, as other
    features do (ADR-523).
  * **A plan without the conversions API gives no token.** It is refused on the token's field,
    naming the plan; one given before stays, and may be changed.
  * **The pixel alone sends no orders.** The storefront loads it as before (ADR-144). No
    moments are recorded for a dataset without a token, and the worker finds no dataset to send
    to. A token given later sends the orders placed from then on.
  * `MetaConversions.accessTokenHint` is null with the pixel alone.
* **Consequences:**
  * Starter's owners see their storefront's visits and add-to-carts in Meta's ads; Growth's add
    orders from the server.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A separate pixel setting:** a second place for the same dataset's ID, to keep in step.

## ADR-532 · The admin's Meta settings connect the pixel without a token, saying orders then go to no conversions API, and the plan cards say which plans have the pixel

* **Context:** A dataset may be connected without a token, for the pixel alone (ADR-531). The
  admin's Meta form required one.
* **Decision:**
  * **Online store → Meta:** the access token is optional, its hint saying that without one the
    storefront loads the pixel alone and orders don't go to the conversions API, which is on
    Growth and bigger plans.
    * Connected without a token, the page says so, and lists no moments sent to Meta.
    * The core's refusal of a token on Starter, or of the pixel on Free, shows in its words.
  * **The plan cards** add a line: "The Meta pixel on your storefront", or "No Meta pixel"
    (ADR-524).
  * English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:**
  * An owner on Starter connects the pixel where Growth's connect both, and learns which plan
    adds the rest.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **A separate pixel form:** two places for one dataset.

## ADR-533 · Each plan includes AI credits a month, kept by billing: each draft the AI gives, of a product's copy or of translations, spends one, and none are drafted past them until the month in Pakistan's time turns

* **Context:** The pricing includes AI credits a month: Free 10, Starter 50, Growth 150, Pro
  600. AI drafts of products' copy (ADR-471) and of translations (ADR-463) were limited only to a
  hundred a day each, the same on every plan.
* **Decision:**
  * **Billing keeps the credits.** Plans say how many they include; migration 0250's
    `billing.ai_credit_uses` holds one row per credit spent, with what it was spent on.
  * **`AiCredits` in `@hatti/api`** is how other modules ask: a shop's balance this month, and
    spending one. Billing provides it globally, as it does `PlanAllowance`; without it, as in
    most tests, drafts are not counted.
  * **A draft asks first, and spends on success.** With no credit left, the draft is refused
    before the AI is asked, naming the plan and saying they come back on the 1st. A draft the AI
    gives spends one; a refusal or a failure spends none.
  * **The month is Pakistan's**, from midnight on the 1st in Karachi, for every plan.
  * The daily hundred stays, against a runaway script.
  * `productCopyDrafting` and `translationDrafting` say the credits left and the plan's month's;
    `billingAiCredits` gives the balance, and `BillingPlan.aiCredits` each plan's.
* **Consequences:**
  * What AI costs Hatti follows what each plan pays. New AI features spend from the same
    credits by asking `AiCredits`.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Counting each module's own drafts:** modules don't read each other's tables, and a shop's
    credits are one balance whatever they're spent on.
  * **The shop's billing period:** Free has none, and a calendar month is easier to say.

## ADR-534 · The admin's AI drafts say the plan's AI credits left this month, and draft none once they are used; the plan cards say each plan's

* **Context:** AI drafts spend the plan's AI credits a month (ADR-533). The admin said only the
  day's drafts left.
* **Decision:**
  * **Write with AI** on a product's form says the credits left of the plan's month's, where
    they are counted, instead of the day's drafts; with none left, its button is off and it
    says they come back on the 1st, or a bigger plan gives more.
  * **Draft with AI** on the Urdu pages adds the same to its hint, and is off with none left.
  * **Add from a photo** drafts nothing with none left, as it does past the day's.
  * **The plan cards** add a line: "150 AI credits a month" (ADR-524).
  * English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:**
  * Owners see what they have left before asking, not after a refusal.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Showing the balance on the billing page alone:** owners draft on the product's form and
    the Urdu pages, and would learn there only from a refusal.

## ADR-535 · Anyone may ask on the status page to be emailed its updates: a link to confirm first, a link to stop in every email, and the worker sending both, each once

* **Context:** The status page shows what goes on (ADR-498) to those who look. Shops and their
  people want to be told without looking, as status pages let them subscribe.
* **Decision:**
  * **Asking:** the page has a form for an email address, posting to `/status/subscribe`. Its
    answer is the same whatever came of it, so no one learns who is subscribed.
  * **Confirming first:** migration 0251's `trust.status_subscribers` keeps each address in
    lower case with a link's secret. The worker emails the link to confirm, again an hour on at
    most if asked again, 50 a sweep at most; nothing else goes to an address until it is
    confirmed.
  * **The link, `/status/subscription/<token>`,** opens a page with a button to confirm, or to
    stop once confirmed; opening it changes nothing, as mail scanners open links. Stopping
    forgets the address. The pages are never cached, and send no referrer.
  * **Updates:** each update posted is taken once by the worker, `incident_updates.mailed_at`
    marking it, and emailed to every confirmed address with its link to stop: the title, the
    status, what it touches and what Hatti said, in English and Urdu, with the page's address.
    Updates missed for over a day are not sent late; those posted before are marked sent.
  * **The secret is kept as is,** for the worker to put in each email: it can only confirm or
    stop one address's emails.
  * The core's pages use the application's login, which now writes the table; the worker's
    sweeps the system's. Without SES, the worker takes nothing, to send once it is set up.
* **Consequences:**
  * Shops hear of incidents and maintenance as they're posted, without signing in.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Emailing every shop's owner:** many don't want it, and the people who do aren't always
    owners. Asking keeps it to those who want it.
  * **Sending the link from the request itself:** the API process would need the email sender,
    and a slow SES would slow the page; the worker's next sweep is within a minute.

## ADR-536 · The worker checks addresses given for Hatti's parts, posts an outage on the status page after three failed checks in a row, and resolves it when the part answers again

* **Context:** The status page says what Hatti's people post (ADR-498). When a part stops
  answering at night, nothing is posted until someone notices.
* **Decision:**
  * **`STATUS_PROBES`** gives the worker an address for each part to check, as
    `part=address` pairs; without it, nothing is checked.
  * **A check** asks the address and takes any status below 500 within ten seconds as an
    answer: a page that says "not found" still answers. Each sweep checks each part, at most
    once a minute.
  * **Three failed checks in a row** post an incident, down, for that part, as "Hatti's checks",
    in English and Urdu; one already open by the checks for that part means no second. An answer
    between failures starts the count again, so one slow answer posts nothing.
  * **An answer again** resolves the checks' incident, saying so. Incidents Hatti's people post
    are theirs to end.
  * The counts are kept in the worker's memory: a restart starts them again, which costs at
    most three more checks.
  * What the checks post goes to the page, its history (ADR-528) and its emails (ADR-535) like
    anything else.
* **Consequences:**
  * A part that goes down is on the status page within minutes, and off it when it's back.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **An outside monitor posting through the command:** another service to run and keep in
    step; the worker already sweeps every minute.
  * **Posting on the first failure:** one slow answer would post and resolve an incident, and
    email every subscriber twice.

## ADR-537 · Hatti's order templates go to each shop's own WhatsApp account for approval, and a shop's customers' order news goes from its own number for each one Meta approves there

* **Context:** A shop that connects its own WhatsApp number (ADR-419) sends broadcasts from it
  (ADR-422). Its customers' order news still came from Hatti's number, under Hatti's name. 07 §2.2
  says Hatti's template library is sent to each connected account for approval, and order news
  moves to the shop's number once it is approved.
* **Decision:**
  * **The library** is Hatti's utility templates to a shop's customers: the order's news from
    placed to delivered, cancelled and paid, the confirmation and its reminder, the payment
    reminder, store credit, and the request for a review. That is 17 kinds, each in English and
    Urdu, so 34 templates. Some messages stay on Hatti's number:
    * codes, which take Meta's authentication category;
    * the gift card's code, kept nowhere once sent;
    * what goes to the shop itself;
    * marketing.
  * **The templates' names** are the ones they have on Hatti's number, so the code sends a message
    the same way whichever number it goes from.
  * **The words** are the messages' own. Each variable is numbered in the order the words name it,
    so a variable named twice is two variables. The shop's number sends values in that order; on
    Hatti's number the templates stay numbered as they were. Meta refuses a body that begins or
    ends with a variable, so a greeting goes before one that would begin with one and a full stop
    after one that would end with one. Buttons:
    * answer buttons are worded for what they answer;
    * the link button opens the order's page.
  * **The worker** checks each round for accounts missing some of the library, a few shops a
    round. It asks Meta for the account's templates, then:
    * keeps one the account already has by its name and language, as for a shop that connected
      before;
    * sends the rest to Meta in the utility category.

    What Meta refuses is logged, and the account is tried again the next day, at most once a day.
    Connecting a number again tries it at once.
  * **Kept with the shop's templates:** each template is a row in the shop's templates, marked
    with the kind of message it carries. Meta's webhook, and asking Meta again, keep its status
    as for any other template. They are not among the templates the shop lists or deletes, and a
    shop's own template cannot take a name beginning `hatti_`.
  * **Sending:** a message of the library's kinds on WhatsApp goes from the shop's own number when
    Meta has approved its template, in its language, on the account the shop has now. Otherwise it
    goes from Hatti's number. Everything else is as before: it falls back to SMS, retries the same
    way, and is paid for as before, as ADR-422 does for broadcasts.
