  * **The admin's WhatsApp page** says which number order news goes from:
    * this number;
    * this number for those Meta has approved, Hatti's for the rest;
    * Hatti's, while Meta looks at the templates or before they are sent.

    It also says how many Meta refused.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop with its own number has its customers' order news in its own name, with no step of
    its own, as Meta approves the templates.
  * A template Meta refuses or pauses leaves that kind on Hatti's number, so nothing goes unsent.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Sending the library as the shop connects:** connecting would wait on 34 requests to Meta,
    and one refused would have no second try.
  * **Hatti's own numbering of the variables:** some templates would name a variable out of order
    or twice, which Meta may refuse.
  * **Moving all the news at once when all 34 are approved:** one refused template would keep the
    other 33 on Hatti's number.

## ADR-538 · A shop's own images are served at the widths and in the formats browsers take, each made once and kept beside its file, and removed with it

* **Context:** Products' images are served at nine widths, in AVIF or WebP where browsers take
  them (ADR-158). A shop's own images were served as uploaded: its logos (ADR-198, ADR-205),
  articles' images (ADR-213), its sharing image (ADR-243) and its themes' pictures (ADR-326).
  A phone's photo chosen as a banner reached every shopper at full size, and a theme's
  `image_url` asked for widths that nothing made.
* **Decision:**
  * **Asking:** each of those addresses takes `?width=`, made at the next of products' widths and
    never wider than the image, and the browser's Accept header, which gives AVIF, else WebP. A
    browser that takes neither gets the image's own format, and PNG for WebP.
  * **Making and keeping:** each size and format is made the first time it is asked for, two at
    a time, and kept in storage under the file's own folder, in `shown/`. Removing the file
    removes that folder too.
  * **Left as they are:**
    * an image asked for at no width, in a format it already has, as an email's reader may ask;
    * a GIF, which may move;
    * an image the decoder cannot read.
  * **What is made has no metadata:** an image is encoded anew without the camera's data, and a
    browser asking for AVIF or WebP always gets one made this way.
  * **Caching:** answers vary by Accept, cached as they were.
  * **Theme pictures:** the storefront passes the width a theme asked for, and its browser's
    Accept, on to the core, so a theme's `image_url` gets the size it asks for.
* **Consequences:**
  * Shoppers get banners and logos at the sizes their screens need, in AVIF or WebP.
  * Each size is encoded once.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Cleaning each file on upload, as products' images are:** the files module would need the
    worker's image pipeline, and PDFs and videos share it. Making sizes when asked costs nothing
    for files never shown.
  * **Making each answer anew, kept by the edge alone:** every edge miss would encode again.

## ADR-539 · A shop buys AI credits a hundred at a time from its message credit, and they last until spent, after the month's own

* **Context:** Each plan includes AI credits a month (ADR-533), and a shop that spent them had to
  wait for the 1st or choose a bigger plan. A shop that drafts a whole new collection in one week
  needs more without changing plans.
* **Decision:**
  * **A pack** is 100 credits for Rs 500, and the owner buys one to ten at a time
    (`billingAiCreditsBuy`), having signed in lately, as for anything that spends the shop's money.
  * **Paid from the message credit** (ADR-155), at once. The credit must hold the price; otherwise
    nothing is bought and the shop is told what the credit holds. The payment is an entry of its
    own in the credit's history, `AI_CREDITS`, saying how many were bought, and the purchase is
    on the activity log.
  * **Bought credits last until spent.** A draft spends the month's own first, then one bought;
    each use says which it spent, so the month's own come back on the 1st and those bought stay.
    Uses are counted one draft at a time, under a lock per shop.
  * **A shop's balance** now says what is left of the month's own and of those bought, with the
    pack's size and price. The message a shop gets with none left says it may buy more.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop never waits for the 1st to keep drafting, and pays only for what it uses beyond its
    plan.
  * There is no new way to pay: the message credit already takes Hatti's gateway and transfers.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **An invoice for each pack:** a payment, and a wait, for Rs 500.
  * **Bought credits ending with the month:** a shop would lose what it paid for.

## ADR-540 · The admin's billing page shows the shop's AI credits, the month's own and those bought, and its owner buys more

* **Context:** The admin showed the plan's AI credits only on the plan card (ADR-534), and buying
  more had no screen (ADR-539).
* **Decision:**
  * **Settings → Billing** has an AI credits section under the message credit. It shows what is
    left of the month's own and when they come back, and how many bought credits are left, which
    last until used.
  * **The owner buys** one pack at a time with a button that names its size and price, confirming
    who they are first if the core asks.
  * **The credit's history** names AI credits bought.
  * **The AI's drafting screens** count what is left of both, beside the plan's monthly number.
    With none left, they say the plan's come back on the 1st, or that more can be bought in
    Settings → Billing.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop that runs out finds where to buy more from the message that says so.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Buying from the drafting screens themselves:** every screen that drafts would carry
    payment. Billing is where the shop's money is spent.

## ADR-541 · Orders placed through checkout go to TikTok's Events API from the worker beside Meta's, the shop connecting its TikTok pixel with a token, each moment waiting in Postgres as Meta's do

* **Context:** Orders reach Meta's ads from the server (ADR-143), but many Pakistani shops sell
  through TikTok's ads, which learned nothing of the orders that turned out. TikTok's Events API
  takes web events from a server much as Meta's conversions API does.
* **Decision:**
  * **The shop connects its TikTok pixel** with its code and an access token Events Manager made
    for the Events API (`tiktokEventsUpdate`), both needed. The token is sealed for the shop alone
    and never shown again; changes are audited, the token never; a code for test events may be
    set while the shop tries it out. A plan without the conversions API connects none, as for
    Meta (ADR-523).
  * **The same moments** as Meta's: an order placed through checkout is recorded for each
    platform connected when it is placed, and its confirming and delivery follow it to the same
    platforms. A row of `marketing.conversions` is one moment for one platform, so the two are
    sent and settled apart.
  * **The worker sends them** a shop at a time, a hundred in a request to each platform. TikTok's
    events are web events: the moment the shop chose as its purchase goes as `CompletePayment`,
    the others as `PlaceAnOrder`, `OrderConfirmed` and `OrderDelivered`. Each carries the order's
    total and its items by variant, the customer's number in E.164 and email hashed with SHA-256,
    their ID with the shop hashed, the browser's address and user agent, and TikTok's click ID
    (`ttclid`) from the latest visit whose address had one. The event's ID is the order's number
    and the moment, so TikTok keeps one however often it goes.
  * **What TikTok says** settles them as Meta's are: taken, sent; over its limits, in trouble, or
    the token refused, tried again on the same backoff while seven days have not passed; anything
    else, failed with TikTok's code and message. TikTok's request ID is kept as the trace.
  * **Disconnecting** forgets the token and skips the moments waiting for TikTok; Meta's go on.
  * **The Admin API** reads the pixel (`tiktokEvents`), connects and changes it, disconnects it,
    and lists the moments by platform (`conversionEvents(platform:)`).
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop advertising on TikTok tells its ads which orders were real, confirmed or delivered,
    as it does Meta's, without a script in checkout.
  * TikTok's browser pixel is not loaded on the storefront yet: events from the server alone.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **TikTok's pixel in the browser only:** ad blockers and checkout's scriptless page lose the
    orders that matter most.
  * **A table of moments per platform:** the same waiting, claiming and settling twice.

## ADR-542 · The admin's online store has a TikTok tab: the pixel connected, changed and disconnected, and the moments sent to TikTok listed apart from Meta's

* **Context:** The Events API had no screen (ADR-541).
* **Decision:**
  * **Online store → TikTok**, for those who set Meta's (owners, managers and marketers): the
    pixel's code, the access token (needed to connect, then left blank to keep the one ending as
    shown), which moment is TikTok's purchase with what each choice means, and a test event code.
    Saving confirms who they are first when the core asks; disconnecting asks whether they mean
    it.
  * **Sent to TikTok** lists the latest moments sent to TikTok alone, by status, each with
    TikTok's request ID; Meta's tab lists Meta's alone.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop connects TikTok the way it connects Meta, in English or Urdu.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **One tab for every ad platform:** two long forms on one screen, for most shops one unused.

## ADR-543 · A shop's storefront loads its TikTok pixel while TikTok is connected, beside Meta's, for the steps shoppers take before checkout, and the order keeps the pixel's browser ID for the Events API

* **Context:** Orders go to TikTok's Events API from the server (ADR-541), but TikTok's ads learn
  more from the steps before an order, which only the browser sees, and match the server's events
  best to the browser its pixel named.
* **Decision:**
  * **While the shop has TikTok connected,** shoppers' pages load TikTok's pixel, its own base
    code with the pixel's code, beside Meta's when the shop has both (ADR-144). Previews and the
    theme editor load neither.
  * **The same steps as Meta's:** the page; `ViewContent` on a product's page, by the catalog
    feed's IDs; `AddToCart` from forms adding to the cart, valued when the page prices the
    variant; and `InitiateCheckout` for the cart's checkout button and links to checkout. One
    listener code serves both pixels. Checkout's pages still run no scripts.
  * **The pixel's browser ID,** its `_ttp` cookie, goes with the order placed through checkout
    beside Meta's, kept only in TikTok's form, and the order's events send it as `ttp`.
  * **The shop's document names the pixel's code,** published again when the code changes or
    TikTok is disconnected, and every page kept at the edge is purged then.
* **Consequences:**
  * TikTok's ads optimise for the steps shoppers take on the shop's pages and match orders to
    them, as Meta's do.
  * Shoppers' browsers load another script while the shop has TikTok connected; a consent banner
    is still to come.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **The shop pasting TikTok's code into its theme:** no pixel code in the theme to keep in step
    with the connected one, and its order events would name no browser.

## ADR-544 · Every shop hears on WhatsApp when an outage of Hatti's begins and ends, at its alerts number and at Hatti's cost, each update once

* **Context:** Hatti's status page (ADR-498) shows outages, the admin carries a banner, and anyone
  may be emailed its updates (ADR-535). A shop owner away from the admin, whose checkout is down
  in the middle of a sale, hears of it from customers first.
* **Decision:**
  * **What is sent:** of an incident or maintenance that puts a part out of service (impact
    `outage`), the update that opened it (or set the maintenance ahead) and the one that ended it.
    What is said while it lasts, and slow or partial trouble (`degraded`), reach shops by the page,
    the banner and the emails alone.
  * **To whom:** every shop with an alerts number, on WhatsApp from Hatti's number, a notice the
    shop cannot turn off and Hatti pays for (`status_update`), as its bills' notices are
    (ADR-169). It names the shop, what Hatti called the trouble, where it stands and the parts it
    touches, in the shop's language (Urdu where Hatti wrote the title in Urdu too), and links to
    the status page.
  * **Once each:** an update is marked told once every shop has it queued, each queued with a key
    of its own, so a shop that failed is tried again next sweep and none hears it twice. An update
    missed for six hours, as while the worker was down, is put aside and never sent.
  * Updates posted before this are not sent.
* **Consequences:**
  * An owner hears of an outage, and of its end, where they read their alerts.
  * At most two messages for each outage and shop, at Hatti's cost.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Every update to every shop:** an outage of hours would send each shop several messages.
  * **Only shops that ask:** the shops least in the admin, who most need it, would not.

## ADR-545 · What customers write to a shop on WhatsApp is kept as a conversation for each customer's number, the shop found by the number written to, the message answered or the last shop to write, for its staff to read, mark read and close

* **Context:** WhatsApp's webhook (ADR-146) hears what customers write, but kept only their
  answers to buttons and their stop words; the rest was dropped. Customers ask about sizes,
  delivery and payment on WhatsApp first, and a shop could not read what they asked (MSG-05).
* **Decision:**
  * **Kept:** every message a customer writes, its words or the kind of thing it held (a photo,
    a voice note) where it had no words, in the shop's conversation with the customer's number,
    one for each number. A message WhatsApp delivers twice is kept once, by WhatsApp's ID for it.
    A reaction, holding neither, is not kept.
  * **Whose:** a message to a shop's own number (ADR-419) is that shop's. One to Hatti's shared
    number is the shop's whose message it answers, else the last shop to write to the customer, as
    stop words are (ADR-146); one no shop wrote to is no one's and is not kept. The webhook finds
    the shop through functions that see no shop's rows.
  * **The inbox:** each conversation is open or closed, with how many of its messages are unread.
    The Admin API lists them the latest written first, a page at a time, the unread or the
    closed alone; counts those with unread messages; and gives a conversation's messages, the
    latest first. Staff mark it read, or close it, which reads it; the customer writing again
    opens it again, unread. Numbers are shown as the caller may see them (ADR-027).
  * **Scopes:** `read_conversations` and `write_conversations`. Owners, managers and confirmation
    agents work the inbox; marketers read it.
  * **Customers' data:** an erased customer's numbers' conversations go with them, and their own
    file has what they wrote.
  * This slice keeps and reads. Replies, within the 24 hours WhatsApp lets a shop answer freely,
    and the admin's inbox page come after.
* **Consequences:**
  * Nothing a customer writes to a shop is lost, and staff see what waits for an answer.
  * A customer who writes to the shared number about one shop, having heard last from another,
    lands with the other, as their stop words would.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Keep only messages to shops' own numbers:** most shops send from Hatti's shared number,
    and their customers would go unheard.
  * **A conversation for each order:** customers write before they order and about several
    orders; the number is what both sides know.

## ADR-546 · The inbox's staff answer a customer in their own words within the day WhatsApp allows after the customer last wrote, sent at once from the number the customer wrote to, and followed to delivery as the webhook says

* **Context:** The inbox keeps what customers write (ADR-545), but a shop could only read it.
  WhatsApp lets a business write to a customer in its own words, not a template, for 24 hours
  after the customer's last message to that number, and charges nothing for it (MSG-05).
* **Decision:**
  * **Who and when:** owners, managers and confirmation agents (`write_conversations`) answer a
    conversation while the day after the customer last wrote lasts; after it, the reply is
    refused (`WINDOW_CLOSED`), and the shop writes again through its templates. The API says
    until when each conversation may be answered.
  * **From where:** the number the customer last wrote to: the shop's own, while it is still
    connected (ADR-419), else Hatti's shared number. A reply is never sent from a number the
    customer did not write to, where WhatsApp would refuse it anyway.
  * **At once:** the API sends the reply through WhatsApp's Cloud API as staff send it, not
    through the worker's queue: staff wait for it, and are told at once if WhatsApp refused it
    (`NOT_SENT`) or could not be reached (`UNAVAILABLE`), to try again. Only what WhatsApp took
    is kept: its words, who wrote it and WhatsApp's ID for it. Sending marks the conversation
    read.
  * **Followed:** WhatsApp's webhook moves each reply on as it moves the shop's other messages
    (ADR-146): sent, delivered, read, or failed with why, never back. A status the webhook names
    before the reply is kept is given back to Meta to send again, as for messages.
  * **Free:** replies are not charged to the shop's credit (ADR-155): WhatsApp charges nothing
    for them.
* **Consequences:**
  * A customer's question is answered where they asked it, and the shop sees it read.
  * An inbox reply waits on WhatsApp's answer, a second or so.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Queue replies for the worker:** staff would not know a reply failed until later, and a
    reply sent in the last minutes of the day could miss it.
  * **Answer past the day with a template:** a different act, with its cost and approval; the
    shop's templates and broadcasts (ADR-420) already do it.

## ADR-547 · Orders placed through checkout go to Google Analytics' Measurement Protocol from the worker beside Meta's and TikTok's, the shop connecting its web stream with an API secret, for Google Ads to import its purchase as a conversion

* **Context:** Orders reach Meta's and TikTok's ads from the server (ADR-143, ADR-541), but
  Google's ads, search and YouTube among them, learned nothing of the orders that turned out
  (MKT-10). Google Ads' own conversion upload needs a developer token and each shop's Google
  account signed in through OAuth; Google Analytics takes events from a server with a stream's
  measurement ID and a secret the shop makes in a minute, and Google Ads imports its events as
  conversions.
* **Decision:**
  * **The shop connects its Google Analytics web stream** with its measurement ID and a
    Measurement Protocol API secret (`googleAnalyticsUpdate`), both needed. The secret is sealed
    for the shop alone and never shown again; changes are audited, the secret never. A plan
    without the conversions API connects none, as for Meta and TikTok (ADR-523).
  * **The same moments:** an order placed through checkout is recorded for Google when it is
    placed, if the shop has it connected, and its confirming and delivery follow, as for the other
    platforms, a row of `marketing.conversions` for each.
  * **The worker sends them** a request for each moment, as Google takes one browser's events
    in a request. The moment the shop chose as its purchase goes as Google's recommended
    `purchase`, the others as `order_placed`, `order_confirmed` and `order_delivered`, each with the
    order's number as the transaction, its total and its items by variant, dated when the moment
    happened. The customer's number in E.164 and email go hashed with SHA-256 as user-provided
    data, and their ID with the shop, hashed, as the user and, shortened, as the browser, so that
    one customer's orders read as one visitor's until the storefront's Google tag names the
    browser.
  * **Three days:** Google dates an event at most 72 hours back, so a moment that could not go
    within them expires, where Meta's and TikTok's wait seven days.
  * **What Google says:** it answers every well-formed request alike and says nothing of events it
    drops, so a request taken is sent; Google in trouble, over its limits or unreachable, tried
    again on the same backoff; anything else, failed with Google's answer. A request refused
    stops the shop's others for the round, and those sent before it go again with it; Google
    keeps one purchase for each transaction.
  * **Disconnecting** forgets the secret and skips the moments waiting for Google.
  * **The Admin API** reads the stream (`googleAnalytics`), connects and changes it, disconnects it,
    and lists Google's moments with the others' (`conversionEvents(platform: GOOGLE)`).
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop advertising on Google tells its ads which orders were real, confirmed or delivered,
    once it marks the purchase as a key event and imports it into Google Ads.
  * Google's tag is not on the storefront yet: events from the server alone, and an order is not
    tied to the ad click that brought it until the tag names the browser.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Google Ads' conversion upload by click ID:** ties each order to its click, but asks every
    shop to sign Hatti into its Google Ads account and Hatti to hold a developer token.
  * **Google's tag in the browser only:** ad blockers and checkout's scriptless page lose the
    orders that matter most.

## ADR-548 · The storefront loads the shop's Google tag while it has Google Analytics connected, tracking the same steps as Meta's and TikTok's pixels, and checkout passes the `_ga` cookie on so that an order's server events are the browser's that came from the ad

* **Context:** Orders go to Google Analytics from the server (ADR-547), but as a visitor of their
  own: the customer's ID shortened stands in for the browser, so Google cannot tie an order to the
  ad click and the visit that brought it. Meta's and TikTok's pixels are on the storefront, and
  their browser IDs go with the order (ADR-144, ADR-542); Google's tag was not.
* **Decision:**
  * **The storefront loads the shop's Google tag** (`gtag.js` with its measurement ID) on every
    page while the shop has its web stream connected, the ID published with the shop's document;
    connecting, changing the ID and disconnecting republish it. The secret never leaves the core.
  * **The same steps:** a product's page sends `view_item`, adding to the cart `add_to_cart` and
    going to checkout `begin_checkout`, each with the variant, its price and the shop's currency, as
    the other pixels track them; the purchase is the server's alone, so it is counted once.
  * **The browser's ID goes with the order:** checkout passes the `_ga` cookie on with Meta's and
    TikTok's, kept only when it reads as Google's (`GA1.n.<number>.<number>`); the worker sends the
    order's moments with the client ID it holds, the customer's shortened ID still where there is
    none.
* **Consequences:**
  * An order's purchase is the visit's that came from the ad, so Google Ads credits the campaign that
    brought it, and the shop sees its visitors' steps in Google Analytics.
  * Like the other pixels, the tag loads without a consent banner yet.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Google Tag Manager's container:** lets a shop add any tag, Hatti's checkout no longer knowing
    what runs on its pages.

## ADR-549 · The admin's inbox lists a shop's WhatsApp conversations open, unread or closed, and a conversation's page reads it as it opens, closes and reopens it, and answers within the day WhatsApp allows, for those who work it; marketers read it alone

* **Context:** The core keeps what customers write to a shop on WhatsApp as conversations
  (ADR-545) and sends the shop's replies within the day WhatsApp allows (ADR-546), but only through
  the API: no one in a shop could see or answer them.
* **Decision:**
  * **Inbox in the admin's navigation,** beside the Confirmation Desk, for owners, managers,
    confirmation agents and marketers, as the API's scopes allow; packers and accountants see none.
  * **The list:** the latest first, a page at a time, in three tabs, open, unread and closed, each
    conversation with the customer's number as the API shows it to the one reading, its last
    message (or what it carried, a photo or a voice note, which stays on the customer's phone), who
    wrote it, and its unread messages counted; the heading counts the conversations unread.
  * **A conversation's page:** its messages oldest at the top, older ones a page at a time, each
    reply with how far WhatsApp took it, and which number the customer wrote to, the shop's own or
    Hatti's.
  * **Those who work the inbox** (owners, managers and confirmation agents) read it as it opens,
    close it or open it again, and answer in their own words, up to WhatsApp's 4,096 characters,
    until the day after the customer last wrote, the page saying until when; once it has passed, a
    note says the customer must write again. Why WhatsApp would not take a reply is said in words,
    whether to try again among them. A marketer reads the conversation, leaving it unread for those
    who answer.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop answers its customers' questions where it confirms and ships their orders, and each
    reply is kept with who wrote it.
  * The list does not refresh by itself yet, nor does a phone hear of a new message.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **The inbox inside the Confirmation Desk:** the desk is a queue of orders, and most
    conversations are about none.

## ADR-550 · The admin's online store has a Google tab: the web stream connected with its measurement ID and API secret, its purchase moment chosen, disconnected once asked, and the moments sent to Google listed apart

* **Context:** A shop's orders go to Google Analytics and its storefront loads the Google tag once
  the shop connects its web stream (ADR-547, ADR-548), but the stream connected only through the
  API, while Meta's and TikTok's have their tabs (ADR-542).
* **Decision:**
  * **A Google tab** in the online store, for owners, managers and marketers, as Meta's and
    TikTok's.
  * **Connecting:** the stream's measurement ID and a Measurement Protocol API secret, both needed
    the first time, and which moment of an order is Google's purchase, each moment's hint saying
    what Google learns from it; saved once the member confirms who they are, only what changed
    sent. The secret is never shown again: its last four characters say which one is kept, and
    leaving it blank keeps it.
  * **Once connected,** the tab says to import the purchase into Google Ads as a conversion, and
    lists the latest moments sent to Google, all or those of one status, apart from Meta's and
    TikTok's; Google gives no trace of a request, so none is shown.
  * **Disconnecting** asks first, saying the storefront stops loading the tag and the moments
    waiting are not sent.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop advertising on Google connects it as it does Meta and TikTok, without the API.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Signing in with Google to pick the stream:** saves copying two values, but needs Hatti to
    hold each shop's Google access, as ADR-547 chose not to.

## ADR-551 · A shop may ask its shoppers before its ad platforms' pixels load: a banner until they accept or decline, kept in a cookie of the shop's, the pixels waiting for the answer, and an order placed by one who did not accept sent to no ad platform

* **Context:** A shop's pages load Meta's and TikTok's pixels and Google's tag while it has them
  connected (ADR-144, ADR-543, ADR-548), and its orders go to them from the server (ADR-143,
  ADR-541, ADR-547), with no banner asking the shopper first. A shop selling to countries whose
  laws ask for one, or that would rather ask, had no way to.
* **Decision:**
  * **A preference of the online store's** (`consentBanner`), off unless the shop turns it on, on
    any plan: asking is not a feature to sell.
  * **The banner:** while it is on and the shop has a pixel, each page's head carries a script
    before the pixels that shows a bar at the foot of the page until the shopper answers, in the
    page's language, English or Urdu, right to left in Urdu, linking the shop's privacy policy when
    it has one. Pages are the same for every shopper and kept at the edge, so the browser decides
    whether to show it, from the answer kept in the shop's `hatti_consent` cookie for some six
    months.
  * **The pixels wait:** each runs only once the shopper accepts, at once on later pages; declining,
    or not answering, loads none, so their cookies are never set.
  * **The order:** placed by a shopper who did not accept while the shop asks, it keeps that alone,
    with no browser's IDs, and the worker skips its moments for every platform, saying the shopper
    declined.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop that asks tells its ads less; one that does not is as before.
  * The banner does not come back once answered, short of the shopper clearing the cookie: no link
    reopens it yet. The visits' first-party cookie (ADR-139) is the shop's own analytics and does
    not wait for it.
  * The admin does not set it yet: the API does.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Google's and Meta's consent modes, the pixels loaded but told to hold back:** they still
    load the platforms' scripts before the shopper answers.
  * **A banner the theme renders:** every theme would need one, and the pixels are the platform's.

## ADR-552 · The admin's storefront preferences turn the consent banner on and off, saying what each choice means for the shop's pixels and its orders

* **Context:** A shop may ask its shoppers before its pixels load (ADR-551), but only through the
  API.
* **Decision:** **Cookie consent** in the online store's storefront tab, for owners and managers as
  the tab's other preferences, a box to ask shoppers first, its hint saying what each choice does:
  asking, a banner until each shopper answers, pixels loading only once they accept, and orders of
  those who did not going to no ad platform; not asking, the pixels on every page as before. Saved
  on its own, as the tab's other forms are.
* **Consequences:** A shop turns the banner on where it sells into countries that ask for it,
  without the API.
* **Alternatives:** **Beside each platform's tab:** the banner holds back every platform alike, so
  it is the storefront's.

## ADR-553 · A shop records what it spends on its ads, day by day, by platform and campaign, and the sales report takes it off the orders' profit and sets their sales against it

* **Context:** True profit takes off what goods, couriers and write-offs cost (ADR-141), but not
  what the ads that brought the orders cost (ANL-03, MKT-12), so a shop selling at a loss on its
  ads saw a profit. The platforms' reporting APIs each need an ad account's access, and many
  Pakistani shops pay for ads in dollars by card, or boost posts from a phone, so what they paid
  in rupees is theirs to say.
* **Decision:**
  * **Ad spend is recorded by day** in the shop's time zone, by platform (Meta, TikTok, Google or
    other) and, where the shop says, by campaign as its links' `utm_campaign` names it, in rupees
    as it paid (`adSpendSet`, up to 400 at a time, all or none): each replaces what that day had,
    campaigns in any letter case being one, and 0 takes it away. Days from 2020 to today, a day
    ahead allowed for a shop already in tomorrow.
    Listed a span of up to 366 days at a time (`adSpendEntries`). Kept by marketing, recorded by
    those who connect the ad platforms (`write_pixels`): owners, managers and marketers.
  * **The sales report** counts each period's days: its `adSpend`, taken off `profit`, and its
    `returnOnAdSpend`, net sales for each rupee spent. By campaign, each row has its campaign's
    spend, and a campaign spent on without an order is a row of none; by channel or by where
    visits came from, the spend is not split, so those rows' is null. On plans without true
    profit, null, as its other lines are (ADR-529).
  * **Orders read it through marketing's public functions** (`adSpendByPeriodIn`,
    `adSpendByCampaignIn`), in the report's own transaction.
* **Consequences:**
  * A shop sees whether its ads paid, for the shop and campaign by campaign.
  * Rows by channel or visit source add up to the totals but for the ad spend.
  * The admin does not record it yet, nor are the platforms asked for it.
* **Alternatives:**
  * **Pulling spend from Meta's and Google's reporting APIs:** exact for the platforms that give
    it, but needs each shop's ad account access and turns dollars into rupees at a rate the shop
    did not pay; it can fill the same days later.
  * **Splitting a platform's spend over visit sources:** Meta's spend covers Facebook, Instagram
    and Messenger alike, with no honest way to share it.

## ADR-554 · The admin records ad spend a day at a time under Marketing, and analytics shows the spend and the sales each rupee of it brought, beside true profit

* **Context:** A shop records its ad spend, and the sales report takes it off profit (ADR-553), but
  only through the API.
* **Decision:**
  * **Ad spend** under Marketing, for owners, managers and marketers, as the other ads settings
    are. A form takes the platform, the day (today in the shop's time zone at first, and none
    after it), the campaign as its links' `utm_campaign` names it, or none for the platform's day
    as a whole, and the amount. Each entry is saved alone; one given again replaces the last.
  * Below it, the last 30 days, the latest first, with their total, and each entry removed in a tap,
    as an amount of nothing does.
  * **Analytics** shows the period's ad spend and its return on ad spend, the net sales for each
    rupee spent, after profit. Both are shown only where true profit is (ADR-529) and something
    was spent, and each is compared with the period before.
* **Consequences:** A shop sees what its ads cost against what they sold, without the API.
  Entries are typed by hand: what the platforms say they spent is not pulled from them.
* **Alternatives:** **A grid of days by platform:** most shops pay one or two platforms, and an
  entry at a time also fits a phone. **Spend shown without true profit:** it is part of what
  profit takes off, so it shows where that does.

## ADR-555 · A Tier-1 shop connects its POS to FBR, and each invoice and credit note it issues is reported to FBR's IMS as it is issued, tried again while FBR cannot be reached

* **Context:** A Tier-1 retailer must report each sale to FBR as it makes it, from a POS FBR has
  registered, and print the number FBR gives it, with its QR code, on the customer's invoice
  (POS-04, TAX-04). A shop issues its invoices on first print (ADR-495) and its credit notes with
  refunds (ADR-496), and keeps its Tier-1 status with its tax settings (ADR-500), but nothing
  reached FBR.
* **Decision:**
  * **The connection.** The tax module keeps the shop's POS as FBR registered it: the POS ID, the
    access token FBR gave for it, sealed for the shop alone and never shown again, FBR's sandbox or
    the real service, and one PCT code its items are reported under until variants have codes of
    their own (CAT-19). Connecting needs all four, and Pro, whose plan includes FBR's connectors;
    changes are audited, the token never. `fbrPos`, `fbrPosUpdate` (staff confirm who they are
    first, as for the ad platforms' tokens) and `fbrPosDelete`, under the settings scopes.
  * **What is kept.** While connected, each invoice the orders module issues, and each credit note,
    is kept in the same transaction as FBR's IMS takes it: its USIN the shop's own number, its time
    in the shop's zone, each line at what was paid for it after its share of the discount with its
    tax as the order worked it out, the delivery charge and fee for paying on delivery as one line
    more, and its totals added up from its lines, so they always match the invoice. A credit note
    is FBR's credit invoice, naming the invoice it corrects, with the refund as its one line. Cash
    on delivery is cash; whatever was paid ahead goes as card, FBR's modes having no transfer.
    Nothing of the customer goes: FBR asks none of a retail sale. The POS ID and PCT code go in as
    each is sent, so a code put right applies to those sent again. Invoices issued before
    connecting are not reported late.
  * **Reporting.** The worker reports those due, the oldest first, each in a request of its own
    with the POS's token. FBR's number settles it; a refusal fails it, saying why; FBR unreachable,
    busy or refusing the token leaves it pending, tried again after a minute, doubling to six
    hours, for a week, and then failed. A new token or POS sends those waiting at once.
  * **The shop's view.** `fiscalInvoices` lists them, the latest first, by status, with FBR's
    number or why not; `fiscalInvoiceRetry` sends again one refused, or one disconnecting left
    unsent, once the POS is connected. Disconnecting forgets the token and leaves what waits
    unsent.
* **Consequences:** A Tier-1 shop's invoices reach FBR without a POS vendor of its own. FBR's
  number is not yet printed on the invoice, nor its QR code, and the admin has no FBR page; FBR's
  Rs 1 POS service fee is not charged; and FBR's digital invoicing for sales-tax-registered
  sellers, through a licensed integrator, remains (TAX-04).
* **Alternatives:** **Reporting while the invoice prints:** FBR answering slowly would hold the
  series' lock and every print behind it; kept in the transaction and sent after, an invoice is
  never issued without being kept, nor kept without being issued. **The customer's name and
  number:** FBR asks none, and none kept is none to erase. **A PCT code each variant:** waits for
  the catalog's FBR fields (CAT-19).

## ADR-556 · A Tier-1 shop's invoices and credit notes print FBR's number and its QR code once FBR has numbered them, and say they await FBR until then

* **Context:** A Tier-1 shop's invoices and credit notes are reported to FBR as they are issued
  (ADR-555), and FBR asks that the number it gives each, with its QR code, be printed on the copy
  the customer gets. The documents had no QR codes, and the orders module did not read how its
  invoices stood with FBR.
* **Decision:**
  * **QR codes** in the documents package: byte mode, error correction level M, versions 1 to 10
    (up to 213 bytes, as FBR's numbers need far less), the smallest version that holds the value
    and the mask the standard's penalty rules find easiest to read, drawn as one SVG path with
    its quiet zone. Written for the package rather than taken from a library, as its Code 128
    barcodes were; it was checked module for module against the Python qrcode library, at every
    mask of every version, and a test keeps that library's matrices.
  * **Printed:** an invoice, and each credit note, issued while the shop's POS was connected,
    prints FBR's invoice number and its QR code, with a line saying to scan it in FBR's Tax Asaan
    app, once FBR has numbered it; until then, that it awaits FBR, to be printed again once FBR has
    numbered it. One issued before the POS was connected prints as before. English and Urdu.
  * **In the API,** an order's invoice says how it stands with FBR, `fbrStatus`, and FBR's number,
    `fbrInvoiceNumber`, read through the tax module's facade.
* **Consequences:** A Tier-1 shop prints FBR-compliant invoices once FBR has answered, usually
  within the worker's first round; one printed at once waits for its number.
* **Alternatives:** **Reporting before the first print:** FBR answering slowly would hold the
  invoice series' lock and every print behind it (ADR-555). **A library for QR codes:** the
  package keeps no dependencies, and the encoder is a few hundred lines checked against one.

## ADR-557 · An inventory item keeps its HS code, Shopify's harmonizedSystemCode, and FBR is sent each item's own PCT code from it, the shop's for those without

* **Context:** FBR asks each item a POS reports to name its PCT code, the 8-digit heading of
  Pakistan's customs tariff. ADR-555 sent the one code the shop gave with its POS for every item,
  which is right only for a shop selling one kind of thing. Shopify keeps an HS code on each
  inventory item, `harmonizedSystemCode`, for customs, and Pakistan's PCT codes are HS codes to
  eight digits.
* **Decision:**
  * **Kept on the inventory item:** `harmonizedSystemCode`, 6 to 13 digits, as Shopify's, typed
    with or without its dots and spaces ("6204.42.00") and kept as digits; set, changed and cleared
    with the item's other settings, and recorded in its change event. CAT-19.
  * **Sent to FBR:** an invoice's or credit note's items name the PCT code of their variant's
    item, when it has 8 digits; others, and its delivery, go under the shop's code, as before. The
    codes are read through the inventory module's facade as the invoice is issued, and kept with
    it, so a code changed later does not change what was issued.
* **Consequences:** A shop selling clothes and shoes reports each under its own heading; one
  importing products from Shopify keeps the codes it had there.
* **Alternatives:** **Codes on products:** a product's variants can be different goods, and
  Shopify keeps them on the item. **Taking 6-digit codes as PCT codes:** FBR takes 8 digits, and
  padding a 6-digit heading guesses the subheading.

## ADR-558 · The admin connects a Tier-1 shop's POS to FBR on the sales tax page, lists what was reported and sends again what was not, and an order's page says how its invoice stands with FBR

* **Context:** A Tier-1 shop's POS is connected to FBR, and its invoices are reported and printed
  with FBR's number (ADR-555, ADR-556), but only through the API.
* **Decision:**
  * **FBR POS** on the sales tax page, for owners and managers, as the shop's other settings are:
    its POS ID, the access token FBR gave it (sealed, never shown again; left blank to keep it),
    FBR's sandbox or production, and its PCT code. Connecting and changing it ask the member to
    confirm who they are; only what changed is sent; a problem with a field shows under it, and a
    plan without FBR reporting says so. Connected, it shows what is kept, the token's last four,
    a warning while on the sandbox, and disconnecting, asked first.
  * **Invoices reported to FBR** below it: the latest 50, all or of one status, each with its
    kind, number, status, when issued in the shop's time zone, FBR's number, its tries and error,
    and a link to its order; those refused or not sent are sent again in a tap while connected.
  * **An order's page** says beside its invoice number FBR's number, that it awaits FBR, or that
    FBR refused it. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shop connects FBR and sees what FBR refused without the API.
* **Alternatives:** **A page of its own under Settings:** FBR's POS is part of the shop's sales
  tax, and its Tier-1 status is set on the same page. **Production by default:** a shop trying a
  POS out would report real invoices.

## ADR-559 · The admin's product page takes each variant's HS code with its stock rules, saved as the field is left

* **Context:** An inventory item keeps its HS code, which FBR is sent as the item's PCT code
  (ADR-557), but only the API and Shopify's import set it.
* **Decision:** Each variant's HS code is a field in the product page's stock rules, beside
  whether its stock is counted and sold when none is left, for those who see them. It shows the
  code as kept, takes it with its dots and spaces, and is saved when the field is left, as the
  card's other rules are saved at once; a code that is not one says why under the field, and an
  empty field clears it. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shop gives its products their HS codes without the API, and FBR is told
  each one's own heading.
* **Alternatives:** **A field among a variant's price and SKU:** those are saved with the product,
  and the HS code is the inventory item's, as Shopify keeps it, saved as stock rules are.

## ADR-560 · What a shop's staff write to Hatti's support WhatsApp number is kept as a request of their shop, threaded, and Hatti's answer goes back on WhatsApp within the day

* **Context:** Plans from Starter reach Hatti's people on WhatsApp (ADR-508), but what was written
  there was kept nowhere: Hatti's people answered from a phone, the shop's requests in the admin
  did not show it, and nothing flagged one left unanswered (ADR-525).
* **Decision:**
  * **Hatti's support line** is its own WhatsApp number, set by the host
    (`SUPPORT_WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID` and its token), apart from the shared notifications
    number. WhatsApp's webhook gives what is written to it to billing, through a port the
    messaging module defines, never to a shop's inbox or its opt-outs.
  * **Who wrote:** the active account whose proved number wrote, and its active memberships, through
    a function of identity's that tells billing no more; a number no account proved is not kept.
  * **Where it goes:** to their open request last written about, in any of their shops, as a
    message of its thread; else a new request, topic other, in the shop they last asked in, else
    the one they joined first, at its plan's priority, in Urdu if they wrote Urdu letters, else in
    their account's language. A shop with five open adds to its newest. A message WhatsApp sends
    twice is kept once.
  * **Answers:** Hatti's people answer from their command as before; for a request written about
    on WhatsApp, the answer is also sent from the support line if they wrote within the last 24
    hours, as WhatsApp allows, kept in the thread and followed to delivery as the webhook says;
    the command says whether it went, could not, or failed and why.
  * **In the API,** a request says where it was asked, `channel`, and gives its thread, `messages`,
    the latest 50.
* **Consequences:** What shops write on WhatsApp is answered in order of their plans, flagged when
  late, and shown in the admin; a word after an answer opens a new request, as the answered one is
  done.
* **Alternatives:** **Finding the shop by asking the sender:** a menu on WhatsApp is a step
  between staff and help, and most staff have one shop. **The shared number:** customers write to
  it about orders, and a shop's staff are customers too.

## ADR-561 · The admin's Help page shows a request asked on WhatsApp with its thread, the answer once with how it went on WhatsApp, and says the shop can write there too

* **Context:** What staff write to Hatti's support WhatsApp number is kept as requests, threaded,
  and answered back on WhatsApp (ADR-560), but the Help page showed only a request's first words
  and its answer.
* **Decision:**
  * A request asked on WhatsApp says so, quietly, beside its topic and status.
  * Its thread follows, oldest first: who wrote, when in the shop's time zone, what (a photo or
    voice note named, as Hatti keeps no files), and for Hatti's messages how WhatsApp delivered
    them, with why when it could not.
  * Nothing shows twice: a thread that opens with the request's own words stands for them, and the
    message Hatti sent with the answer's words is the answer, shown once where it was sent, with
    its WhatsApp status; an answer not sent on WhatsApp follows the thread as before.
  * On plans with WhatsApp, the form says they can also write to Hatti's number from their own
    proved mobile, and it shows here. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shop sees in one place what it asked, however it asked, and whether Hatti's
  answer reached its phone.
* **Alternatives:** **A link between the answer and its message in the API:** the answer's words
  match the message sent with them, and an unmatched one still shows, in full, after the thread.

## ADR-562 · A sales-tax-registered shop reports its invoices through FBR's digital invoicing instead of the POS integration, by the same worker, its credit notes left to its return

* **Context:** FBR asks sales-tax-registered persons to issue their invoices through its digital
  invoicing (DI), PRAL's API, apart from the POS integration Tier-1 retailers report through
  (ADR-555). The shop's NTN, STRN and province are kept with its tax settings (ADR-190, ADR-500).
* **Decision:**
  * **One connection to FBR, of either system:** the shop's FBR connection says whether it reports
    through the POS integration or DI; for DI, the security token FBR issued the seller through
    IRIS, sealed as the POS's is, FBR's sandbox or production, and its default PCT code, and no
    POS ID. Connecting DI needs the shop's NTN, STRN and province. Each invoice is kept for the
    system it was issued under; switching leaves the other system's waiting ones unreported, and
    neither is sent to the wrong one.
  * **What DI is sent:** a sale invoice with the seller's NTN, name, province and the address it
    ships or is collected from, the buyer as an unregistered consumer with the order's name,
    address and province (the seller's where the order has none), and each item with its HS code
    as "dddd.dddd" (its own, ADR-557, else the shop's), rate, unit, value without tax, tax, total
    and discount, the delivery charge an item of its own. The sandbox is sent the scenario a sale
    to an unregistered buyer is tested under. FBR's constants are in one place, after its DI
    technical specification (v1.12), and proved by FBR's sandbox scenarios before production.
  * **What FBR said:** taken only when the invoice and every item are valid and FBR numbered it;
    refused, with FBR's codes and errors item by item, is not retried; a token refused, FBR down
    or not answering is tried again, for a week, as for the POS (ADR-555). A retry reads the
    seller's details afresh, so a corrected NTN is sent.
  * **Credit notes** are not sent to DI, which has no credit notes: they are kept as not reported,
    for the sales tax return, and their printed copy shows no FBR block.
  * In the API, the connection and each invoice say their system.
* **Consequences:** A registered online seller's invoices carry FBR's number and QR code, as
  Tier-1 retailers' do (ADR-556), from the same worker, list and retries.
* **Alternatives:** **A connection and list of its own for DI:** the token, environment, retries
  and printing are the same, and a shop reports through one system at a time. **Sending a refund
  as a debit note:** a debit note raises a supply, the opposite of a refund.

## ADR-563 · The admin's FBR card connects a shop through FBR's digital invoicing or its POS integration, chosen from the shop's tax profile, and switches between them with a new token

* **Context:** A shop reports to FBR through its POS integration or its digital invoicing
  (ADR-562), but the admin's card (ADR-558) knew only the POS.
* **Decision:**
  * **Reporting to FBR** on the sales tax page asks first which way: the POS integration, for
    Tier-1 retailers, or digital invoicing, for sales-tax-registered sellers; the POS if the tax
    profile says Tier-1, else digital invoicing if the shop has an STRN, else the POS.
  * For digital invoicing, no POS ID: the security token FBR issued through IRIS, the
    environment and the PCT code, with a line saying the seller's details come from the tax
    settings above and the address orders ship from, and that credit notes go in the sales tax
    return. A shop not registered is told what its tax settings lack, under the choice.
  * Switching a connected shop asks for the new way's token, and a POS ID for the POS, and warns
    that what waits for the old way is not sent. The connected view says which way it reports.
  * The invoices list says each one's way when it shows both, and sends again only what the way
    now connected takes. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A registered seller sets up digital invoicing without the API.
* **Alternatives:** **A card for each way:** a shop reports one way at a time, and the token,
  environment and invoices are shared.

## ADR-564 · A shop connects its Meta ad account and the worker pulls each day's spend by campaign, what the shop typed by hand kept over what Meta says

* **Context:** A shop records its ad spend by hand, a day at a time (ADR-553, ADR-554), and most
  Pakistani shops spend it on Meta, which reports it campaign by campaign.
* **Decision:**
  * **The ad account:** a shop on a plan with true profit gives its Meta ad account's ID and a
    token that may read its ads, checked with Meta as it is saved, sealed, with its last four
    shown; an account billing in another currency than rupees is refused, as the shop's spend is
    recorded in rupees. Connecting and disconnecting are audited; disconnecting keeps what was
    pulled.
  * **Pulling:** the worker asks Meta, every three hours by default, for each connected shop's
    spend by campaign and day, the last seven days, as Meta revises recent days, and thirty on the
    first pull; it is pulled at once on connecting, and the shop may pull again once a minute.
    Each day is Meta's, in the ad account's time zone, which Pakistani accounts share with their
    shops. Spend is kept to the paisa, a campaign under its name as Meta has it.
  * **Typed by hand wins:** each day's spend says where it came from. A pull replaces what was
    pulled before for its days, and leaves alone a campaign's day, or Meta's whole day, that the
    shop typed; typing over a pulled day makes it the shop's.
  * **Failing:** a token refused, Meta's limits or Meta down are kept as the account's last error,
    and the next round tries again; nothing pulled before is lost.
* **Consequences:** True profit and the return on ad spend follow Meta's figures without typing.
  TikTok and Google are still typed by hand.
* **Alternatives:** **Pulling through the conversions API's settings:** their token sends events,
  and reading ad spend needs another permission, often another token. **Meta's figures over the
  shop's:** a shop types a day by hand to correct it, or to add what Meta does not see.

## ADR-565 · The admin's ad spend page connects the shop's Meta ad account, pulls it now, and says which days came from Meta

* **Context:** The worker pulls a shop's Meta ad spend once its ad account is connected
  (ADR-564), but only through the API.
* **Decision:**
  * **A Meta ad account card** on the ad spend page, for those who see the page: its ID and a
    token that may read its ads, sealed, after the member confirms who they are; a field's
    problem under the field. Connected, it shows the account, its currency, the token's last
    four, when it was last pulled, and Meta's last error as a warning, as the worker tries again;
    it pulls now, changes the token, or disconnects, asked first, keeping what was pulled.
  * **The list** says which days came from Meta, and the form says that a figure typed over them
    is the shop's from then on, Meta's whole day typed keeping Meta's campaigns out. English and
    Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shop connects Meta once and its true profit follows Meta's spend.
* **Alternatives:** **The card in the settings:** it belongs with the spend it fills, where the
  shop sees what came from Meta.

## ADR-566 · A shop connects its TikTok advertiser account and the same worker pulls its spend by campaign under Meta's rules, shared between the two

* **Context:** Meta's ad spend is pulled (ADR-564); TikTok is the other platform Pakistani shops
  spend on, and its Business API reports spend by campaign and day.
* **Decision:**
  * **The advertiser account:** its ID and a long-term token of TikTok's Marketing API, checked
    with TikTok as it is saved, sealed, its last four shown; an account billing in another
    currency than rupees is refused. On a plan with true profit, audited, as Meta's.
  * **One set of rules for both:** saving an account, disconnecting, which are due, and the pull
    itself (seven days each round, thirty at first, the platform asked outside the transaction,
    what the shop typed kept, what the platform no longer reports dropped, errors kept) are one
    module, set up for each platform; each day's spend says which platform it was pulled from.
  * **TikTok's report:** spend by campaign and day, page by page, the day TikTok's in the
    advertiser's time zone; a campaign without a name kept under its ID, as no name is the
    platform's whole day. A token refused, TikTok's limits or TikTok down are kept as the
    account's last error and tried again next round. TikTok's codes are in one place, as best
    known.
  * The worker pulls Meta and then TikTok each round; the API connects, disconnects and pulls
    now, as for Meta.
* **Consequences:** True profit follows both platforms' spend; Google's is still typed.
* **Alternatives:** **One table for every platform's accounts:** Meta's would be moved and its
  queries rewritten for no change in what they do; the rules, not the rows, are what is shared.

## ADR-567 · The admin's ad spend page connects the shop's TikTok advertiser account as it does Meta's, one card for both, TikTok's folded until it is wanted

* **Context:** TikTok's ad spend is pulled once its advertiser account is connected (ADR-566),
  but only through the API; the page had Meta's card alone (ADR-565).
* **Decision:**
  * **One card, set up for each platform:** the connect form, the connected view, pulling now,
    changing the token and disconnecting are one component, given each platform's operations,
    field and words; Meta's behaves as before.
  * **TikTok's** below Meta's: its advertiser ID and a long-term token of TikTok's Marketing API
    with access to its reports. Not connected, its form is folded behind a button, so a shop that
    runs no TikTok ads has a short page on a phone.
  * The list says which days came from TikTok, and the form's word on typing over pulled days
    shows for TikTok too. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shop connects both platforms from the page its spend is on.
* **Alternatives:** **Both forms open:** most shops run one platform, and two forms asking for
  tokens read as two steps to take.

## ADR-568 · A shop chooses its storefront's filters, their order and their words, filters on its products' and variants' custom fields among them, and none chosen keeps every filter as before

* **Context:** Collection and search pages filter by every filter there is, in one order
  (ADR-478, ADR-479); Shopify's Search & Discovery lets a shop choose its filters, name them, and
  filter on its products' metafields.
* **Decision:**
  * **The shop's filters,** kept with its online store's preferences: up to 25, in its order, of
    availability, price, product type, brand, an option by its name, the eastern-wear attributes,
    and a product's or variant's custom field of a definition the shop has, of text, a list of
    text, or yes and no; each with words of its own in English and Urdu, or the built-in ones (an
    option's as the page's products name it, a custom field's its definition's name). None chosen
    is every filter as before; an empty list is no filters.
  * **Checked as saved:** a filter twice, a custom field the shop has no definition of, or one of
    a type filters cannot read is refused under it; an option no product has yet is kept. A
    change is audited and republishes the shop's storefront.
  * **On the storefront,** the shop's document carries its filters; pages show them in its order,
    in the page's language, and read only their parameters, a hidden filter's ignored. Custom
    fields filter as Shopify's do, `filter.p.m.<namespace>.<key>` and `filter.v.m.<namespace>.<key>`,
    a list's items each a value, yes and no as `true` and `false`. A translated option is still
    found by its own name.
  * The API gives the shop's filters and those it could choose.
* **Consequences:** A shop selling lawn shows fabric first and hides what its products do not
  vary by; a theme's `collection.filters` follows without a change of theme.
* **Alternatives:** **Filters in the theme's settings:** each theme would ask again, and a
  shop's filters are of its catalog, not its look.

## ADR-569 · The admin's online store has a Filters tab: every filter as before, or the shop's own list, ordered, named in English and Urdu, its custom fields' filters added

* **Context:** A shop may choose its storefront's filters (ADR-568), but only through the API.
* **Decision:**
  * **A Filters tab** in the online store, for those who edit its menus and preferences: every
    filter (the default), shown as the storefront now shows them, or the shop's own list.
  * **Choosing** starts from what the storefront shows, so the shop edits what it sees; each
    filter moves up or down, takes words of its own in English and Urdu, or is removed; a
    filter is added from the built-in ones, the products' options, and the product's and
    variant's custom fields. Up to 25; an empty list is said to show none. A chosen list is
    fixed: options added later join it only when the shop adds them, as the page says.
  * Saving sends the whole list, or the default; a problem shows under its filter. English and
    Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shop arranges its filters without the API.
* **Alternatives:** **Dragging to reorder:** buttons to move a filter work by keyboard and on a
  phone, and say what they do to a screen reader.

## ADR-570 · A shopper signs in to a shop's storefront with a code to their mobile, and the session reads their orders and store credit, the storefront's pages to follow

* **Context:** Hatti's shoppers have no accounts (CUS-02): a customer is the shop's record of a
  number, and checkout proves a number with a one-time code (CHK-09, ADR-148, ADR-186). Shopify's
  customer accounts sign in by a code too, and show the shopper their orders.
* **Decision:**
  * **Signing in:** the storefront asks for a code to a mobile number, sent by WhatsApp or SMS as
    checkout's are, worded as a sign-in code in English and Urdu; it answers the same whether or
    not the number is anyone's. A code signs in once, within ten minutes and five tries, and is
    kept apart from checkout's: neither proves the other. The two share checkout's limits, a
    number's day and an address's hour.
  * **The session:** 32 random bytes, given to the storefront once and kept as their digest; it
    lasts 30 days from its last use and never 90 past signing in, signing out ending it at once.
    It follows the number: a number with no orders takes on its customer with its first, a
    merged customer's sessions move to the one kept, a number moved away ends its sessions when
    next read, and erasing a customer deletes them and its codes.
  * **The account:** the number, the customer's name, their latest 20 orders with this shop, of
    every number merged into them, with their state, total and whether they have a page, and
    their store credit with what expires first. An order's page opens with the link its messages
    carry, or one the session opened before, else a new one, as messages make them.
  * **In the checkout module,** which already owns the codes and reads customers, orders and
    messaging through their facades, which cannot read one another the other way.
* **Consequences:** The storefront's sign-in and account pages need only render what the API
  gives. The WhatsApp template for the code is to be registered with Meta before it is used.
* **Alternatives:** **A password:** shoppers pay by cash on delivery from phones and remember a
  code better than a password. **Accounts in the customers module:** it is read by messaging and
  orders, so it cannot read them.

## ADR-571 · The storefront signs shoppers in with a code and shows their account, the pages never cached and every other page as it was, Hatti Base's customer templates in both languages

* **Context:** A shopper signs in with a code and the storefront API reads their account
  (ADR-570), but the storefront had no pages for it, and themes no `customer`.
* **Decision:**
  * **Signing in,** at `/account/login` and its Urdu twin: a mobile number, by WhatsApp or SMS,
    then the code sent to it, the number kept meanwhile in a cookie of ten minutes the page cannot
    read; a code wrong, run out or tried too often, a number that is not one, or codes asked too
    often says so in the page's language. Signed in, the session's cookie is set, the page cannot
    read it, and the shopper goes to their account, or back where they came from on the same shop.
    Sign-in forms posted from another site are refused, and an address may post them 20 times a
    minute.
  * **The account,** at `/account`: their name and number, their store credit and what expires
    first, and their orders with their state and total, each opening its order's page; signed
    out, it asks them to sign in. Signing out, by a link or a form, ends the session.
  * **Never cached:** the account's pages are private and kept by no cache, and only they know who
    is signed in. Every other page is the same for everyone and cached as before; its header
    says "Sign in", and a cookie of no secret, as the cart's count does, turns it to "Account".
  * **Themes** get Shopify's `customer` there: its name, number, orders with their states' words,
    totals and links, and its store credit, and `routes.account_login_url` and
    `account_logout_url`; Hatti Base's `customers/login` and `customers/account` templates, in
    English and Urdu. Shops' themes may keep templates under `customers/`, as Shopify's do.
* **Consequences:** A shopper sees their orders and credit at any shop they bought from, on any
  phone, without a password.
* **Alternatives:** **Who is signed in on every page:** each page would be a request to the core
  and none could be cached; the header's word is the only thing that differs.

## ADR-572 · A signed-in shopper downloads their data and asks for its erasure from their account, through the requests staff make, the file kept a day and linked for minutes

* **Context:** Staff export a customer's data and file their erasure (CUS-05, ADR-123, ADR-110,
  ADR-132); a shopper now has an account (ADR-570, ADR-571) but could ask for neither.
* **Decision:**
  * **Their file:** asked from the account, the customers module's own export is made, as the
    customer, and kept in storage for a day, a second ask that day giving the same file; the
    account links to it, and each click is given a signed link of five minutes, so the page holds
    none. A worker sweep deletes files past their day; a merge or erasure stops their links at
    once. Each file is audited, the customer its actor.
  * **Their erasure:** filed through the customers module's intake, the customer recorded as who
    asked, once while one is open; it waits ten days, which the shop may cancel within, and is
    held while an order is open or store credit is left, as staff's are. The page says so first,
    and that orders stay for the shop's accounts without a name, number or address, and asks the
    shopper to say they understand.
  * **The account** says what was asked and how it stands. The storefront's forms are refused from
    another site and limited per address; their outcome is said in the page's language.
  * Staff see who asked an erasure, staff, an app or the customer, and the activity log shows a
    customer as its actor.
* **Consequences:** A shopper exercises their rights without asking the shop. The shopper is not
  yet told when their erasure is done (ADR-110).
* **Alternatives:** **The file sent on WhatsApp:** a message is not a safe place for every order
  and address a customer has. **A link kept on the page:** a page copied or cached would carry it.

## ADR-573 · The admin says who asked each waiting erasure, and shows a customer who acted in the activity log, linked to their page

* **Context:** A shopper asks for their data and its erasure from their account, recorded as the
  customer's own requests (ADR-572); the admin knew only staff and apps as who asked or acted.
* **Decision:**
  * **Erasures waiting** say who asked: the customer from their account, staff, or an app.
  * **The activity log** shows a customer as "The customer", linked to their page, and a customer
    downloading their data in their own words; staff's exports read as before. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** Staff know an erasure came from the shopper before they cancel it.
* **Alternatives:** **The customer's name as the actor:** an erased customer's name is gone, and
  their page says who they are.

## ADR-574 · A shopper buys an order again from their account: what can still be sold goes into their cart at the order's quantities, and the cart says what could not

* **Context:** A signed-in shopper sees their orders (ADR-570, ADR-571); Shopify's accounts let
  them order the same again (CUS-02). Cart permalinks (CH-07) make a cart of their own and go
  straight to checkout.
* **Decision:**
  * **The account's orders give their items** as sold, each with whether it can be bought again:
    its variant still there, its product active and its stock not out, a bundle's from its parts.
    Gift cards are left out. A bundle is found again as the shop's bundle of those parts in those
    quantities, or cannot be bought again.
  * **Buy again** is a form on each order with something to buy: posted, it adds what can be sold
    to the shopper's own cart at the order's quantities, as much as the stock allows, and opens
    the cart, which says if some could not be added, or none. Refused from another site, limited
    per address, for the order's own shopper alone.
  * Hatti Base's account lists each order's items, says which are not available now, and offers
    Buy again. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shopper reorders their usual in two taps, and changes the cart before paying.
* **Alternatives:** **A cart permalink:** it would leave the shopper's cart aside and skip to
  checkout, where nothing can be changed. **A link that adds to the cart:** a link fetched ahead
  by a browser or a preview would fill the cart.

## ADR-575 · A signed-in shopper's wishlist is kept with their account and follows them across devices, the browser's list still what pages show, so every page stays cacheable

* **Context:** Hatti Base keeps a shopper's wishlist in their browser (OS-12): another phone, or a
  cleared browser, has none. Shoppers now sign in (ADR-570, ADR-571); Shopify's accounts keep it.
* **Decision:**
  * **Kept by customer:** a signed-in number's list is its customer's, so every number of theirs
    sees one list and a merge joins two; a number with no customer yet keeps its own, which moves to
    the customer it becomes when next read. At most 100 products, the oldest making room; another
    shop's or an unknown product is skipped, a deleted one drops out when read. Erasure deletes
    it, the customer's data file includes it, and a number's own list goes with its last session.
  * **The storefront** reads, adds and removes by product handle, as Hatti Base's script knows them,
    in JSON, for the same site alone, limited per address and kept by no cache.
  * **Hatti Base's script,** for a signed-in shopper, once a tab merges the browser's list into the
    account's and takes the account's back, and tells the account of each heart pressed; the
    browser's list is still what pages render from. Signed out, nothing changes. The account page
    may link to the wishlist page, a setting off until the shop has the page.
* **Consequences:** A shopper's wishlist is the same on their phone and their laptop once they
  sign in, and no page is made per shopper.
* **Alternatives:** **The wishlist rendered by the server:** each product page would be per shopper
  and uncacheable for a heart.

## ADR-576 · The Admin API costs each query before it runs and meters it per app or member of staff in each shop, Shopify's leaky bucket, refusing what would overdraw it and saying the cost

* **Context:** The Admin API had no limits, to come before any third-party app has a token; shops'
  custom apps have had tokens since DEV-04. Shopify costs each GraphQL query and meters it with a
  leaky bucket per app and shop, saying the cost in `extensions.cost`.
* **Decision:**
  * **The cost, before it runs,** as Shopify counts it: scalars and enums nothing, an object 1 and
    what it selects, a connection or paged list 2 and its page times one item and what it selects,
    a page of `first` or `last` or else 50, a mutation 10 each and its payload, fragments merged as
    executed, an interface or union its costliest type, `@skip` and `@include` heeded, and
    introspection 1. An app's query over 1,000, or its bucket, is refused before it runs; a member of staff's is
    held to their whole bucket, as the admin's costliest page, a courier's statement of 250 lines,
    costs about 1,009.
  * **The bucket:** in Redis, one for each app, member of staff or support agent in each shop, an
    atomic script restoring with time and taking a query's cost only if all of it is there: an
    app 1,000 points restoring 50 a second, staff 2,000 restoring 100, all set by the host. What
    a query did not use, its connections returning fewer than asked, is given back after.
  * **Refused** queries take nothing and say `THROTTLED`, with what is left and when to try again,
    or `MAX_COST_EXCEEDED`; a mutation refused with an idempotency key frees the key, so trying
    again runs it. Every answer says its cost and the bucket's state.
  * **Open when Redis fails:** the query runs unmetered and a warning is logged; the API and every
    shop's admin stay up.
* **Consequences:** No app can starve a shop's API, or another shop's, and apps pace themselves by
  the cost they are told. Lists that come whole with their parent, a product's variants, are
  counted as one item; buckets by plan are to come.
* **Alternatives:** **Requests a second:** a page of 250 orders and one product would weigh the
  same. **Closed when Redis fails:** an outage of the cache would stop every shop's admin.

## ADR-577 · The admin waits out a throttled request and sends it again, saying it is busy meanwhile, and gives up after three tries with plain words

* **Context:** The Admin API refuses a query that would overdraw its caller's bucket, saying how
  much is left and how fast it fills (ADR-576); the admin showed any refusal as an error.
* **Decision:**
  * **Throttled:** the admin's client waits the time the bucket needs for the query's cost, at
    least a second and at most 30, and sends the request again as it was, a mutation with its
    idempotency key, up to three times; then it says Hatti is busy for the shop, to try again in a
    moment. The query cache does not retry on top.
  * **Too costly a query** is never sent again, and says so in plain words.
  * **While waiting,** the notices every page shows say Hatti is busy and count down the seconds.
    English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A burst of pages, or a member of staff clicking fast, waits a second instead
  of failing.
* **Alternatives:** **Retrying at once:** a throttled request would be refused again until the
  bucket fills, each refusal one more round trip.

## ADR-578 · A shop makes roles of its own, each narrowed from a preset, and what was checked by a role's name is checked by capabilities each preset holds as before

* **Context:** Staff have six presets (ADM-01); custom roles are V1's, with a permission to see
  customers' numbers (security §2.1). About twenty checks across the modules asked a role's name,
  so a role of the shop's own could not be fitted in without changing what they ask.
* **Decision:**
  * **Capabilities** name what those checks allowed: seeing customers' numbers whole, revealing
    them, exporting orders, managing others' export schedules, refunding, assigning orders,
    moderating comments, seeing staff's performance, reconciling payments, claiming from couriers,
    managing staff, apps, billing, verification and support access. Each preset holds exactly what
    its checks allowed before, a table test proving it; numbers whole, revealed or masked follow
    the first two.
  * **A custom role** is named by the shop, based on any preset but the owner's, which it keeps,
    and holds a subset of its preset's scopes, the read of what it writes counting, and of its
    capabilities: it never grants more. Up to 50 a shop, their names apart; owners and managers
    make them for the roles they manage, and a change asks who they are. A member or an invitation
    holds one, the database keeping its role its preset; one in use is not deleted.
  * **Access** is read each request: a role's change counts from the member's next, intersected
    with its preset as it is then. The owner's actions, MFA and alerts stay by preset.
  * The API gives the shop's roles, the presets with their scopes and capabilities, and a member's
    or invitation's role.
* **Consequences:** A shop gives a packer who also confirms, or an accountant who may not export,
  exactly that.
* **Alternatives:** **Roles of any scopes:** a role could grant what no preset does, beyond the
  owner's say. **Roles by name in every check:** each new role would mean changing each module.

## ADR-579 · The admin's staff page has a Roles tab to make a shop's roles from a preset, and invitations and role changes offer them beside the presets

* **Context:** A shop may make roles of its own, narrowed from a preset (ADR-578), but only
  through the API.
* **Decision:**
  * **A Roles tab** beside People, for those who manage staff: the shop's roles with their preset
    and how many members hold each, changed or deleted, the deletion asked first and refused with
    the core's count when the role is in use.
  * **The editor:** a name, the preset it is based on (fixed once made), and what the preset holds,
    all ticked at first: its permissions in plain words, grouped as customers' numbers, orders,
    money, and team and shop, and its areas, each to view or edit, the view of what it edits
    allowed alone. It says a role can only narrow its preset; saving asks who they are.
  * **Assigning:** inviting and changing a member's role offer the presets and the shop's roles,
    and members and invitations show their role's name, and quietly its preset. English and Urdu.
* **Consequences:** A shop makes and gives its own roles without the API. The admin's own pages are
  still shown by a member's preset, the core refusing what their role does not allow.
* **Alternatives:** **One list of every scope:** grouped by area, view and edit read as a shop
  thinks of its work.

## ADR-580 · The admin shows each member what their own scopes and capabilities let them use, a custom role's member no more than it holds

* **Context:** A shop's own roles narrow a preset's scopes and capabilities, and the core checks
